text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing ill-conceived plans to rapidly increase detention capacity, and the total will likely rise due to ongoing mismanagement, congressional investigators warned Thursday.

READ MORE: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' immigration detention center has closed, governor says

The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented costly problems in several initiatives ICE has pursued since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 and ordered the mass arrest and deportation of people who are in the country illegally.

Among the misspending was nearly $3 million to erect tents at Guantanamo Bay that were never used, $20 million to maintain purchased warehouses that are now being sold without having housed a single detainee, and excessive rates paid to hold detainees at a deficient and now-shuttered Florida lockup.

ICE has no strategic plan for spending its windfall

Congress gave ICE an unprecedented $45 billion to expand detention capacity last year as part of the Trump-backed One Big Beautiful Bill, but the agency still lacks a comprehensive strategic plan for how to spend it wisely, the report warned. The detainee population has increased from 39,000 in January 2025 to 67,000 as of July 30.

"Without taking action to manage detention investments in accordance with program and project management practices, ICE will likely continue to make uninformed decisions and risk further inefficiency and wasted resources," warned the GAO, a nonpartisan agency that investigated at the request of congressional Democrats.

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, told GAO it would develop a plan to guide its detention expansion by Aug. 31, 2027, but that may be too late to prevent more waste, the report said.

ICE and DHS offered no immediate additional comment on the report.

The government scrapped a plan for mass detention at Guantánamo Bay

Shortly after Trump returned to the White House, the government began blowing money by hastily pursuing plans to detain more people who were in the U.S. illegally, the report found.

After the White House directed officials to use the military base in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for immigration detention in January 2025, the Department of Defense assembled enough tents to hold 5,000 people there at a cost of $2.85 million, the report said. But DHS found that the tents didn't meet detention standards, and they were removed before they housed a single detainee.

The plan for mass detention at Guantánamo Bay was later found to be "infeasible" and scrapped because of the costs of building facilities that could meet federal standards. Instead, the agency housed an average of 16 detainees daily there this year, at a cost of millions of dollars, the report found.

ICE is wasting millions of dollars on empty warehouses

Earlier this year, ICE purchased 11 large warehouses across the country for $1.07 billion as part of a plan backed by former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to increase detention capacity. But that idea was scrapped amid public opposition before any detainees were housed in them because the department didn't conduct "appropriate due diligence and planning," according to the GAO report. DHS is now planning to sell seven of the facilities.

ICE has spent $20 million on costs and services related to those seven warehouses that it will not recover, including zoning assessments, title insurance, utilities and security, and will need to sell them for the total purchase price of $707 million to avoid more waste, the report said.

ICE has also "incurred significant costs" for the four warehouses that it plans to keep, including a $426 million outlay to renovate facilities in Arizona and Maryland that is on hold due to legal challenges.

Report finds waste on 'Alligator Alcatraz' and other plans

After the warehouse initiative faltered, ICE launched a plan to purchase facilities owned by private contractors that were already housing detainees, saying it would give more control over infrastructure and limit local governments' ability to restrict their use.

The agency spent $1.5 billion to buy two of them in July and could buy more even though ICE has "not assessed the long-term affordability of owning these facilities," the report said.

The report found fault with other initiatives. ICE never reached a contract with the state of Florida to operate the facility nicknamed "Alligator Alcatraz," which housed detainees for a year until it was closed in June following reports of substandard and abusive conditions.

Instead, DHS agreed to reimburse the state through a special $608 million Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that authorizes a charge of $249 per detainee per day — 171% higher than ICE's normal rate of $92, the report found. DHS is also paying the state the higher rate for a second facility that's still open in Sanderson, Florida.

ICE is also facing high costs under an agreement in which the Bureau of Prisons is housing detainees at eight facilities. The agreement requires ICE to reimburse the full cost, which has ballooned because of overtime and other staffing assignments, and pay a rate of $182 per detainee per day, the report said.

text:
In an emergency request Thursday, the Trump administration urged the Supreme Court to revive its policy of deporting some migrants to places other than their country of origin, a practice that was struck down by a lower court on the grounds that it violates deportees' due process rights.

The Justice Department asked the high court to pause a February 2026 order from a federal judge, largely upheld by an appellate court last week, that requires federal immigration officials to give deportees more due process. The courts said deportees need to get notice and a chance to challenge their deportation before any attempt to remove them to a so-called "third country" where they have no ties.

Such a pause would allow the Department of Homeland Security to continue a policy that empowers officials to send detainees to third nations, without providing them notice or a chance to challenge that deportation, if the receiving country has made blanket assurances that they will not persecute or torture the deportees.

Justice Department lawyers said DHS already had to cancel a flight to three third countries for 70 would-be deportees, some of whom have criminal records, in the wake of the adverse rulings from Boston-based judges.

In the emergency appeal, Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote that the third-country removal policy has allowed the Trump administration to remove "thousands" of individuals in recent months. He estimated that "thousands more" are eligible to be deported to third countries.

"These include some of the worst of the worst criminal aliens — whose home countries refuse to take them back," he wrote. "The order below would again obstruct DHS from efficiently removing aliens — this time under a policy that has been in force for 15 months" because of earlier court orders.

Sauer also said that the lower court's decision "undermines our standing abroad."

"Finding third countries willing and able to accept aliens is a delicate diplomatic endeavor," Sauer wrote. "By interjecting itself in that process, and potentially disrupting those carefully negotiated arrangements, the lower courts' actions 'will cause significant and irreparable harm to U.S. foreign policy.'"

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who handles emergency appeals from Massachusetts and other states in the region, gave lawyers for the immigrants challenging the policy until Monday afternoon to respond.

Sauer asked Jackson to provide the administration with temporary relief while it considers the emergency appeal.

As part of its far-reaching crackdown on illegal immigration, the Trump administration has brokered agreements with dozens of countries around the globe, mainly in Africa and Latin America, that have agreed to accept deportees from the U.S. who are not their citizens.

Some of the African nations that have agreed to such deportations include countries plagued by repressive governments, armed conflict, human rights abuses and widespread poverty, such as Equatorial Guinea, the Central African Republic and South Sudan.

While some countries, like Eswatini and South Sudan, have received deportees from the Trump administration who have violent and serious criminal histories, other nations, like Liberia, have accepted deported migrants from Latin America and other places across the world with no known criminal records, beyond immigration violations in the U.S.

In Liberia, CBS News interviewed men and women from Brazil, Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and Venezuela who were deported to the West African country last month and described feeling stateless. All of them said they were deported to West Africa without being notified in advance or given an opportunity to challenge the deportation.

Immigration officials have mainly targeted two categories of individuals in their third-country deportation campaign: immigrants who won limited legal protections in U.S. immigration courts barring ICE from deporting them to their homelands, and detainees whose home countries limit or reject U.S. deportations.

The dispute over the third-country removals has already been before the Supreme Court, though during an earlier stage in the case.

In a divided decision last year, the high court allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations to third countries while legal proceedings continued. Then, the Supreme Court lifted an order from the federal judge in Boston overseeing the challenge that had prevented the administration from removing immigrants without first giving them the chance to raise fears of torture or persecution.

text:
International human rights organization Amnesty International has called for the abolition of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in a new report alleging human rights abuses in the Trump administration’s immigration operations.

The report focuses on documenting human rights violations in ICE operations in the Twin Cities, Chicago, New Orleans and Washington, DC, including racially discriminatory immigration enforcement; unjustified use of force by federal agents; unlawful killings by federal agents; repression of protests through tear gas and pepper spray; unlawful surveillance; and inhumane detention conditions.

It’s the first time the organization has called for the abolition of ICE. Amy Fischer, Amnesty’s director of refugee and migrant rights, said it’s rare move for the organization to call for an agency to be fully abolished, but that the report shows the agency has reached a tipping point after decades of “mass impunity.”

“There are simply no reforms that would bring this agency into alignment with United States right human rights obligations,” Fischer said in a press call Thursday.

The report is over 100 pages and gathers information from laws and policies, legal cases, news articles, academic papers and official communications and reports to document the four immigration operations. The organization interviewed 154 people across the four cities as part of its research, including Reformer reporter Madison McVan.

ICE was established in 2003 following the September 11 attacks. The movement to abolish ICE gained mainstream traction on the left during Trump’s first administration and has been galvanized by Trump’s second administration’s immigration operations. In Minnesota, the winter’s chaotic surge of thousands of federal agents, who killed two U.S. citizens, shot a Venezuelan immigrant and violently arrested others, led to mass protests against ICE, attended by tens of thousands in subzero temperatures.

The organization is also calling for immediate independent investigations into all human rights violations in the four operations; investigations into the killings of Renee Good, Alex Pretti, Silverio Villegas González and others killed during immigration enforcement; and the end of facial recognition surveillance technologies.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to again clear the way for continued quick deportations of immigrants to third countries where they have no ties.

The government asked for an immediate halt to lower court orders finding that people must have the chance to object before the U.S. government deports them to countries other than their homelands.

The justices previously allowed the deportation flights to temporarily continue when the case came before them last year. Since then, an appeals court has upheld a Boston-based judge’s final ruling that migrants must have a meaningful chance to argue a third-country deportation would put them in danger of persecution or torture.

The ruling didn’t prohibit those deportations outright but it lengthens the process. The government argues it has already led to the cancellation of a flight carrying 70 people with criminal convictions to three different countries.

“The government has been able to remove thousands of aliens to third countries in recent months, and thousands more are eligible for such removal,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

Trump’s Republican administration has said that it sends people to third countries when it is unable to quickly return them to their homelands. Those third-country governments provide assurances that people won’t be persecuted or tortured, attorneys said.

The lower courts’ legal requirements would mean cascading delays and could force the reworking of agreements with foreign countries, attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of people under a series of agreements with nearly two dozen countries, including South Sudan, Equatorial Guinea and Panama.

This month, lawyers for two men deported to Equatorial Guinea said they were beaten and held at gunpoint in a hotel-turned-detention center by police who covered their heads with bags.

The case comes amid a sweeping immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which has pledged to deport millions of people who are living in the United States illegally.

description:

text:
A Haitian pastor who received a brief reprieve from deportation after he was abruptly removed from a flight to Haiti last week was returned to the country on Thursday.

Molis Augustave was deported to Haiti along with dozens of other people despite several legal efforts to halt his removal and reverse a decision by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services denying his application for permanent residence filed by his wife, who is a U.S. citizen.

Augustave, who was arrested on Sept. 4 while driving for DoorDash, has become an example of the growing uncertainty facing Haitians in the U.S. following the end of their humanitarian protections.

After the Supreme Court cleared the way this summer for the Trump administration to revoke Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status designation despite ongoing litigation in federal courts, immigration advocates say they are seeing an increase in people with pending immigration claims — including through marriage and other family-based adjustments — being detained and deported.

“Before, it used to be if someone got taken by ICE we had a few weeks, a few months to get an attorney and see what kind of bond or legal relief we could get them,” said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, one of the groups that that advocated for Augustave’s release. “But now within a couple of days from being taken by ICE, they are being sent either to their country or a third country. Now they have completely removed any access to due process, and they are targeting and attacking people who have very strong possibilities of an adjustment of status.”

Augustave, who entered the U.S. in 2016 and had his asylum application denied, had been issued a final order of removal before applying for TPS, which protected him from deportation.

Days after his arrest, his wife received word that her petition filed on his behalf to begin the process of getting him permanent residence had been approved. But shortly after application for a green card was denied.

When he landed back in Haiti on Thursday, a motion to reopen his removal proceedings was pending before the Board of Immigration Appeals along with a pending habeas corpus petition before a federal court in Louisiana.

An immigrant rights organizer, Augustave walked off the aircraft in Haiti on Thursday wearing a red T-shirt with the logo of his organization, We Are CASA, turned inward, and sporting a beard. He did not give interviews and said he first wanted to change his clothes.

In an opinion piece he wrote before leaving the U.S., Augustave wrote: “I now understand something I did not understand before I was detained: For every person whose name becomes known, there are so many others whose names we never hear. People knew my name. Reporters told my story. Advocates fought for me. My wife fought for me. My community prayed for me. People I had never met cared about whether I would be put on that plane. That is a blessing I will never forget.

“But what about the other 89” who were on the first deportation plane he had been scheduled to be on? he wrote. “Who knows their names?”

Jossie Flor Sapunar, national communications director of We Are CASA, said: “The Trump administration deported a shepherd.”

She added: “The federal government feared a Black man from Haiti who loved his wife, cared for his children, pastored a congregation, and made a people-powered movement...They evicted him and so many other Black immigrants from this country. But they cannot deport a legacy. The love he poured into his family, his church, and his community spread throughout the United States, despite the hate that the Trump administration spews.”

Ama Frimpong, chief of services and legal advocacy at We Are CASA said that in denying Augustave’s green card application, the Trump administration rubber-stamped a predetermined decision to deport him.

“This is what happens when a government decides that due process is a privilege it can revoke at will,” she said.

Not the only one

Johnny Jules, another detained Haitian, also showed up on the manifest for Thursday’s deportation flight, even though he too had been pursuing an adjustment of his immigration status through his U.S.-citizen wife.

Jules was arrested on Sept. 15 in Columbus, Ohio, after reporting for a mandatory ICE check-in, his wife said. On Thursday, she was desperately trying to determine whether he was aboard the deportation charter flight, which originated in Alexandria, Louisiana, stopped in Miami and arrived in Cap-Haïtien at 2:25 p.m.

Jules had been transferred to Louisiana and called his wife Wednesday evening. But the call abruptly ended, she said. Soon, his information disappeared from ICE’s online detainee locator.

“He said, ‘Hello, how are you’ and then the call dropped,” Lourdes Miya Dorsonne said. “I tried calling him back, and I couldn’t get him.”

The couple married in 2024 after being together for years. They have two children, a 1-year-old son and a 3 -year-old daughter.

“I am suffering,” Dorsonne said. “We’ve just been suffering since all this happened.”

Jules came to the U.S. after nearly drowning at sea, his wife said, after a boat carrying him and dozens of other Haitian migrants capsized in 2022 in the Mona Passage off Puerto Rico. Eleven women died. Jules was detained after surviving the wreck, and eventually released. As part of his release, he had to periodically report to ICE.

When Haiti was redesignated for TPS by the Biden administration, Jules applied, Dorsonne said. He began working as a truck driver but remained subject to ICE’s check-ins.

In 2025, Dorsonne said, she petitioned to have his status adjusted through marriage. They brought the documents along, she said, when Jules reported for his ICE appointment this month.

“Even though we showed it to them, they still held him,” Dorsonne said. “The children keep asking where their father was. The minute they hear the garage door open, they run thinking it’s him.”

Dorsonne said she never imagined that complying with an ICE requirement would lead to her husband’s detention – or that she would spend the week after his arrest desperately trying to locate him in the detention system.

“He followed the law and did everything they asked. This is why he’s in this situation because he went to his appointment,” Dorsonne said.

Pompano Beach mother of seven detained

When TPS ended in late July, Haitians went back to the status they had held before the designation. In the face of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, that has meant being vulnerable to deportation to Haiti based on final order of removals they had prior to getting TPS.

As Thursday’s flight prepared to depart Miami, a group of immigration advocates with the advocacy groups Faith In Action and Faith In Florida were trying to stop the deportation of another Haitian with U.S.-born children, and who once had a green card, according to her family.

Sirena Prosper, a longtime Pompano Beach resident and mother of seven, was arrested by ICE on Sept. 14 in front her kids and is currently being held at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, a facility where advocates say there were two deaths this summer.

Like the others, Prosper has U.S.-born children, three of whom are minors aged 14, 12 and 10. She also had legal residency, her family said. The case has caused indignation in South Florida.

Prosper’s family and advocates note that she owns a beauty salon in Pompano Beach after having turned her life around. A prayer vigil was held on Tuesday outside her Royal Hands Salon to call for her release and a pause on her deportation.

Marie Prosper, her niece, told the Miami Herald that her aunt was born in The Bahamas in the late 70s and came to the United States six months later.

In a statement to the Herald, an ICE spokesperson pointed to her criminal history, which it said includes convictions for burglary of a residence and larceny.

“Prosper entered the country legally and adjusted, but on Jan. 9, 2002, was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge. She will remain in ICE custody pending her removal from the country,” the ICE spokesperson said.

Prosper’s family says that she had served her time for the decades-old convictions and checked in with ICE for years.

One of her children died by suicide during COVID, said Marie Prosper, and now the rest of the siblings are navigating the uncertainty of their mother’s potential deportation. The family is worried that her immigration records may incorrectly say she was born in Haiti, Marie Prosper said.

“She’s never been to Haiti.”

text:
Every year, millions of taxpayers file a Form 1040, the most commonly used federal tax document that has long been viewed as a routine calculation of income, deductions and credits. But next year’s form could include a new question on citizenship and work-authorization, marking the first time ever that an individual's tax return asks filers to affirm their immigration status.

Immigrants, including undocumented immigrants, are required to file taxes and use the same IRS forms that U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents file. Paying taxes has long ​been seen as a key criteria for undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status.

The IRS published a draft of the 2026 Form 1040 that includes a question on status asking whether the filer — or their spouse, if filing jointly — are U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, or are legally authorized to work in the country. The yes-or-no question appears below the filing status section, in a box titled “other information.”

The draft was released for public review and has not been finalized. Legal experts warn that if the rule is implemented, if could deter undocumented immigrants from filing, which not only impacts their ability to obtain legal status but also has fiscal consequences for the U.S. Treasury.

It remains unclear how the information would be used, and the IRS did not respond to requests for comment.

It comes as the Trump administration ramps up its sprawling immigration enforcement effort. Last year, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, signed a controversial information-sharing agreement which allows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to submit names and addresses of immigrants inside the U.S. illegally to the IRS for cross-verification against tax records. The arrangement has been the subject of multiple lawsuits and led to the resignation of the IRS's acting commissioner.

What could the IRS do with this information?

Joseph Malouf, a Maryland attorney and legal contributor for Telemundo, said the proposed question could be tied to determining which taxpayers qualify for certain tax credits.

In August, the Treasury Department and the IRS proposed regulations aimed at limiting eligibility for certain federal tax credits, including the Child Tax Credit, the American Opportunity Tax Credit, the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Adoption Tax Credit.

“That’s the excuse they’re using to try to implement those changes, saying, ‘Look, the reality is we can’t calculate correctly without the information,’” Malouf said in an interview with "Noticias Telemundo Ahora."

However, federal ​law already prohibits undocumented immigrants from many entitlement programs, including Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and other benefits covering ​education funds and housing. In fact, research from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy shows that undocumented immigrants pay billions in annual taxes — including federal, state, local and sales taxes — that funds those programs despite being barred or having limited access to those public benefits.

The proposed question also raises concerns about privacy and about how the information collected by the IRS could be shared with other government agencies.

Malouf said he believes the proposal could face legal challenges based on federal laws governing the confidentiality and sharing of taxpayer information.

Section 6103 of the Internal Revenue Code generally protects the confidentiality of tax returns and taxpayer information, though it sets out some exceptions that allow those data to be shared under certain circumstances.

Earlier this year, a federal judge determined that the IRS had broken the law “approximately 42,695 times” by illegally disclosing information from thousands of taxpayers to ICE as part of the two agencies' information sharing agreement.

Malouf also raised a concern related to the Fifth Amendment, questioning whether the form could force some people to provide information that could later be used against them.

“The government has described people who are undocumented as people who have committed a crime: being in the country illegally. The first question I ask myself is how this form is consistent with the Fifth Amendment in terms of you admitting that you’re undocumented in the country; that would be admitting to a crime,” Malouf said.

The changes to the form could also scare some immigrants and discourage them from filing their returns, Malouf said.

“This is going to make a lot of people not file their tax forms out of fear they’ll be deported if they do,” he said.

NBC's Danielle Abreu contributed to this report.

Rochester, N.Y. — Advocates gathered on the University of Rochester Medical Center campus Thursday to rally in support of immigrant healthcare workers.

The rally was part of the national "Healthcare Needs Us All" day of action, calling on Congress to protect those workers and the patients who depend on them.

The advocates said tens of thousands of healthcare workers are at risk under the Trump administration's immigration policies.

BACKGROUND: Trump administration expands immigration crackdown with worldwide visa pause | Trump flexes executive power with unprecedented flouting of lower court rulings

"Almost 20% of the nation's essential caregivers and providers in hospitals, nursing homes, and home and community-based case were born outside of the U.S.," said Tracey Harrison, 1199SEIU vice president for the Rochester area. "When we cancel temporary protected status for countries, fail to renew work permits for DACA recipients and implement new travel bans on other immigrants, we're losing doctors who treat us during a crisis and provide preventative care; home care workers who help our parents, grandparents and loved ones with disabilities live at home with dignity; support tech workers who help keep hospitals, nursing homes and other healthcare facilities sterile to prevent the spread of diseases."

The advocates called on Congress to restore legal status for TPS holders and other immigrants, pass the Dream and Promise Act to create a pathway to citizenship, end discriminatory travel bans and processing delays, and prioritize healthcare funding over ICE and deportations.

description:

text:
In a new report released today, Amnesty International documented widespread human rights violations committed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and other federal agencies during the Trump administration’s large-scale, militarized immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St. Paul, New Orleans and Washington, DC.

The report, “We Had Whistles, They Had Guns”: Human Rights Violations in U.S. Immigration Enforcement Operations and the Case to Abolish ICE, demonstrates that the Trump administration is implementing a mass detention and deportation system, fueled by racist, xenophobic and false narratives, whose objective is to detain and deport as many migrants, asylum seekers and refugees from the United States as possible and spread fear throughout immigrant communities more broadly.

“Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities,” said Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA. “ICE’s record of violating human rights is nothing new, but our report shows many of these abuses have reached a perilous new level.”

Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities.”

Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.

The Trump administration has committed a host of human rights abuses, including unlawful killings, some of which may amount to extrajudicial executions; arbitrary and discriminatory incommunicado detentions, including possible enforced disappearances, in some cases in conditions of confinement that may violate the prohibition on torture; violent repression of peaceful protests, and more. Based on these findings, Amnesty International is joining the chorus of community voices calling for ICE to be abolished, immediately.

ICE must be abolished

Amnesty International’s findings demonstrate that the violations documented across the four operations were not isolated or exceptional incidents, but part of recurring patterns of abuse with devastating consequences for immigrants and entire communities.

“Masked and armed federal agents attacking people in the streets with impunity doesn’t make our communities safer — it puts everyone in danger,” said Daar. “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”

ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”

Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.

ICE was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001 attacks, and an extremely problematic security framework was adopted in the years following. Amnesty International and other organizations have documented human rights violations committed by ICE and a troubling lack of oversight and accountability since its creation in 2003. However, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels.

Human rights violations

The four operations resulted in human rights violations against immigrants, asylum seekers and refugees, people profiled as immigrants, Black and Brown communities, and those who came to their aid and challenged the conduct of the Trump administration. They also created a pervasive climate of fear that extended throughout entire communities.

Across all four operations, Amnesty International documented:

· Racially discriminatory immigration enforcement operations and arbitrary detention

· Harassment, intimidation, degrading treatment and unjustified use of force by federal agents

· Use of lethal force and unlawful killings by federal agents, which should be investigated as extrajudicial executions

· Repression of protests and use of less lethal weapons, including tear gas

and pepper spray, by federal agents

· Unlawful surveillance and facial recognition technology

· Inhumane detention conditions and denial of due process, which should be investigated as torture

· Unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance

As the report documents, ICE agents operated within an institutional environment – openly supported and expanded by the Trump administration – in which violent and racially discriminatory immigration enforcement practices were encouraged by senior government officials, including President Trump. Agents frequently operated with masks and without identification; safeguards intended to prevent and address misconduct were weakened or dismantled; and human rights violations were rarely followed by meaningful investigation or accountability.

The report details an account from Minnesota State Representative Liish Kozlowski, who is Obijwe-Latine, who said: “My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”

“My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”

This is just one example from dozens in the report where ICE agents appeared to be engaging in explicit racial profiling.

“Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International. “These practices violate human rights and cause fear and psychological distress and long-lasting health concerns to children, other family members and entire communities.”

Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,”

Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.

The report also highlights how communities came together to resist and protect one another. These networks played an essential role in documenting human rights violations, and being there for their neighbors, through mutual aid networks, constitutional observer trainings, rapid response networks, walking school buses, and more in order to stand by and protect those most directly impacted. Protests were one important tool of resistance, but were frequently met with additional acts of lawlessness by ICE and Border Patrol agents.

For example, in Chicago, the Broadview facility became a focal point for protesting against ICE and Border Patrol’s actions in the city. Reverend David Black, who frequently went to the Broadview facility to do ministry, said, “The escalation of violence by ICE and CBP at Broadview when we were just praying and chanting was terrifying.” During one ministry service he led at the facility, Reverend Black, who was dressed as Clergy, was calling on three federal agents who were standing on the facility’s roof to repent, when the agents suddenly shot him in the face, arms and torso with exploding pellets of pepper spray. He is one of the numerous people whose experiences are documented in the report.

The report highlights numerous additional human rights violations during these cruel immigration enforcement operations. Amnesty International researchers interviewed 154 people across the four locations, allowing the organization to analyze how immigration enforcement operations affect diverse communities across different political, legal, and historical contexts, and to conclude that the human rights violations documented reflect broader national patterns rather than being isolated local incidents.

“It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants,” said Daar. “I’m also hopeful – communities have rallied around those targeted and in some instances forced the Trump administration to back down. We must hold accountable those government officials responsible for this reign of terror, and we must keep fighting for an immigration system that is grounded in human rights and dignity, not cruelty.”

It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants. We must hold accountable those government officials responsible for this reign of terror, and we must keep fighting for an immigration system that is grounded in human rights and dignity, not cruelty.”

Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.

text:
By Andrew Chung and Nate Raymond

Sept 24 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump’s administration asked the US Supreme Court on Thursday to allow it to continue to deport migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face — a key tool in his immigration crackdown.

The administration in an emergency filing asked the justices to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy’s ruling ​that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful, while it appeals to the Supreme Court.

The dispute ‌escalated quickly after the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals, which upheld Murphy’s decision on September 18, put that decision into effect late on Wednesday.

More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.

The Supreme Court previously sided with the administration, lifting a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals.

The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump’s goal of mass deportation. The Republican ‌president has ​enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration — among his top priorities — since returning to office last year.

The administration has ⁠carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, ⁠which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.

In its filing on Thursday, the Justice Department told the Supreme Court that the rulings by lower courts disrupt “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens.”

The Justice Department said the administration already has canceled flights or plans for removals to ​various countries, and warned of harms to diplomatic arrangements and US foreign policy.

“While certain aliens may benefit from stalling their removal, the nation does not,” the filing stated.

Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said in an interview the fact that the administration opted to take the case to ⁠the Supreme Court was not surprising, as “they have repeatedly and publicly stated an intention to do so.”

Realmuto ⁠said the 1st Circuit’s order on Wednesday night “makes crystal clear no flights or buses should carry out third-country removals.”

STEPPING UP ​DEPORTATIONS

The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation ​orders. Immigrant rights groups filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of a group of migrants seeking to prevent their removal to such ‌third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.

The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.

In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and ⁠due process protections under the US Constitution’s Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.

The administration has said these deportations are needed to expel migrants who commit crimes and are considered “some of the worst of the worst illegal aliens in this country” because ⁠their countries of origin are often unwilling to take them ‌back.

But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal ⁠protection from being sent back to their home countries.

The policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by third ​countries back to ‌their home countries, while others have been abused, detained or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.

The ​1st Circuit upheld most ⁠of the judge’s ruling on September 18. On Wednesday, at the behest of the plaintiffs, the 1st Circuit dissolved a pause it had placed on Murphy’s ruling during the Justice Department’s appeal.

The 1st Circuit acted after the challengers to the policy reported that the government had planned to fly a group of migrants to several countries in Africa on Thursday.

The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the government “repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate” his orders.

Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated his order requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; Additional reporting by Nate Raymond ​and Katharine Jackson; Editing by Will Dunham)

text:
A federal judge slammed ICE for what he called "inhumane and unconstitutional" conditions at a New York City detention center and issued a permanent injunction imposing sweeping standards on the facility.

Why it matters: The ruling echoes other court decisions tied to President Trump's rapid expansion of immigration arrests and detention.

Kaplan found that ICE had repeatedly ignored his previous orders and misled the court about its compliance, saying officials had sometimes "intentionally concealed or recklessly disregarded the truth."

What they're saying: "The conditions of confinement to which ICE subjected immigration detainees at 26 Fed during the summer of 2025 were inhumane and unconstitutional," U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan wrote in a scathing 127-page opinion.

"By detaining far more persons in the hold rooms than ever was intended and for far longer than ever was intended, ICE objectively deprived detainees of sleep, sanitary living conditions, basic personal hygiene needs, sufficient food and water, and adequate medical care."

Catch up quick: The holding rooms at 26 Federal Plaza in NYC are meant to be short-term facilities that house detained immigrants for "12 hours or less," but ICE routinely held people for extended periods.

"Fed 26 is not unique," Kaplan wrote, noting that "comparable litigation" has been brought against other facilities.

26 Federal Plaza's immigration court and the Department of Homeland Security didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Zoom in: Kaplan said the "overwhelmed" center "confined many of those arrested in overcrowded, squalid, and degrading rooms for excessive periods of time."

He also noted that detained immigrants were "severely restricted" from accessing counsel in a "meaningful way," and that those who were able to make phone calls could do so for only a few minutes at a time.

ICE staff or contractors were typically close enough to overhear phone conversations, leaving at least one person "fearful and powerless" and scared of "speak[ing] freely."

The intrigue: Kaplan said ICE's disregard of previous court-ordered capacity limits had been "persistent, egregious, and, at a minimum, reckless, if not willful."

What's inside: The court's permanent injunction requires ICE to provide at least 50 square feet of qualifying floor space per person — excluding space within eight feet of a toilet — and keep hold rooms between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit.

Kaplan also required ICE to provide detainees three daily meals, each with bottled water, and adequate supplies of soap, toilet paper, and oral and feminine hygiene products. Immigrants held overnight must receive a clean bedding mat or mattress, pillow and blanket.

He also directed ICE to keep a licensed medical professional on-site at all times, and provide detainees with a basic medical screening to identify and begin treating any acute or chronic medical conditions.

ICE must also give immigrants a way to make confidential, unmonitored and free telephone calls to their attorneys or potential attorneys.

Zoom out: The ruling highlights growing tensions between the courts and Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown.

The administration insists that nearly all unlawfully present noncitizens it arrests are incarcerated pending removal proceedings, putting the policy on a collision course with limited detention capacity.

More than 300 judges have rebuffed Trump's mandatory detention policy, with many ruling it is illegal or unconstitutional.

Some immigration advocates say the goal is likely to make detention so brutal that immigrants are willing to self-deport immediately rather than endure harsh conditions for years while fighting their cases.

text:
SEPTEMBER 24, 2026

Contact: media@haitianbridge.org, Paige Censale, pcensale@haitianbridge.org

SAN DIEGO, CA — Haitian Bridge Alliance is demanding a full and independent investigation into the death of Carlos Josué Marchena Marchena, a Costa Rican national who died in ICE custody after his family reported that he repeatedly complained about inadequate care for his diabetes. His death raises serious questions about the medical care he received, whether his complaints were properly addressed, and whether timely intervention could have prevented his death.

Far too many people have died in immigration detention. Each death represents a human life lost while in the custody and care of the United States government—and each deserves more than an internal review and unanswered questions.

“Carlos Josué Marchena Marchena should not have had to die in custody while reportedly asking for medical care,” said Guerline Jozef, Executive Director of Haitian Bridge Alliance. “Far too many people have died in immigration detention, and we continue to see families left searching for answers after their loved ones are gone. The government has a duty to protect people in its custody under both domestic and international law. We demand a full accounting of what happened to Carlos, whether his death could have been prevented, and accountability for any failures that contributed to it.”

HBA is calling for the immediate preservation and independent review of all medical records, medication records, sick-call requests, surveillance footage, incident reports, and other evidence concerning Mr. Marchena Marchena’s detention and death. This investigation must also examine the broader failures in the immigration detention system that are placing medically vulnerable people at risk.

People in immigration custody are not disposable. Their lives, their health, and their dignity must matter. HBA stands with Mr. Marchena Marchena’s family in demanding transparency, justice, and accountability.

text:
Federal immigration officers were a half-mile away when a man who was illegally in the U.S. crashed a car at high speed and died in Michigan last weekend, authorities said Thursday.

The Department of Homeland Security appeared to try to counter any claim that officers were aggressively pursuing the vehicle when the crash happened Sunday in Grand Rapids. The death of Mario Coronado Juarez has angered friends and activists, and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has directed state police to investigate.

Juarez, a native of Guatemala, apparently was not the specific target of officers. But he was driving a car that was registered to another person from Guatemala who was also in the U.S. illegally and wanted back in his home country, Homeland Security said in a statement.

“As officers attempted the stop to confirm the identity of the driver, the driver of the vehicle fled at a high rate of speed,” DHS said. "In the interest of public safety, ICE officers immediately discontinued the enforcement action.

“A short time later, officers saw smoke nearly half a mile from the attempted stop and discovered the vehicle had crashed into a tree and caught fire,” DHS said.

The agency said officers tried to help Juarez and put out the fire before Grand Rapids first responders arrived. Juarez, who was in his 30s, died at the scene.

He was supporting a wife and three children by working construction in Grand Rapids and was saving money to build a home for them in Guatemala where they live, said Gema Lowe, an immigrant rights activist.

She led a chant of Juarez' name at a plaza outside city hall Tuesday and said he had died because of ICE's “vicious persecution of immigrant workers.”

The Trump administration will ask the U.S. Supreme Court to allow it to continue swiftly deporting immigrants to third countries that are different from their country of origin, Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday.

Blanche's announcement follows a federal appeals court ruling on Wednesday that cleared the way for a lower court decision blocking the rapid removal of migrants to third countries without a "meaningful opportunity" to contest their deportations.

"Without even allowing the government a chance to respond, and in the dark of night, a federal appeals court blocked us from conducting all third-country removals of illegal aliens, an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration," Blanche wrote Thursday on X. "We will immediately seek relief from the Supreme Court, which previously granted a stay in this very same case."

Attorneys representing people who have been deported to third countries told ABC News that several third-country removal flights that were scheduled for Thursday were canceled.

Last week, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled that immigrants were not receiving adequate notice before being deported to nations where they have no connections.

"An individual's right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination," wrote Circuit Court Judge Seth Aframe.

About 25,000 people have been deported to so-called third countries during the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, according to the immigrant rights organization Human Rights First.

The Department of Homeland Security's general counsel said on X Wednesday that third-party deportations are an "essential public safety tool" that's utilized in cases where a migrant's country of origin won't accept them; when they cannot remain in the U.S. but also can't go back to their home country; and when there are "logistical problems" associated with removing them to their country of origin.

According to immigration lawyers and advocates, third-country removals are not new, but they are rare. In recent months, the Trump administration has ramped up third-country deportations after creating a web of formal deals with nearly three dozen countries to deport asylum seekers, refugees, and migrants with criminal records with little to no warning.

ABC News previously interviewed a group of Latin American men who were deported to the Central African Republic, which the U.S. has classified as an extreme-risk destination for Americans due to armed conflict, violent crime and the threat of terrorism. The men said they were not informed of their destination until several hours into the flight.

"I feel kidnapped," one of the men, Aristides Fernandez Garcia, said. "They have violated all the rights that exist in life, because we are human beings."

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing ill-conceived plans to rapidly increase detention capacity, and the total will likely rise due to ongoing mismanagement, congressional investigators warned Thursday.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented costly problems in several initiatives ICE has pursued since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 and ordered the mass arrest and deportation of people who are in the country illegally.

Among the misspending was nearly $3 million to erect tents at Guantanamo Bay that were never used, $20 million to maintain purchased warehouses that are now being sold without having housed a single detainee, and excessive rates paid to hold detainees at a deficient and now-shuttered Florida lockup.

ICE has no strategic plan for spending its windfall

Congress gave ICE an unprecedented $45 billion to expand detention capacity last year as part of the Trump-backed One Big Beautiful Bill, but the agency still lacks a comprehensive strategic plan for how to spend it wisely, the report warned. The detainee population has increased from 39,000 in January 2025 to 67,000 as of July 30.

“Without taking action to manage detention investments in accordance with program and project management practices, ICE will likely continue to make uninformed decisions and risk further inefficiency and wasted resources,” warned the GAO, a nonpartisan agency that investigated at the request of congressional Democrats.

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, told GAO it would develop a plan to guide its detention expansion by Aug. 31, 2027, but that may be too late to prevent more waste, the report said.

ICE and DHS offered no immediate additional comment on the report.

The government scrapped a plan for mass detention at Guantánamo Bay

Shortly after Trump returned to the White House, the government began blowing money by hastily pursuing plans to detain more people who were in the U.S. illegally, the report found.

After the White House directed officials to use the military base in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for immigration detention in January 2025, the Department of Defense assembled enough tents to hold 5,000 people there at a cost of $2.85 million, the report said. But DHS found that the tents didn’t meet detention standards, and they were removed before they housed a single detainee.

The plan for mass detention at Guantánamo Bay was later found to be “infeasible” and scrapped because of the costs of building facilities that could meet federal standards. Instead, the agency housed an average of 16 detainees daily there this year, at a cost of millions of dollars, the report found.

ICE is wasting millions of dollars on empty warehouses

Earlier this year, ICE purchased 11 large warehouses across the country for $1.07 billion as part of a plan backed by former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to increase detention capacity. But that idea was scrapped amid public opposition before any detainees were housed in them because the department didn’t conduct “appropriate due diligence and planning,” according to the GAO report. DHS is now planning to sell seven of the facilities.

ICE has spent $20 million on costs and services related to those seven warehouses that it will not recover, including zoning assessments, title insurance, utilities and security, and will need to sell them for the total purchase price of $707 million to avoid more waste, the report said.

ICE has also “incurred significant costs” for the four warehouses that it plans to keep, including a $426 million outlay to renovate facilities in Arizona and Maryland that is on hold due to legal challenges.

Report finds waste on ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ and other plans

After the warehouse initiative faltered, ICE launched a plan to purchase facilities owned by private contractors that were already housing detainees, saying it would give more control over infrastructure and limit local governments’ ability to restrict their use.

The agency spent $1.5 billion to buy two of them in July and could buy more even though ICE has “not assessed the long-term affordability of owning these facilities,” the report said.

The report found fault with other initiatives. ICE never reached a contract with the state of Florida to operate the facility nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz,” which housed detainees for a year until it was closed in June following reports of substandard and abusive conditions.

Instead, DHS agreed to reimburse the state through a special $608 million Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that authorizes a charge of $249 per detainee per day — 171% higher than ICE’s normal rate of $92, the report found. DHS is also paying the state the higher rate for a second facility that’s still open in Sanderson, Florida.

ICE is also facing high costs under an agreement in which the Bureau of Prisons is housing detainees at eight facilities. The agreement requires ICE to reimburse the full cost, which has ballooned because of overtime and other staffing assignments, and pay a rate of $182 per detainee per day, the report said.

After spending much on warehouses to use for detention, that initiative has faltered, the report found. It has sold a lot of the property it bought but ICE has also “incurred significant costs” for the four warehouses that it plans to keep, including a $426m million outlay to renovate facilities in Arizona and Maryland that is on hold due to legal challenges.

ICE launched a plan to purchase facilities owned by private contractors that were already housing detainees, saying it would give more control over infrastructure and limit local governments’ ability to restrict their use.

The agency spent $1.5bn to buy two of them in July and could buy more even though ICE has “not assessed the long-term affordability of owning these facilities”, the report said.

The report found fault with other initiatives. ICE never reached a contract with the state of Florida to operate Alligator Alcatraz in the Everglades, which housed detainees for a year until it was closed in June after reports of substandard and abusive conditions.

Instead, DHS agreed to reimburse the state through a special $608m Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) grant that authorizes a charge of $249 per detainee per day – 171% higher than ICE’s normal rate of $92, the report found. DHS is also paying the state the higher rate for a second facility that’s still open in Sanderson, Florida.

ICE is also facing high costs under an agreement in which the Bureau of Prisons is housing detainees at eight facilities. The agreement requires ICE to reimburse the full cost, which has ballooned because of overtime and other staffing assignments, and pay a rate of $182 per detainee per day, the report said.

Permanent injunction comes months after documents revealed that ICE violated court order to reduce overcrowding at temporary holding facility in New York

September 24, 2026 2:34 pm

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

NEW YORK – A U.S. District Court granted a permanent injunction today that requires Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to improve detention conditions and mitigate overcrowding at 26 Federal Plaza. Notably, the order prohibits ICE from detaining people in overcrowded holding rooms and also requires that ICE provide adequate sanitation and hygiene, as well as adequate meals and medical care for all people detained at the facility. It also orders ICE to allow all detained people to make confidential, unmonitored, and free telephone calls to their attorneys within an hour of arriving at the facility, among other protections.

In September of 2025, the court granted a preliminary injunction prohibiting ICE from holding people in abusive conditions at 26 Federal Plaza after the American Civil Liberties Union, New York Civil Liberties Union, Make the Road New York, and Wang Hecker LLP filed a class action lawsuit. Despite the order, damning evidence presented at a bench trial in May 2026 showed that ICE repeatedly violated the preliminary injunction and exceeded the court-imposed capacity limits in temporary holding rooms at the facility.

The temporary holding facility became a flashpoint in the Trump administration’s aggressive mass deportation and detention campaign last summer, after ICE held more than 100 people, sometimes for weeks, in inhumane, overcrowded, and unsanitary conditions without beds, showers, or adequate medical support. The government also banned in-person legal visitation, any confidential phone or video communication, and confidential exchange of written documents, in violation of people’s First and Fifth Amendment rights.

Quotes from co-counsel are as follows:

“While we applaud the court’s decision to issue permanent protections requiring ICE to improve conditions at 26 Federal Plaza, it shouldn’t take a federal lawsuit to get the government to comply with the law,” said Carmen Iguina Gonzalez, deputy director of immigration detention for the ACLU’s National Prison Project. “As our legal teams have argued before, the conditions at this facility were entirely a crisis of ICE’s own making. We will continue to hold ICE accountable and ensure that people’s rights are upheld.”

“Today’s order rightly affirms that ICE cannot continue subjecting people to dehumanizing, abusive conditions at 26 Federal Plaza,” said Molly Biklen, Legal Director at the New York Civil Liberties Union. “We’ll continue to hold the Trump administration accountable and fight to end ICE’s cruel, unconstitutional detention conditions across New York.”

“The horrific detention conditions inside 26 Federal Plaza are emblematic of this administration's contempt for the rule of law and hostility toward immigrants. Today's decision is a testament to the courage of those who endured and spoke out against conditions no human being should ever be forced to bear: severely overcrowded cells, a lack of medical care, and the denial of basic hygiene and human dignity. Thanks to the bravery of those who came forward to support this lawsuit, this ruling will help ensure that no one else is forced to endure the same inhumane treatment at 26 Federal Plaza. At the same time, we are clear-eyed that these abuses did not occur in isolation. They are part of a broader pattern of cruelty and lawlessness that has characterized this administration's treatment of immigrants over the past year, fueling fear, inflicting profound harm on communities, and undermining the rights and safety of citizens and noncitizens alike. Today's decision is a firm reminder that the Constitution demands better,” said Harold Solis, Co-Legal Director of Make the Road New York.

"We are thrilled that the Court has imposed permanent, expanded protections to ensure that nobody will ever again have to experience the inhumane, traumatizing, and punitive conditions that our clients were subjected to at 26 Federal Plaza," said Heather Gregorio, a partner at Wang Hecker LLP. "We will stay vigilant to make sure that ICE complies.”

text:
The Administration is reshaping the H-1B visa program through higher proposed costs, wage-based selection, closer scrutiny of employer layoffs, and expanded investigations into alleged fraud and worker exploitation. Together, these actions raise the stakes for employers that rely on global talent while intensifying the policy debate over how to protect US workers without weakening the country’s ability to attract specialized skills.

The Administration extended the required $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, but actual payment of the fee is on hold pending the outcome of litigation. Together with a proposed $103,265 H-1B petition fee, wage-based selection system, and pending prevailing-wage changes, policy changes raise the costs and potential risks for companies sponsoring H-1B visas.

A new Executive Order also directs agencies to consider sponsors’ recent and planned layoffs of similarly situated US workers, linking H-1B review more closely to employers’ broader workforce decisions and adding risks for employers. Federal investigations are also expanding scrutiny of H-1B and permanent residency application practices, including wages, recruitment, worker placement, “benching,” and third-party staffing relationships.

The effects will vary by employer and sector. Based on the current distribution of H-1B visas, impact would be felt particularly in technology and engineering roles and on smaller entities for whom any fees could deter using these workers. Impacts will also vary depending on access to domestic workers, ability to locate work outside the US, reliance on specialized foreign talent, and how agencies will ultimately interpret the link between H-1B visas and a company’s broader employment practices.

From a Talent Program to a Broader Employer Review

The H-1B program allows US employers to hire foreign workers temporarily in “specialty occupations” that generally require at least a bachelor’s degree in a related field. Congress established an annual cap of 65,000 new visas, plus 20,000 slots for workers with qualifying advanced degrees from US institutions; universities and certain research organizations are generally exempt. Supporters argue that H-1B workers address specialized skill shortages and strengthen innovation, while critics contend that some employers use the program to suppress wages, displace US employees, or eventually transfer jobs abroad.

The Administration has recently acted to reinforce its policies on the use of H-1B visas. On September 18 it extended to September 21, 2027, a restriction first imposed in 2025: certain H-1B workers outside the US may not enter to begin employment unless the sponsoring employer makes a $100,000 payment.1 The Secretary of Homeland Security may grant national-interest exceptions covering an individual worker, a company, or an industry.

The same day, the President issued an Executive Order that may have broader implications for employers’ workforce decisions. The Departments of State, Labor (DOL), and Homeland Security (DHS) must now consider whether a sponsoring employer directly or indirectly conducted layoffs during the preceding year—or plans future layoffs—that negatively affect similarly situated US workers.2 The order also requires those agencies to consult with the Departments of Commerce and Education and the Small Business Administration on wage, employment, academic, industry, and other economic information relevant to the H-1B program. Agencies may therefore assess an H-1B visa request not only by the job and required wage but also in the context of a sponsoring company’s layoffs, contractors, compensation practices, and broader workforce strategy.

H-1B Fees: What Is Blocked and What Is Proposed?

On July 24, the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined to stay a ruling that that the $100,000 fee is an unauthorized tax and exceeds the President’s authority.3 In response, US Citizenship and Immigration Services confirmed that it would not collect the payment now.4 That result conflicts with an earlier district court ruling which upheld the policy under the President’s authority to restrict entry. The US Chamber of Commerce and the Association of American Universities appealed that decision to the DC Circuit. The September decision extends the policy’s duration but does not restore collection. Therefore, employers are currently not required to make the payment, although another court decision could change that result.

The $100,000 fee is distinct from a $103,265 H-1B fee DHS proposed in August.5 The proclamation for the fee invokes the President’s authority to restrict entry and focuses principally on workers outside the US who need admission to begin employment. The DHS proposal instead relies on DHS’s authority to recover immigration-system costs and would apply to most new petitions subject to the annual H-1B cap, including workers seeking to change from student to H-1B status without leaving the country.6 DHS projects that its proposed fee would raise approximately $8.8 billion annually for immigration adjudication, vetting, courts, enforcement, and other functions. The proposal anticipates fewer petitions and significant economic effects on more than 11,000 small entities. Because these policies rest on different authorities, cover different groups, and remain at different stages, it is premature to assume employers will ultimately pay both charges.

Program Redesign and Enforcement

Higher costs are one element of the Administration’s broader strategy on visa reform. DHS replaced the randomized H-1B cap lottery with a system favoring higher-wage positions, while DOL proposed increasing prevailing-wage requirements for H-1B and permanent-residency sponsorship. In response, applications from the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms fell from 24,946 to 2,055 between FY2026 and FY2027, while the share of visaholders with at least a US master’s degree rose from 45.1% to 66.1%.

Enforcement is also expanding. In July, DOL’s Office of Inspector General (OIG) opened an investigation into alleged fraud and human trafficking involving H-1B and PERM, the labor-certification process generally required for employment-based permanent residency. The investigation covers alleged falsified applications, below-wage employment, wage kickbacks, fraudulent recruitment, and unpaid or underpaid “benching.”7

Business Implications

The Administration’s approach makes visa sponsorship a broader enterprise issue. Information supplied by HR, compensation teams, recruiters, business units, and staffing firms may now trigger immigration, wage, civil-rights, or criminal scrutiny if filings are inconsistent with actual duties, wages, worksites, recruitment, or workforce decisions.

Employers should assess whether recent or planned layoffs involve positions comparable to those filled by H-1B workers. Because the new policy does not define “similarly situated,” companies should coordinate closely with leaders planning restructurings or reductions in force. Companies should also review staffing firms and labor brokers for recruitment, wage, placement, and “benching” practices. Even businesses that are not formally petitioning for a visa could face exposure through their relationships with intermediaries.

The economic effects vary by employer and industry sector. In the current distribution of H-1B visas, the impacts fall most heavily on technology, engineering, and computer-related roles and positions at universities and in health care. Higher costs and enforcement may discourage low-wage outsourcing and worker exploitation, but they could also constrain specialized hiring—particularly for smaller employers, health systems, universities, and research organizations with limited alternatives. Some companies may also be able to avoid the need for H-1B sponsorship if they can locate work outside the US, though this might also affect their ability to attract recent graduates who are foreign nationals. The outcome of the Administration’s policy changes and their effects on business will depend on pending litigation, as well as how broadly agencies ultimately connect visa sponsorship to employers’ wider workforce decisions.
