text:
WASHINGTON — The Department of Justice defended President Trump's recent media ban, arguing that reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico on a wide range of issues — from the White House ballroom construction, to the reported depletion of ammunition during the Iran war, and the Republican midterm convention — jeopardized national security and spread falsehoods.

In a late Tuesday court filing, in response to the lawsuit filed on Monday by the three media organizations, the DOJ asked the court to deny the request of the news outlets to have their access to the White House restored.

The filing from the Department of Justice included White House letters, dated Sept. 22, where it accuses the three barred media outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."

The DOJ response came just hours before an emergency session by the federal court in Washington, D.C., planned for Wednesday afternoon in a case that will further test the First Amendment protections under the Trump administration.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit against Trump on Monday for violating their constitutional rights after his administration revoked White House press credentials to the outlets' journalists.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," said the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C.

The lawsuit cites the news organizations' First Amendment rights not to be punished by the federal government over their news coverage. It also cites their Fifth Amendment rights to due process: the government cannot take away rights or privileges without any warning or process to intercede or appeal the decision.

In its Tuesday's filing, the DOJ argued that Trump revoked access to White House grounds to the three media outlets because he "concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum" and for "publishing sensitive or classified information."

"After all, access to the White House is a privilege—not a right," the DOJ argued.

In letters to CNN and MS Now, the White House alleged that the news outlets had jeopardized national security or spread falsehoods by publishing details relating to the construction of the White House's East Wing bunker to depletion of U.S. ammunition stockpiles during the Iran war.

The instances cited in the White House letter to Politico sought to contest the outlet's reporting on the Trump administration's lifting of sanctions against Russia, and rebuked Politico's reporting on the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas as "a disaster."

The letters were dated Sept. 22, four days after Trump denied outlets access to the White House. The White House set a Friday deadline for the banned media to submit written complaints to contest Trump's decision.

The ban on three news organizations is the latest instance of Trump's attempt to restrict the press. In his first term, he revoked press credentials for Jim Acosta, then a CNN White House correspondent. Trump denied access to the Oval Office and Air Force One to the Associated Press over its refusal to call the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name of Gulf of America, and that case is still in the courts.

On Friday, he told reporters at the White House that his decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico had not been sparked by any specific reporting but the accumulation of what he called two years of unfair and negative coverage.

Background on the $100,000 H-1B fee and a Federal Court Injunction A July 2026 court order from the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit barred USCIS from collecting the $100,000 H-1B fee.
This approach will surely result in immediate litigation in order to clarify the validity of the $100,000 fee.
Which H-1B Petitions Are Subject to the $100,000 Fee?
Which H-1B Petitions Are Exempt From the $100,000 Fee?
text:
On September 18, 2026, President Trump issued a proclamation that extends through September 21, 2027 a $100,000 fee for H-1B petitions that are filed as consular petitions or are only approvable for consular notification. This follows President Trump’s September 2025 proclamation that imposed a $100,000 fee on H-1B consular petitions filed from September 21, 2025 through September 21, 2026. More details on the 2025 proclamation can be found in our prior alert.

Background on the $100,000 H-1B fee and a Federal Court Injunction

A July 2026 court order from the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit barred USCIS from collecting the $100,000 H-1B fee. A USCIS appeal of this decision remains pending with the Federal Appeals Court.

Based on the language in the new proclamation, it appears that USCIS may immediately implement this fee despite the existing federal court order. We expect USCIS to argue that the new proclamation is not impacted by the July 2026 Federal District Court decision. This approach will surely result in immediate litigation in order to clarify the validity of the $100,000 fee.

To strengthen its legal position, the administration argues that the combined effects of the 2025 proclamation and the weighted H-1B selection process have increased access for highly skilled, highly paid workers, citing H-1B filing statistics from the past year.

Which H-1B Petitions Are Subject to the $100,000 Fee?

The new proclamation requires that the employer pay an additional $100,000 filing fee for an H-1B petition filed on behalf of a person who “must seek admission to the United States to effectuate the approval of a petition described in section 1 of this proclamation, including through consular notification, notification at a port of entry, pre‑flight inspection, or pre-clearance.”

As with the prior proclamation, the $100,000 fee applies only to “new” H-1B petitions filed on or after September 21, 2026:

for beneficiaries who are outside the United States and do not have a valid H-1B visa; or

for any H-1B petition that requests consular notification, port of entry notification, or pre-flight inspection for a beneficiary who is in the United States.

Which H-1B Petitions Are Exempt From the $100,000 Fee?

The $100,000 fee does not apply to any H-1B petitions for beneficiaries:

who have an H-1B visa or an approved H-1B petition submitted prior to September 21, 2026; or

who are in the United States and are being sponsored for an H-1B amendment, change of status, or extension of stay.

Based on a plain reading of the USCIS update, the $100,000 fee also does not apply to a beneficiary who has an H-1B visa issued prior to September 21, 2026 or an approved H-1B petition that was filed prior to September 21, 2026.

Mintz is closely following all policy developments and litigation related to the H-1B program. Please contact a member of the Mintz Immigration Team for more information: https://www.mintz.com/industries-practices/immigration

text:
The shooting of a man in Austin by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has become the latest flashpoint in America's divide over enforcing immigration law.

Protests erupted in Texas' capital city on Sept. 20 after an ICE agent shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, a Venezuelan DoorDash driver.

CNN reported that bystander video shows an ICE agent’s vehicle striking Garcés Pérez’s car, followed by gunshots. At a Sept. 21 news conference, calling in from detention, Garcés Pérez denied running from the agent, disputing the Department of Homeland Security’s account of a foot pursuit.

According to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez was released from the hospital straight into ICE custody, with no pain medication. She told reporters he entered the United States in 2024 through the Biden-era CBP One app, had a work permit and was seeking asylum, but received a deportation order in absentia after a hearing notice was sent to the wrong address.

Garcés Pérez should not be deported until the investigation is complete.

DHS revoked CBP One parolees' status when President Donald Trump returned to office, though a federal judge has since ordered it restored pending litigation.

In a lengthy statement released on Sept. 22, DHS refuted claims that Garcés Pérez was not receiving proper medical care, stated that his work permit expired in 2025, and reminded the public that resisting arrest and evading officers is dangerous for all involved.

The Austin American-Statesman reported that video footage calls into question Garcés Pérez's claim that he didn't flee agents.

DHS posted on X that it is investigating with the FBI, maintaining that Garcés Pérez "illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal."

CBS News reported that the ICE officer who shot him has been placed on administrative leave.

Austin's Democratic leaders reacted with fury. Mayor Kirk Watson said he wants the city's police department to participate in the investigation as a third party. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar went further.

"The vast majority of people being pulled over have zero criminal records," Casar told reporters Sept. 21. "ICE has not made us more safe by arresting 5-year-olds, by shooting delivery drivers, by raiding construction sites. We will all be more safe when ICE gets the hell out of Austin, Texas."

Democrats continue to oppose enforcing immigration law

I support ICE, and incidents like this still frustrate me. The use of force here is troubling, and there are two competing accounts of what happened and Garcés Pérez's legal status.

Texans deserve the truth. Democrats are right to demand answers about the Austin shooting. They're wrong to treat ICE itself as illegitimate. Local officials should be pushing federal agents to enforce the law well, not undermining the agency tasked with our security.

On Sept. 22, the ranking members of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform held a hearing on the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. Good and Pretti were U.S. citizens who interfered with ICE operations.

The congressional hearing also reviewed other deaths, including Ruben Ray Martinez and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.

ICE’s critics have legitimate concerns. These cases deserve answers, and ICE agents should be held accountable while DHS works to prevent unnecessary casualties. But even with all the questions I have about the Austin shooting, it's frustrating to watch Texas Democrats immediately condemn ICE wholesale, telling the agency in no uncertain terms to "get the hell out."

In January, Casar urged Senate Democrats to reject ICE funding, part of a broader pattern of Democrats calling to defund or abolish the agency after incidents like this one. Treating ICE as illegitimate is irresponsible. Enforcing immigration law is a legitimate function of government – one of its most important.

ICE is necessary to maintain law and order

A city or state that won't enforce the law isn't safe for its citizens. A country without secure borders is ripe for crisis and chaos. I'm glad Trump is reining this in through ICE, even though there have been mistakes.

Successful efforts rarely make news, even as they make communities safer. ICE said a recent five-day Indiana operation led to 426 arrests of people here illegally, including some with criminal histories involving sex crimes and assault. Its Dallas field office announced 39 people indicted or charged after a child exploitation operation. And in July, ICE made nearly 50,000 arrests, the highest monthly total of Trump's second term.

Democratic lawmakers rarely applaud these successes, and they show little of the same sympathy for the victims of illegal immigration.

They're right to demand answers about the Austin shooting. But they're wrong to call for ICE to leave Texas. Secure borders and safe cities depend on it staying.

text:
An attempted traffic stop by federal immigration officers ended in a deadly crash Sunday after the driver fled and smashed his car into a tree in Grand Rapids, Michigan, according to police.

The driver, a Guatemalan national, was pronounced dead at the scene.

Rosario Ovando, consul general of Guatemala in Chicago, which serves Michigan, identified the man killed in the crash as Mario David Coronado Juárez.

Ovando told NBC News on Wednesday that Coronado, 36, was originally from the Guatemalan city of San Marcos.

Coronado had been employed in the U.S. as a construction worker to provide for his wife and three young children, who are back in Guatemala, according to Karla Barberi and Gema Lowe, both members of the advocacy group Movimiento Cosecha in Grand Rapids.

“Mario was a hard-working man for the working class. He lived a humble life. I’m showing you here who Mario is,” Lowe said, holding a picture of Coronado while speaking at a press conference Tuesday. “In his car, he only has tools to work here and just to be working for his family.”

“If ICE was chasing him and caused his death, we want justice,” Barberi said.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE have not responded to requests for comment.

At approximately 7:10 a.m. Sunday, Grand Rapids police responded to reports of a car that had crashed into a tree and caught fire. Coronado “was pronounced deceased at the scene,” police said in a statement Sunday.

In a follow-up statement Tuesday, Grand Rapids police said, “Prior to the crash Sunday morning, Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel attempted to stop the involved vehicle and the driver fled.”

Police Chief Joseph A. Trigg requested assistance from Michigan State Police in the investigation. Col. James Grady II, the state police’s director, confirmed to NBC News that the agency is “investigating what led to Sunday’s deadly crash” in collaboration with Grand Rapids police.

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer also directed the state police “to conduct an independent review of the law enforcement actions surrounding this situation,” her spokesperson, Kaylie Hanson, told NBC News in a statement.

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., sent a letter to acting ICE Director David Venturella on Tuesday requesting information about the agency’s actions in connection with Coronado’s death.

“No traffic stop should end with a fatality. Something went wrong, and we need to know what and how,” Scholten said in a statement, adding that she will be demanding “a transparent investigation into facts we don’t yet know.”

Scholten’s letter to Venturella demands a response by Sunday, as well as an immediate briefing on the situation.

“The purpose of federal law enforcement is to make our communities safer. We must make sure that is happening,” she added.

Ovando said the Guatemalan Consulate will assist Coronado’s family with the repatriation of his body whenever authorities conclude their investigation into the incident.

A community vigil in Coronado’s name is planned for Thursday night at the site of the crash, according to Movimiento Cosecha in Grand Rapids.

Coronado is survived by his wife, two daughters, a son and his parents, all of whom are in Guatemala.

text:
Where the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has challenged a U.S. District Court judgment regarding “third-country removals,” the judgment must be vacated in part based on a lack of standing.

“The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (‘DHS’) appeals a final judgment in favor of a class of noncitizens with final removal orders who, pursuant to DHS policy documents issued in March and July of 2025 (collectively, ‘the Guidance’), face removal to countries neither designated in their removal orders nor identified in writing during prior removal proceedings as potential countries of removal. Following the parties’ lead, we call these removals ‘third-country removals.’

“The final judgment contains five declarations that, together, construe applicable law to require DHS to take three actions when executing third-country removals that are not contemplated by the Guidance: (1) to seek first to remove class members to countries they have designated or of which they are subjects, nationals, or citizens; (2) to provide class members with effective notice of DHS’s intention to remove them to a specified third country; and (3) to provide class members with a meaningful opportunity to contest removal to that third country on the ground that they have a reasonable fear of being persecuted or tortured there. … The judgment also vacates and sets aside the Guidance as unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act (‘APA’). 5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A), (C).

“For reasons we shall explain, the representative plaintiffs lack Article III standing as to their ‘sequencing’ claim. This requires us to vacate the two declarations regarding DHS’s obligation first to seek to remove class members to countries they have designated for removal or of which they are subjects, nationals, or citizens. Otherwise, we affirm the judgment. …

“The complaint in this case did not contain allegations that DHS unlawfully failed to engage in sequencing prior to carrying out third-country removals. Rather, the issue appears to have first arisen during the summary-judgment stage of the proceedings. DHS presents several arguments about this procedural irregularity, including an argument that none of the representative plaintiffs possessed Article III standing to litigate the issue. We agree with DHS that this claim must be dismissed, and the declarations based on this claim vacated, because the representative plaintiffs lack Article III standing. …

“For the reasons stated, we vacate on standing grounds the two declarations pertaining to DHS’s statutory obligation to seek to remove class members to countries they have designated, or of which they are subjects, nationals, or citizens, prior to removing them to third countries. We otherwise affirm the final judgment.”

D.V.D., et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 01-215-26) (55 pages) (Aframe, J.) Appealed from a decision by Murphy, J., in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Sarah E. Welch, with whom Matthew P. Seamon, Mary L. Larakers, Drew C. Ensign and Brett A. Shumate were on brief, for the defendants-appellants; Matt A. Crapo, Christopher J. Hajec, Edwin E. Aldana Madrid, Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, Anwen Hughes and Human Rights First were on brief, for the plaintiffs-appellees; Daniel Bowman, Rachel A. Romaniuk, Esther G. Back in Salazar’s district, several Republican voters said that they approved of the Trump administration’s deportation efforts.
And to some of these voters, Salazar’s ad was proof that she’s trying to stay in power by having it both ways.
text:
MIAMI - In South Florida, Rep. María Elvira Salazar’s latest campaign ad seems to be all voters can talk about.

The Republican’s video, released last week, was shot in front of the White House, not in the sun-blazed streets of Miami-Dade County. Though aimed at frustrated voters, it was framed as a direct appeal to President Donald Trump.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar says while looking directly at the camera. She goes on to tell Trump that his advisers are giving him bad advice, and that his immigration policies are weakening Republicans’ standing with the Latino voters who helped power GOP gains in 2024.

But many Latino voters in Salazar’s district said she has misread their sentiment and that their support for Trump has not wavered. Their support for their congresswoman, however, has waned, they said - and the ad did nothing to restore their confidence.

“She’s out of line,” said Hector Rubio, a resident of Miami’s wealthy enclave of Key Biscayne. Rubio, a longtime Republican voter who supported Salazar in the past three races, said in Spanish that Trump “is doing what he can, and he could do even more.” As he watched his wife shop in the neighborhood’s busy farmers market on Saturday morning, Rubio advised Salazar to stick close to Trump.

Even those who agreed with Salazar’s message seemed to find fault in it, with many saying the lawmaker should have made her appeal to Trump earlier.

“Her blind support of Trump has me very disturbed. She’s not thinking for herself,” said Charles Parsons, 83, another Key Biscayne resident who voted for Salazar in the past but said Saturday that he will not support her this year, even though he plans to vote for other Florida Republicans on the ballot. “All she’s thinking about is her political survival, and this ad … does nothing more than exacerbate the wound for me.”

In a statement to The Washington Post, Salazar defended her video, saying it “represents her long-standing conviction on the matter.”

Still, the ad suggests that what initially seemed like a relatively easy race for Salazar in a district Trump won by nearly 15 points in 2024 may be more complicated.

“[The ad] told me that she’s desperate,” said political analyst Ana Navarro, a former Republican strategist who became a fierce Trump critic, and a resident of Salazar’s district. “This was a pretty much ho-hum race. I think most people weren’t paying much attention to it. And all of a sudden this ad comes out, and it’s like: ‘Whoa, what’s going on here?’ And then you look at the polls, and you realize she’s tied.”

Salazar faces Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez who, like the lawmaker, is a former TV anchor. Both are well-known among Miami’s Hispanic population, with Salazar spending roughly 35 years at Spanish-speaking outlets like Univision and Telemundo. Rodriguez, meanwhile, spent 25 years at CBS Miami. He retired from the network in December, three months before launching his campaign.

The two are children of Cuban refugees who fled the island as communism took over the Caribbean nation - a history shared by many residents in southern Florida.

Their district spans wealthy waterfront communities like Key Biscayne, working-class immigrant neighborhoods like Little Havana, and tourist-heavy corners like Coconut Grove. Nearly 75 percent of the district’s residents are Hispanic - and more than half were born outside of the United States, according to the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey.

In 2024, Trump solidified years of Republican growth in Florida by drawing in a larger share of Hispanic voters in the state. But those gains are now being tested in districts like this as his popularity plummets nationwide.

Riding on a golf cart as he canvassed through Key Biscayne on Saturday, Rodriguez said he found Salazar’s ad “strange.”

“I was not expecting that, but it tells me that they’re nervous,” Rodriguez said. “She seems to have opened her eyes, but it’s too late. After you vote for all of this, after you vote to fund ICE, after you go ahead with Trump’s tariffs?”

Rodriguez questioned whether Salazar’s internal polling shows a race within the margin of error. He said that could be why she filmed an ad pushing back on Trump this close to the election, a hypothesis some analysts floated as well.

While Salazar’s campaign did not make her available for an interview, in a statement, Salazar dismissed speculation about what her polling shows.

“Every cycle around this time, the Democrat campaign will surface their polling analysis and come November the voters prove them wrong,” she said.

Democrats maintain the ad has been a boon. The Rodriguez campaign said it recorded a haul of about $120,000 last week, double the candidate’s take the week before. But he faces an uphill climb against the well-funded Salazar: According to Federal Election Commission numbers from July, the congresswoman is sitting on a war chest of about $2 million.

Democrats point out that it wasn’t too long ago that the area went blue - the county voted for their party in every presidential election between 1992 and 2020. A new congressional map has changed the shape of the district this year, however, and the area is now home to many of the Latino voters that helped lead Republicans to victory in 2024. The Cook Political Report still rates the race as “likely Republican.”

For his part, Trump chided Salazar for the ad on Friday, arguing that she would not have been elected had it not been for his endorsement. But the president notably spared Salazar from the louder, more aggressive reprimands he has unleashed against others in his party who have publicly criticized him.

Sunday, Salazar told CBS that she had “a fantastic conversation” with Trump following the ad, and that she reiterated the message she shared in the video. Salazar said Trump was “very receptive” to her message about the need for a new deportation strategy and broader immigration restructuring.

The Trump administration’s immigration enforcement activities have had a marked effect on Salazar’s district. Venezuelan, Haitian, Cuban and Nicaraguan immigrants make up a vast swath of the immigrant workforce in the area. Tens of thousands of these immigrants, who were living across South Florida legally under humanitarian parole programs and Temporary Protective Status, lost their immigration protections after the Trump administration ended them.

Residents complained about immigrant-owned businesses shutting down and neighbors being deported following intense Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations.

Nationally, the administration has said it deported 2.5 million people as of December 2025. The administration’s critics say the effort has been overly aggressive, and its deportation strategy drew widespread scrutiny following the deaths of Americans during enforcement actions in Minnesota in 2026.

Back in Salazar’s district, several Republican voters said that they approved of the Trump administration’s deportation efforts.

“The people who voted for Trump - the 70 or so million - one of the reasons was because they wanted to get all the illegal people out of here,” said South Miami resident Richard Santos, 80, in an interview outside of the city’s iconic Versailles restaurant. Santos said he voted for Salazar in the past but that he’s no longer supporting her because she challenged the president.

For many of the district’s Republicans, the calculus is very simple: You’re either with Trump or you aren’t. And to some of these voters, Salazar’s ad was proof that she’s trying to stay in power by having it both ways.

“She just did it because she wants to keep her seat in Congress,” said Julio Perez, 54, as he smoked a cigarette outside of Versailles alongside Santos.

text:
EVANSTON, Ill. —

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents mistakenly detained a U.S. citizen in a Chicago suburb Sunday morning, leaving him on the ground with various injuries, according to local authorities.

See footage of the detention in the video player above.

The man was found on the ground by police in Evanston, Illinois, after officers were dispatched around 9:49 a.m. over reports of two men arguing, Evanston Police Department said in a statement.

Several bystanders were helping the man, police said, and an ambulance was called after he reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth. Witnesses told officers they believed ICE agents were attempting to detain the man, who police identified only as an Evanston resident.

The incident marks the latest instance of a U.S. citizen swept up in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown, which has seen federal agents use highly visible, aggressive tactics that have sparked nationwide protests, legal battles, and political backlash.

One year after “Operation Midway Blitz” – the immigration crackdown by ICE officers in Chicago and surrounding areas – legal challenges against the agents’ aggressive tactics are still underway.

While responding to the scene in Evanston, one officer encountered two SUVs near an intersection and spoke with an individual in one of the vehicles, who identified himself as a federal agent conducting a “fugitive investigation,” police said. The person was wearing plain clothes and a vest marked “POLICE” with federal law enforcement markings, according to police.

The individual told the officer that agents had attempted to identify a person who resembled someone they were seeking, but the person refused to provide identification and “resisted detention,” Evanston police said.

The agents later determined the man was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen, after which he was released, police said.

The Department of Homeland Security told CNN that ICE agents conducting a targeted enforcement operation encountered a person who resembled their target and “immediately identified themselves as law enforcement.”

“The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself,” a DHS spokesperson told CNN. “ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself.”

Evanston police said it is investigating the incident, and that officers are preserving available body camera footage and interviewing witnesses.

Video shows struggle with agents

Surveillance video obtained by CNN appears to show two agents and the man in an upright struggle before federal officials pull him to the ground.

It’s unclear what happens after the man is brought to the ground, as the individuals move out of the camera’s view.

Moments later, at least three drivers pull into the nearby parking lot and exit their vehicles, joining other bystanders, some recording.

Evanston police said its officer noticed blood on hands of the agent in the SUV, which the federal official said resulted from an injury he received while trying to detain the man. The agent declined medical treatment.

Evanston’s police chief met with the man at a local hospital, and an evidence technician photographed and documented his injuries.

DHS said the man refused assistance from ICE agents, but did not address the man’s injuries in its statement.

'He was shooken up'

At the time of the incident, five federal agents were operating in separate vehicles to search the area for their target, the agent in the SUV told the Evanston officer.

Miguel Olivares told CNN affiliate WLS he was taking a break while helping out at a Mexican restaurant on Howard Street when he noticed vehicles parked outside and a confrontation unfolding.

“It looked like police vehicles until I started hearing, ‘I’m a U.S. citizen. I’m a U.S. citizen,’” Olivares said, at which point he began filming.

“They were being rough with him; they had him pinned against the floor, and it looked like one of the agents hit him in the face,” Olivares said.

He and others tried to comfort the man after agents released him.

“He was shooken up. He wasn’t really able to talk much. All he said was that he was a .U.S citizen, that he doesn’t know why they targeted him,” Olivares told WLS.

The federal agents later left the area after protesters began to gather, fearing they would be attacked, according to local police.

“ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” a DHS spokesperson said.

text:
Immigrant advocates went to federal court Tuesday seeking an immediate order blocking the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents.

In its federal lawsuit, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and seven Tennessee taxpayers alleged the THP is violating state law and the U.S. Constitution by making traffic stops of motorists suspected of being noncitizens solely based on their ethnic or racial appearance and then allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — riding along or stationed nearby — to demand immigration papers and detain drivers.

“The THP is using its traffic stop powers to help ICE do something that the Supreme Court has forbidden: to conduct ‘roving patrol[s]’ in which officers stop motorists on roads in the interior of the United States to check immigration status absent any substantial reason to think they lack status,” read their motion for a preliminary injunction blocking the joint traffic stops.

State attorneys defending the Tennessee Highway Patrol and the Tennessee Department of Homeland Security argued in court filings that state troopers have only engaged in legal traffic stops, based on probable cause of a traffic or criminal violation, and defended the cooperative effort between state troopers and ICE agents.

“Interagency law enforcement collaboration is not taboo,” they wrote in legal filings. State attorneys urged the court to reject the “extraordinary demand” that THP cease cooperative efforts with ICE . “THP’s collaboration with federal counterparts makes Tennessee safer,” they wrote.

Immigrant rights group sues Tennessee Highway Patrol over motorist stops

The state attorneys also raised procedural objections, arguing the plaintiffs lack legal standing to file the lawsuit, the federal court lacks jurisdiction to hear the lawsuit and the state has sovereign immunity against the legal claims.

In court on Tuesday, Assistant Attorney General Samantha Morris argued that ICE agents riding along with state troopers was not a constitutional violation, noting that interagency collaborations are common. Morris compared the practice to bringing drug-sniffing K-9 dogs on patrol to deploy when troopers conducting stops then have reasonable suspicion of potential drug violations.

Michael Holly, who represents the plaintiffs, said the comparison was apt “in a way.” Except, he said, a “drug dog doesn’t have a salary or an agenda.”

U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger told attorneys Tuesday she hoped to “issue a fairly quick decision.”

The lawsuit was filed May 18, about a year after the THP and ICE conducted a week-long operation they dubbed “Operation Flood the Zone” focused on one Nashville neighborhood with a large immigrant population.

Dashcam and bodyworn camera videos obtained by a consortium of investigative news outlets later revealed troopers made pejorative remarks about their targets, described the Nashville operation as “hunting’ time,” competed among designated teams of ICE officers and troopers to make the most arrests and marked detainees’ arms with sharpies to indicate which team could take credit for the arrests.

Questioned months later by state lawmakers about alleged misconduct during the operation, THP Colonel Matt Perry said the agency has since rejected overtures from ICE to conduct future joint operations.

The Tennessee Highway Patrol, however, continues to work in tandem with ICE and other federal agencies as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, convened last September via an executive order from President Donald Trump. In that role, the THP has conducted tens of thousands of traffic stops in Memphis. Neither the task force nor the THP has released data on how many of those traffic stops led to immigration arrests.

The injunction sought by the immigrant advocates and taxpayers, if granted, would prevent the THP from conducting traffic stops in tandem with ICE in its role as a member of the Memphis Safe Task Force.

text:
Carpinteria is a bit safer and calmer these days, thanks to a recent court ruling. The court ordered that ICE can no longer make the kind of warrantless immigration arrests that brought fear and disruption to our community last year.

The court’s ruling was issued in a lawsuit challenging federal immigration enforcement practices. Carpinteria joined the case at the urging of many, including our organization, the Carpinteria Immigrant Rights Coalition (CIRC). We applaud our city — and the City of Santa Barbara, which also joined the lawsuit — for taking this important step.

On September 2, 2026, federal court Judge Frimpong ruled that the federal government must halt its policy of arresting people without obtaining a warrant and without determining whether the person is likely to escape. The court also made clear that an immigrant’s “mere presence” in the U.S. in violation of immigration law is not, in itself, sufficient to establish the person is likely to escape before the officer can get a warrant.

We are grateful to those who worked on the case and gathered evidence that documented how ICE activity has affected people in our community. Local residents contributed eyewitness evidence about warrantless seizures, including one on a residential street in Carpinteria. Mayor Alarcon submitted a sworn statement describing the teargassing and arrests she saw outside Glasshouse, and the impact of ICE activity on Carpinteria’s workplaces and its economy.

Economic impacts of ICE actions, according to a September 11 Pacific Coast Business Times report [https:/ /www.pacbiztimes.com/2026/09/11/carpinteria-coalition-study-finds-ice-has-hurt-business-workforce/], include substantial lost profits, challenges in hiring and employee retention, and a lack of workplace preparedness compounded by limited access to legal guidance.

The judge’s order is a good start. But Carpinteria can and must do more to protect its workers, their families, businesses and customers. CIRC has made several recommendations for city action.

text:

EVERETT — A woman says she witnessed masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting a man in north Everett on Monday morning, and she captured it on video.

Jennifer Gordon told The Daily Herald on Tuesday that officers attempted to detain two men she’d hired from a local company to do landscaping outside her home near Everett Community College and the Legion Memorial Golf Course.

Gordon said the men were returning from a trip to the store for supplies on Monday morning when she saw flashing red and blue lights then heard shouting outside her home.

A five-and-a-half minute video Gordon recorded of the incident shows five or six suspected federal agents wearing tactical vests that read “Police” in large yellow letters with “Immigration and Customs Enforcement” underneath.

In the video, the men can be heard yelling for help in both English and Spanish as the suspected federal agents pull the men from a work truck. At one point, it appears one of the men ran away from the area while the agents wrestled another man from the truck.

The man being detained can be heard yelling, “They don’t have a warrant” and “Please help me” repeatedly. The man can also be heard saying, “I can’t breathe” while multiple agents lean over him.

Gordon said the officers were in unmarked vehicles, without any identification or badges. Several of the suspected agents were masked during the incident.

In March, state Gov. Bob Ferguson signed a bill prohibiting law enforcement, including federal immigration agents, from hiding their identity by wearing masks while conducting official business in Washington state.

A spokesperson for ICE and Homeland Security Investigations in Seattle said the agency could not provide any information without names or identifying information of the individuals detained.

Gordon said she asked multiple times for the agents to identify themselves.

“No response to that,” she said. “I was told to stand back, stay out of the way a couple times, but no one ever got aggressive with me.”

In the video, one agent can be heard saying to Gordon, “Ma’am, it’s not just our country that wants him,” seemingly alluding to why the man was being detained. The woman asks the agents if they are proud of themselves, to which one replied, “Actually, on this one, very proud.”

The federal agents detained the man in leg shackles and handcuffs before placing him in the back of an unmarked car, according to the video.

After about 20 minutes, Gordon said they were gone, but not without allegedly leaving her a message.

“Before they left, one of the officers was visibly making a point to take photos or videos of my property and my house, with my house number,” she said. “Seemingly, in an effort to threaten or intimidate me, like, ‘Hey, now we’re watching you.’”

After multiple follow-up requests, an ICE spokesperson chose not to answer questions confirming the agency’s presence in Everett or acknowledging the resident’s fears about intimidation, but did respond to questions about the suspected agents wearing masks.

“Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from wearing masks is despicable and a flagrant attempt to endanger our officers,” the ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “To be crystal clear: we will not abide by unconstitutional bans. The Supremacy Clause makes it clear that Washington’s sanctuary politicians do not control federal law enforcement.

“ICE officers wear face coverings for one reason: to protect themselves and their families from real-world threats including agitators.”

State Rep. Julio Cortes, D-Everett, represents the community where Monday’s incident reportedly occurred and was a co-sponsor on the legislation to prohibit law enforcement agencies from concealing their identity during arrests.

The bill gives anyone detained by an unlawfully masked officer the right to take legal action, allowing them to seek compensation, attorney fees and other remedies deemed appropriate by the court, according to the governor’s office.

Cortes said he isn’t aware of ICE operations in the local community beyond what is seen on social media. He said he has received many reports of ICE activity in south Everett, in addition to the video seen from Monday in north Everett.

“I don’t have any information specifically from the federal government or anyone really outside of the community that’s posting videos online, that’s contacting my office,” Cortes said. “It’s unfortunate, because it’s creating a lot of fear.”

Cortes said, despite the state law he sponsored, he expected complications enforcing the legislation due to the current divide between state and federal governments.

“ICE agents are already breaking, I think, a lot of Civil Rights laws,” Cortes said. “So for them to break this additional law, I’m not super surprised.”

He said the bill showed communities that lawmakers weren’t going to stay silent. It’s a first step that Cortes said he hopes will spark additional action to create accountability with legislation that has more teeth.

“Our local officers do this already, so why not federal officers?” he said. “It’s a pretty reasonable request to ensure that people know who is policing them. … Instead, ICE agents are out here creating fear and creating situations where it’s going to be dangerous, not just for the community, but also for the officers, because if they’re not adequately identifiable, it can create a very dangerous situation.”

While ICE would not confirm if federal agents were involved in the incident in north Everett, the Everett Police Department and Snohomish County Sheriff’s Office said their officers had no role in the arrest.

“If there is ever a life safety concern, 911 is a resource available to all of our community members,” Natalie Given, a spokesperson for EPD, said in an email. “While we are unable to interfere with immigration enforcement, per Washington State law, all officers have a duty to intervene if unlawful force is used.

As a Navy veteran and an essential worker, Gordon said the incident in her own front yard dredges up moral questions.

“I’ve been having a really difficult year reconciling the ways we show up to serve our community, and our country, and where the line is between helping and hurting, and what we’re called to do in the face of these unprecedented times and these injustices,” she said.

Gordon said the federal agents disrupted the jobs and lives of people in her neighborhood going about their regular days. She said it’s the least of her concerns when a man was separated from his family and incarcerated, but it shows the impact goes beyond just those in ICE custody.

“We have roving bands of faceless, nameless, supposed federal agents snatching our neighbors,” Gordon said. “But if that’s not enough to make you care, now you also didn’t have someone making sure that the patients were safe that day.”

Cortes is encouraging his constituents to stay educated on their rights and resources if confronted by a situation involving federal agents. He recommended services like the Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network and the Northwest Immigrants Rights Project for assistance and information during situations like these that may be clouded with unknowns.

He also asked the community to record these incidents to have a clearer picture of what’s going on.

“We want to know what’s happening, the community needs to know what’s happening,” Cortes said “If these ICE agents — if they are ICE agents, because again, we don’t know sometimes — if they’re breaking state or federal law we need to capture that on video to hold them accountable.”

After the initial shock of an arrest outside her home, Gordon said she found herself unsurprised based on the uptick in immigration arrests and encouraged others to consider if they are ready for the same thing.

“I think it’s something everyone in Everett should be prepared for,” Gordon said.

text:
Advocates and community leaders gathered on Wednesday at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement office in Miramar to denounce whistleblower allegations that immigrants held there are staying in overly crowded quarters, using filthy bathrooms, sleeping on the floor and being restrained.

“How can this be happening without any transparency, independent supervision, accountability? We have a right to know what’s happening behind these doors,” said Maria Elena Muñoz, a representative of the Miramar Circle of Protection, a group that supports immigrants weekly at the facility.

They called on Florida members of Congress, who can visit the facility unannounced under federal law, to witness the situation for themselves.

“Imagine that conditions are so bad that a whistleblower has come forward,” said Yareliz Mendez-Zamora, the policy coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee of Florida.

READ MORE: Extreme overcrowding and abuse plague Florida ICE facilities, whistleblowers say

The public showing comes days after congressional Democrats published allegations and images from a whistleblower denouncing abusive conditions in Miramar that show people sleeping on the floor, being held in a garage entry, and overflowing toilets. On Wednesday, the activists displayed the photos behind them as they spoke.

The facility at Miramar held 342 people at one point even though it has a maximum capacity of 50, according to claims released by Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability.

Immigrants held in the garage have been shackled while sleeping, the summary of whistleblower allegations continued. They are continuously under bright lights, have no access to basic hygiene products like soap, and must use portable toilets that the facility won’t clean.

The event also follows separate, recently released reports from the Department of Homeland Security’s Inspector General that found severe overcrowding at the Krome Detention Center in Miami and detention standard violations at the now-defunct facility dubbed Alligator Alcatraz in the Everglades. At Alligator Alcatraz, immigrants were held in a cage as punishment.

Also released on Monday were whistleblower allegations about another ICE facility in Orlando, where people are so crammed they are forced to stand up and have no access to the outside for up to two weeks, according to Democrats on the Oversight Committee. The whistleblower claims also allege that officers were told to shackle people around the clock at one point to address a lack of staffing.

READ MORE: Extreme overcrowding and abuse plague Florida ICE facilities, whistleblowers say

The activists also held a press conference in July at the Miramar ICE facilty to denounce conditions there. That’s when Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz visited unannounced and called the conditions she witnessed “horrific.” Last month, a Miami Herald investigation found that 911 medical calls from the facility had risen sharply between July 2025 and July 2026.

Maria Bilbao, the campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee, criticized Miami’s Republican delegation in Congress for not yet having visited the center, which is typically used for routine ICE check-ins. Under the second Trump administration, it has become a detention hotspot. People detained around South Florida are also brought there temporarily before being relocated to other local, long-term detention facilities.

“They’re always talking about human rights in Nicaragua, in Venezuela, in Cuba. When this is happening in their own backyard, where are their investigations?” said Bilbao.

A religious worker who showed up to support the activists said he saw a waste management truck come in Wednesday morning. That’s after photos of a pile of trashbags and dirty toilets emerged as part of the whistleblower’s claims.

In a statement to the Miami Herald, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not address the whistleblower’s allegations and the photos detailing conditions at Miramar.

“Miramar is a processing facility not a detention facility. Illegal aliens are processed and transferred to permanent housing at a detention facility,” said the spokesperson. “If you break the law, you will face the consequences. Illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.”

On Wednesday, the Miramar Circle of Protection set up tables to provide water, coffee and food to immigrants and their relatives awaiting appointments at the check-in office. There were sugar cookies and Argentinian empanadas along with worksheets about what to do if immigration agents showed up at someone’s house and what rights people have in that situation. Nearby, relatives of people already inside the facility for appointments awaited nervously on foldable chairs to see if their loved ones came out. A poster behind them said: “Free them all. All immigrants deserve dignity and respect.”

David Rosa, an evangelical pastor, has been to the facility recently to support a friend with an appointment at Miramar. His friend was desperate to use the bathroom, but the conditions were so dire that she did not. Rosa met a Honduran landscaper, still in his work uniform and detained there for three days, he said.

He recalled witnessing another woman leaving the facility. “She dropped to her knees. She did the sign of the cross in extreme relief. Almost as if coming out of a nightmare,” he said.

Rosa closed out the Wednesday event with a prayer for detained immigrants and their families.

“May we never become so accustomed to suffering that we stop seeing the humanity of those experiencing it.”

text:
Findings Show Concerted Efforts to Censor and Retaliate Against Speech in Support of Palestinian Rights in Colleges and Universities

Today, the American Civil Liberties Union and Amnesty International USA released a new report, “Student Speech Under Attack: Suppression of Pro-Palestine Speech and Dissent on Campus,” analyzing how higher education institutions, the federal government, and policymakers censored and suppressed speech in support of Palestinian rights and critical of the Israeli government. The report documents fierce retaliation against pro-Palestinian speech and expression that began in late 2023 and continues today. This repression has infringed on academic freedom and violated students’ and scholars’ free speech, association, and assembly rights across the country.

The report provides an in-depth review of university and college administrations’ punitive responses to campus protests against Israel’s war in Gaza, which has been declared an ongoing genocide by Amnesty International. The report documents how colleges and universities aggressively enforced campus policies and wielded disciplinary actions against community members based on their viewpoint, such as by suspending students, terminating faculty, and banning student organizations. It also documents how campus police and law enforcement used unlawful and unnecessary force against largely peaceful protesters, often leading to serious psychological harm and physical injuries. This nationwide crackdown has also contributed both to the rise of surveillance on campus to identify those who expressed pro-Palestinian views, and to universities’ failure to protect international students and scholars who spoke out under the Biden and Trump administrations from harassment and immigration enforcement.

The report also details how the Trump administration retaliated against universities and colleges that were sites of pro-Palestinian and anti-genocide activism. Under the guise of applying civil rights laws to combating campus antisemitism, the federal government withheld federal funding and research grants to coerce universities into accepting overly broad agreements that curtailed lawful expression on campus.

“Universities and colleges must take all possible measures to ensure that their campuses are spaces where students may exercise their rights to freedom of speech and expression without fear of unwarranted punishment or retaliation regardless of viewpoint,” said Jennifer Turner, principal human rights researcher in the ACLU’s Human Rights Program. “Schools should resist the pressures placed on them to silence and punish students or faculty who engage in protest or advocacy for Palestinian rights. Instead, they should stand up to the federal government’s intimidation tactics and defend the university’s core mission of fostering free-flowing inquiry and debate.”

The report closely documents the federal government’s targeting of noncitizen students and scholars for arrest, detention, and deportation based on their political views and in direct retaliation for their advocacy for Palestinian rights. Such actions include revoking the visas and green cards of noncitizen students and scholars who engaged in pro-Palestinian advocacy – such as Mahmoud Khalil, Mohsen Mahdawi, and Dr. Badar Khan Suri, among others – and arresting, detaining, and attempting to deport them solely because of their political viewpoints and constitutionally protected expression.

“Universities and colleges should prepare students for open discourse in a pluralistic society. Instead, campus leadership has suppressed free speech and peaceful protest while enabling the Trump administration to advance its anti-rights agenda and seek ideological control over higher education,” said Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA. “The Trump administration’s targeting of students and faculty who oppose Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza is dangerously reminiscent of McCarthy-era censorship and a blatant violation of academic freedom. The Trump administration must stop stifling political expression on campus and end its relentless push for ideological conformity in higher education. Students’ rights must be respected, protected, and fulfilled.”

The report is based on a two-year investigation that covered instances at 46 public and 34 private university and college campuses nationwide, located in 28 states and the District of Columbia. It additionally includes detailed case studies of six universities and colleges that were sites of student activism: the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Michigan; Columbia University; City College of New York; Tulane University; and the University of Texas at Austin.

The “Student Speech Under Attack: Suppression of Pro-Palestine Speech and Dissent on Campus” report concludes with recommendations for college and university leadership, as well as any law enforcement to:

Uphold free speech protections for all students and scholars, regardless of nationality, ethnicity, and race, and ensure that campus policies on political speech and protest are viewpoint neutral.

Refrain from adopting overly broad and vague policies against discrimination and harassment that punish or chill protected political speech.

Resist demands from the federal government that undermine academic freedom and students’ and faculty’s civil and human rights.

Impose strict limits on the deployment of law enforcement and use of less-lethal / crowd-control weapons, especially in the context of protests on college campuses.

The report also includes urgent calls for the Trump administration and Congress to:

Cease the campaign to deport students and faculty involved in Palestinian rights advocacy and end all pending removal proceedings against students and faculty targeted in retaliation for their lawful advocacy in support of Palestinian rights.

Cease the misuse of Title VI investigations to compel universities and colleges to impose unconstitutional policies and measures that violate free speech and undermine academic freedom.

Oppose any legislation that would punish noncitizens for exercising their First Amendment rights.

Oppose any legislation that threatens free expression and academic freedom to suppress criticism of the Israeli government or support for Palestinian rights.

You can read the full report and findings here: https://www.amnestyusa.org/reports/student-speech-under-attack-suppression-of-pro-palestine-speech-and-dissent-on-campus/

text:
A California assemblywoman representing parts of San Francisco and San Mateo County is calling for her staffer to be released after federal immigration agents detained him.

District 19 Assemblymember Catherine Stefani said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Ho Yin Mo, a field representative in her office, last Thursday.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said agents arrested Mo at the Las Vegas airport. The agency said he entered the U.S. in 2020 on a temporary visa but "illegally overstayed his welcome."

In a statement, Stefani said, "I am respectfully calling for Ho Yin Mo’s release as soon as possible. Ho Yin is a selfless public servant and a valued, legal employee of the California State Legislature serving our San Francisco and Bay Area communities. When Ho Yin and I meet our Chinese-American constituents, he brings a unique sense of belonging to so many who watched him as a TV reporter. And his work goes far beyond presence. Ho Yin helps people access affordable health care coverage, child care, and food support."

DHS also released a statement, saying, in part, "Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the United States."

Tincher’s story is just one of the hundreds that the ACLU-MN received from Minnesotans during Operation Metro Surge.
We will not stop fighting for them, and for everyone harmed by Operation Metro Surge, until the government answers for its violent, unconstitutional assault on Minnesotans.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS – On Friday, Sept. 18, a Federal Court dismissed Tincher v. Mullin. This case was brought by the ACLU-MN and pro-bono partners on behalf of protesters, observers, and journalists who were stopped, arrested, brutalized, and detained in the course of exercising their First Amendments Rights during Operation Metro Surge.

The ACLU-MN is disappointed in the court’s decision that plaintiffs lack standing to seek injunctive relief, and we will use every tool at our disposal to continue seeking accountability for the plaintiffs and declarants.

Tincher v. Mullin (then Tincher v. Noem) was filed by the ACLU-MN and pro bono partners Ciresi Conlin, Forsgren Fisher, and Riach Law on Dec. 17, 2025, as Operation Metro Surge was intensifying. In response to unlawful attacks on their neighbors, community members showed up to observe and protest. Federal agents countered their dissent with intimidation and force clearly intended to interfere with people’s exercise of free speech and their right to peaceably assemble and express disagreement with the government.

Susan Tincher, the named plaintiff in Tincher v. Mullin, awoke on Dec. 9 to a notification that an ICE detainment was happening blocks from her house. She quickly drove to the location of the ICE activity and stood on a public street without interfering with the agents. When Tincher asked, “are you ICE,” agents grabbed her, slammed her face-first into the snow and detained her. She was brought to the Whipple Federal building where agents cut off her wedding ring and some of her clothing. Hours after being detained, Tincher was released without charges or an explanation for her arrest.

Tincher’s story is just one of the hundreds that the ACLU-MN received from Minnesotans during Operation Metro Surge. And, while the government declared an end to the operation, we continue to receive reports of federal agents arresting and detaining our neighbors violating Minnesotan’s rights.

“We are reviewing this decision and assessing our next steps,” said Teresa Nelson, ACLU-MN Legal Director. “The plaintiffs and declarants in Tincher v. Mullin were gravely harmed by federal immigration enforcement, and they came forward to tell their stories — despite the federal government's attempts to silence their dissent. We will not stop fighting for them, and for everyone harmed by Operation Metro Surge, until the government answers for its violent, unconstitutional assault on Minnesotans. This fight is not over.”

The ACLU-MN has filed more than fifteen notices under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) seeking accountability and damages on behalf of individuals harmed by federal agents during Operation Metro Surge, including plaintiffs and declarants in Tincher v. Mullin.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA), a member of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations Committees, announced the filing of fifteen additional privileged resolutions to require the Trump-Vance Administration to produce assessments of the human rights situation in Belize, Burundi, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Dominica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Moldova, Palau, Paraguay, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Sierra Leone, and Uganda following reports that the Trump-Vance Administration deported immigrants who are not from those countries to those places. The legislation comes amid new reporting alleging the Administration has pledged at least $410 million to build a vast network of dozens of countries for third-country deportations.

“The American people want the government to focus on lowering their costs, not committing appalling human rights abuses with their tax dollars,” said Kaine. “Yet the Trump-Vance Administration is spending hundreds of millions of dollars—or more—to rip migrants from their homes and families without due process and send them to random countries they have no connection to and where they are being brutally beaten and held in awful conditions. We have a right to demand answers about what conditions are like in those countries and to understand what kind of shady backroom deals are facilitating these shameful removals. We can get those answers by passing these resolutions.”

The resolutions are privileged under the Foreign Assistance Act, meaning Kaine can force the Senate to debate and vote on them. Kaine previously teamed up with Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY) and U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and Alex Padilla (D-CA) to force a vote in the Senate to require a human rights report regarding El Salvador. The move came after President Trump threatened to imprison U.S. citizens there. Kaine has also previously filed resolutions to compel human rights reports regarding Cameroon, Costa Rica, Eswatini, Equatorial Guinea, Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Mexico, Panama, Rwanda, South Sudan, and Uzbekistan after reports of those countries’ involvement in third-country deportations from the United States.

Included here are the full texts of the legislation regarding Belize, Burundi, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Dominica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Moldova, Palau, Paraguay, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Sierra Leone, and Uganda.

title: Temporary Protection, Permanent Precarity - Public Seminar
authors: Nina Glick Schiller, Georges E. Fouron, Peter Dreier, William Milberg, Purushottam Bhandare, Katerina Canyon, Emily Condon, Rachel Charney McKenzie, Thomas Liess, Mitchell Abidor
description:

They had become critical parts of the US workforce, which needed a range of frontline workers from health care to construction to small businesses in underserved communities.
In addition, according to immigration advocates and researchers, TPS holders have contributed an estimated $29 billion to the US economy annually, while paying around $7.8 billion in taxes.
After the termination of Haitian TPS, Rebecca Shi, executive director of the American Business Immigration Coalition reported that its members “were particularly hard hit.
TPS holders could work and pay taxes, but they had no pathway to permanent residence and citizenship.
text:
Human rights activists protest outside a San Francisco US Immigration court, calling for an extension to the TPS program (February 2, 2026) | Phil Pasquini / Shutterstock

In August, The Wall Street Journal reported that in South Florida several home health care agencies were closing, “nursing homes are scrambling to fill vacant positions and restaurants are scaling back operating hours. Hotels, retailers, airport contractors and small businesses are also grappling with new staffing shortages.” Meanwhile, in neighborhoods such as New York’s Flatbush, small businesses reported an alarming decrease in customers, as well as imperiled daily operations owing to the absence of essential staff. As the 2026 school year began, school districts in states such as New York, Minnesota, Florida, California, and Ohio reported reduced enrollments and “disappearing” students.

These disruptions to daily life are all the results of the Trump administration’s crusade to turn over a million people,including factory workers, students, home health care aides, doctors, and nurses, into “illegals” overnight with the cancellation of their Temporary Protected Status. Meanwhile, government officials have continued to justify their daily capturing of migrant workers and their families as protecting public safety, arguing that they are removing “the worst of the worst.” However, the termination of most TPS protected statuses, with its disruption of both urban and rural communities has made it dramatically apparent that Trump’s migration policies benefit the detention-deportation industry and almost no one else. This round-up has also made it clear how inadequate TPS has been at providing people who desperately needed to resettle in safety with a pathway to citizenship, rather than a continuously precarious existence.

By providing time-limited humanitarian relief, Temporary Protected Status (TPS) allowed eligible foreign nationals from countries deemed unsafe due to armed conflicts, environmental disasters, or other extraordinary conditions, to live and work in the US. However, in January 2025, the Trump administration announced that all TPS programs would be ended by October 2026. Despite a number of court challenges, the administration proceeded to implement its goal except, so far, for the Salvadorians, de facto criminalizing all other TPS holders by removing their legal status. The 12 nationalities who have been living, working, and building lives in the US and who have now lost this legal status include: Afghanis, Nepalese, Cameroonians, Nicaraguans, Syrians, Lebanese, Sudanese, Ukrainians, Yeminis, Hondurans, South Sudanese, Burmese, Somalians, Ethiopians, and Haitians. They had become critical parts of the US workforce, which needed a range of frontline workers from health care to construction to small businesses in underserved communities. Notably TPS holders were an important component of the essential workers who risked their lives and were celebrated for supporting communities amid the Covid epidemic lockdown of 2020–2021. In addition, according to immigration advocates and researchers, TPS holders have contributed an estimated $29 billion to the US economy annually, while paying around $7.8 billion in taxes.

An estimated 50,000 TPS holders had been working in the health care sector, a vital part of the US economy already short of workers. Many of these workers had become central to local hospital systems at all levels and to elders, who were able to age at home with the assistance of aides. Before the termination of the program, Amina Dubuisson, who as a vice-president of Ventura Services Florida, oversees nine nursing homes across Miami, said at least 20 to 30 percent of their workers were TPS holders. These men, women, and children who fled countries enmeshed in ongoing wars, civil unrests, and gang violence are now subject to detention and deportation.

Faced with the loss of their legal status, families, who have been living in the United States for years with jobs, homes, and businesses are going into hiding and keeping their children home from school, fearing for their safety. More than 230,000 US born citizen children are facing the loss of at least one parent. The US government is telling former TPS holders to leave immediately, but around the world many countries in the Global North have already closed their borders to new immigrants and asylum seekers, while the homelands of TPS holders, the majority of which are located in the Global South, continue to be places of violence and repression.

So what will happen to over a million people holding TPS when, through no fault of their own, they have unexpectedly lost their right to work, been denied the rights to drive, to have access to the health insurance they have purchased or to the unemployment and social security benefits to which they have contributed? What will happen to the homes they had purchased? What will the banks do about their mortgages? How many of these houses will the banks have to short sell, causing the immigrants and the banks to lose their investments? What will happen to their children, extended transnational families, to their employers, to their cities or towns, and to our whole society?

The 350,000 Haitians who had TPS

The impact of the end of TPS on both migrants and on the cities and towns across the country where they live has become starkly visible with the withdrawal of status from 350,000 Haitians on July 23, 2026. The Haitian example elucidates both the viciousness of TPS cancellations and the widespread damage they have caused. After the termination of Haitian TPS, Rebecca Shi, executive director of the American Business Immigration Coalition reported that its members “were particularly hard hit. A resort hotel in Florida lost more than 150 workers, and a senior center in Massachusetts lost more than 50 employees.”

Haitian TPS holders generated an estimated $5.9 billion each year to the US economy. In addition, annually, they paid $805 million in federal and payroll taxes and $755 million in federal, state, and local taxes. An estimated 50,000 US citizen children have at least one parent who is a Haitian TPS holder; those children now face poverty and emotional harm because a parent has lost their work authorization and lives in fear of detention and deportation. Four days before ICE began hunting and mass-detaining Haitians, the US State Department re-issued its highest level of warning, advising US citizens not to travel to Haiti due to “the immediate risks of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care.” The Haitian domestic situation is so dire that the US State Department has advised travelers to prepare a will if they must travel there.

Almost 1.5 million people have been displaced because of gang violence in Haiti, where more than half of the country’s nearly 12 million inhabitants need humanitarian aid. In 2025, the United Nations verified “2,088 grave violations affecting 1,661 children, including the recruitment and use of 892 children [by armed gangs], as well as killings and maiming, sexual violence, abductions, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access.” As TPS holder Harriett Cecilia Joseph put it, “It’s not that we don’t want to go back to Haiti. It’s just the situation doesn’t allow us to.”

This situation is, in part, a result of direct US involvement in Haiti, which spans two centuries characterized by diplomatic isolation, economic interference, military occupation, and political interventions including undermining democratic grassroots movements. Haitians have long served as disenfranchised and exploited labor in both the US and Haiti, whether as temporary farm labor, workers with TPS, or factory workers in Haitian export-processing zones where the majority of goods are destined for the United States. In such zones, workers work for less-than-living wages and without any form of worker protection or benefits. In addition, the presence of guns and drugs that make it unsafe to travel or live in Haiti can be traced to transnational crime with US connections; Haiti produces neither guns nor drugs. The current unelected leadership of Haiti is in office with US support, and the US is also heavily involved in organizing Haiti’s first general elections in a decade, slated for December, despite the impossibility of holding secure, safe and fair balloting under current conditions. And by eliminating immigrants’ ability to send money to families and communities, the termination of work authorization for Haitian TPS holders will deepen the poverty in Haiti, causing further destabilization. In 2022, remittances sent from abroad accounted for more that 22 percent of Haiti’s GDP; 70 percent of those funds came from the US.

Springfield Ohio and its lessons for US politics

Springfield, Ohio has been a microcosm of both the brutal destructiveness of Trump’s migration policies and the ways local citizens are opposing these policies. Located in south-eastern Ohio, Springfield is a small city of about 60,000. Since the 1970s, the city has faced increasing deindustrialization and depopulation. But following the devastating 7.5 magnitude earthquake that devastated Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, and its surroundings in 2010, thousands of Haitians emigrated to the US, with over 10,000 moving to Ohio. According to The New York Times, “The newcomers staffed auto plants, packed ready-to-eats salads at Dole and sorted packages at Amazon. They filled church pews, enrolled their children in schools, and began to buy homes.” Carl Ruby, pastor of the Central Christian Church in Springfield said, “I’ve seen the city go from a seemingly unstoppable economic and population decline to a thriving locale fully on the upswing. That miracle turnaround was thanks in part to the thousands of Haitians seeking safety, many of them recipients of a little-known legal protection called Temporary Protected Status.”

Standing against the narrative of the Trump Administration, Republican elected leaders including the mayor of Springfield, Rob Rue, and the Republican governor of Ohio, Michael DeVine, called for the continuation of TPS. “It’s Haitians who, many times, are taking care of your mom or your dad who has Alzheimer’s, taking care of family members who might be in a nursing home,” said DeVine. “And to say we’re going to pull all those [people] out, it’s just not in our own self-interest.” While many right-wing extremists have voiced their support for the Haitians’ mass deportation, hundreds of Springfield citizens have attended meetings and demonstrations in support of their Haitian neighbors while developing plans to help them hide, or care for Haitian children if their parents are abducted by ICE.

Outside Ohio, politicians from both sides of the aisle are pushing to see TPS authorizations reinstated, with precisely such self-interest in mind. Republican congressman Mike Lawler, who represents New York’s lower Hudson Valley, has consistently supported extending TPS for Haitian nationals. In July, Lawler publicly urged Senate leadership to take up a bill which would extend TPS until 2029, citing ongoing violence in Haiti and the critical role Haitian workers play in US health care and local communities. Democratic members of Congress such as Laura Gillen of New York have also joined mayors like Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade County, Eileen Higgins of the City of Miami, and Haitian American Mayor Alix Desulme of North Miami in disavowing the end of TPS for Haitian immigrants.

While the official grounds for TPS extensions have always been ongoing danger in TPS holders’ home countries, it has long been tacitly understood that the US government uses TPS workers to meet the labor exigencies of the US economy while bypassing the urgent need to reform the US immigration system to address the socioeconomic needs of the country. These temporary protections also fail to fulfill US treaty obligations to grant asylum to those fleeing repressive regimes. TPS holders could work and pay taxes, but they had no pathway to permanent residence and citizenship.
