text:
September 18, 2026 marks a shift in how USCIS evaluates the public-charge ground of inadmissibility for covered adjustment-of-status applications. DHS's rescission of the 2022 public-charge regulations takes effect that day, and USCIS's revised Policy Manual guidance applies to Forms I-485 subject to the public-charge grounds that are postmarked or electronically submitted on or after September 18, 2026. That said, the change affects how the ground is evaluated, not whether it applies: the statutory ground of inadmissibility under INA § 212(a)(4) remains in place.

Under the revised framework, USCIS officers must evaluate the statutory factors in INA § 212(a)(4), including age, health, family status, assets, resources, and financial status, and education and skills, along with other evidence relevant to whether the applicant is likely at any time to become a public charge. USCIS states that this assessment is individualized and based on the totality of the circumstances.

The change does not establish an automatic bar based on benefit receipt. Instead, for means-tested benefits received on or after September 18, USCIS may consider benefit history together with the applicant's financial circumstances, household circumstances, education and skills, health, and other evidence in the record. For employment-based and investor applicants, that makes the framework, its transition rules, and the scope of evidence USCIS may consider worth understanding in detail.

What Changed, and What USCIS Now Applies

Two related agency actions underpin this change. First, DHS rescinded the 2022 public-charge regulations in a final rule, Public Charge Ground of Inadmissibility, 91 Fed. Reg. 45,324 (July 20, 2026), effective September 18, 2026. USCIS subsequently issued Policy Manual guidance on August 18, 2026, explaining that officers will adjudicate public-charge inadmissibility under the post-rescission framework.

The underlying statute has not changed. INA § 212(a)(4) continues to require officers to consider, at a minimum, five factors: age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.

What has changed is the framework surrounding those factors. USCIS may now consider additional case-specific evidence, including receipt of means-tested public benefits, as part of an individualized totality-of-the-circumstances determination. USCIS directs officers to make case-by-case determinations based on the totality of the circumstances rather than on any single factor.

In other words, the revised framework is not simply a question of whether an applicant has received a particular benefit. Benefits history may be considered alongside financial resources, employability, household circumstances, health, and the rest of the record. USCIS describes its guidance as controlling and intended to guide, rather than prescribe, how officers exercise discretion in individual cases. The guidance also supersedes prior related guidance, including the 1999 Interim Field Guidance.

Transition Rules for Filings and Benefits

The effective date creates two separate questions: which public-charge framework applies to the filing, and which benefits USCIS may consider.

For Forms I-485 subject to the public-charge grounds that are postmarked or electronically submitted on or after September 18, 2026, USCIS applies its revised guidance. The final rule separately addresses how USCIS considers means-tested benefits received before that date.

The timing of benefit receipt is evaluated on its own track. For means-tested benefits received before September 18, 2026, USCIS says it will consider only public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense. For means-tested benefits received on or after September 18, 2026, USCIS states that officers may consider any and all means-tested public benefits as part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

That distinction matters. The date of the I-485 filing determines which framework governs the case, while the date a benefit was received determines the range of benefits USCIS says it may weigh. As a result, a filing made under the revised framework can involve benefit history from before the effective date, with that earlier history evaluated under the narrower transition rule.

Revised Form I-485 Takes Effect Without a Grace Period

A second change is procedural rather than substantive.

Beginning September 18, 2026, USCIS accepts only the 09/18/26 edition of Form I-485. There is no grace period for the previous 01/20/25 edition. USCIS states it will reject the prior edition if it is postmarked or electronically submitted on or after September 18, 2026.

Who Is Subject to the Public-Charge Ground?

Public charge is not limited to family-based immigration.

According to USCIS, all adjustment applicants are subject to the public-charge ground unless their immigration category is exempt. Among the USCIS-listed covered adjustment categories are employment-based priority workers; EB-2 professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability; EB-3 skilled workers, professionals, and other workers; investors; religious workers; immediate relatives and family-preference applicants; and diversity visa immigrants adjusting status.

USCIS also identifies numerous exempt groups, including refugees, asylees, Special Immigrant Juveniles, VAWA self-petitioners, T and U nonimmigrants, certain Cuban and Haitian entrants, Afghan and Iraqi interpreters and certain Afghan and Iraqi nationals employed by or on behalf of the U.S. government, and registry applicants, among others. Because the list contains category-specific exemptions, the applicable adjustment category determines whether the public-charge ground applies in a given case.

The Benefits Inquiry Under the Revised Framework

The benefits inquiry is a central feature of the revised framework.

USCIS's guidance allows officers to consider a broader range of means-tested benefits, meaning benefits granted based on a household's income level. USCIS identifies examples such as cash assistance for income maintenance, housing assistance, food stamps, financial aid for college, and similar benefits.

Still, receipt of a public benefit does not automatically make an applicant inadmissible as a public charge. Rather, it may be one factor within the broader individualized determination.

For that reason, the relevant question is not simply whether a benefit was received. Its timing and type, along with the applicant's household circumstances and broader financial picture, may form part of the record USCIS evaluates.

Employment-Based and Investor Cases Under the Revised Framework

For employment-based and investor adjustment applicants who are subject to the public-charge ground, the statutory factors may make financial and employment-related evidence particularly relevant. USCIS must consider the applicant's age, health, family status, assets, resources, financial status, education, and skills, and may consider other evidence relevant to the likelihood of becoming a public charge.

Depending on the facts of a case, the record may include information relating to current and prospective employment, income, assets and liabilities, business-related financial documentation, household resources, education, professional qualifications, and skills. These are not a separate set of regulatory requirements; rather, they are examples of evidence that may relate to the statutory totality-of-the-circumstances assessment.

The Role of Form I-864 in the Analysis

In many employment-based cases, no Form I-864, Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA, is required. USCIS identifies Form I-864 as a factor it may consider where applicable, while the public-charge inquiry remains individualized and fact-specific. Where Form I-864 is not part of the filing, USCIS may still assess the statutory financial and other factors based on the record before it.

Public-Charge Bonds Remain Available

The revised framework retains the possibility of a public-charge bond in certain circumstances.

If USCIS finds an adjustment applicant inadmissible only on public-charge grounds, an officer may invite the applicant to post a bond using Form I-945. An applicant cannot independently submit Form I-945 for this purpose; USCIS must first issue an invitation in a Notice of Intent to Deny.

When determining the bond amount, USCIS may consider the government assistance the applicant could be eligible for and potentially receive over the following five years. A cash bond or a Treasury-certified surety bond may be used.

Pending Litigation and Potential Developments

The revised framework is already the subject of legal challenges.

On September 14, 2026, New York and a multistate coalition filed a challenge to the DHS final rule in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The complaint is docketed as New York v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, No. 26-cv-7978 (S.D.N.Y.). New York City, joined by local-government plaintiffs including Chicago, San Francisco, Santa Clara County, Seattle, and King County, filed a separate action in the same court. The plaintiffs' claims are allegations and have not been adjudicated.

As of September 18, 2026, this article has not identified an order staying implementation of the final rule. Because procedural developments can occur quickly, the status of the litigation should be checked against the relevant court dockets before publication or republication.

Several questions remain open. Courts could address whether preliminary relief is appropriate. USCIS adjudications and Requests for Evidence may provide more insight into how the guidance is applied in practice. The DHS rule and USCIS guidance discussed here principally concern DHS/USCIS adjudications; immigrant-visa applicants processing abroad should separately monitor Department of State guidance. And, as cases develop, fact patterns involving household benefits, derivative family members, and variable, newly established, or startup-based income may help clarify how the framework operates.

Practical Effects of the September 18 Change

For covered adjustment applications filed on or after September 18, 2026, the operative issues include the applicable Form I-485 edition, whether the adjustment category is exempt from the public-charge ground, and the timing and type of any means-tested benefits reflected in the record. USCIS will accept only the 09/18/26 edition of Form I-485 for forms postmarked or electronically submitted on or after that date; the prior 01/20/25 edition will be rejected if filed on or after September 18.

The revised framework does not replace the statutory requirement to consider the five INA § 212(a)(4) factors. It instead permits USCIS to consider a broader set of relevant evidence, including any means-tested public benefits received on or after the effective date, in a case-by-case totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

text:
He watched immigration agents shepherd other detainees from Venezuela, Cuba, Haiti and Central America across the tarmac towards three sleek white buses on the Mexican side of the port of entry.

Betancourt had no intention of boarding those buses. “I’ll just refuse to go. It’s my right,” he remembers thinking.

By then, Betancourt was used to the vagaries of American immigration enforcement. Since the Venezuelan journalist was detained on July 14, 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had shuttled him between 12 different detention facilities and had already attempted to deport him twice.

The first time had been in late December 2025, when immigration agents bussed Betancourt to San Diego’s border with Tijuana. Betancourt told authorities that they couldn’t obligate him to cross — Mexico wasn’t his country, he was scared of what would happen if he were sent there without any legal status, and deporting him without due process was illegal. The agents relented and returned him to detention.

Then, a month later at Arizona’s Mesa Gateway airport, immigration agents tried to force Betancourt onto a plane to Venezuela. He told them that an immigration judge had granted him protection from deportation to Venezuela in a 2024 court order, a decade after he fled political persecution in Caracas. ICE agents ignored his objections until a U.S. Marshal intervened on his behalf.

In Nogales, though, things unfolded differently. Four armed immigration agents clambered into the van and closed in around Betancourt. “They’ll deport you with punches if it’s necessary,” Betancourt said.

During six months in detention, Betancourt regularly experienced what he described as inhumane and dehumanizing treatment, including periods of up to 25 hours in shackles, and days on end shut with other immigrants in holding rooms so cramped that the detainees had to take turns lying down to rest. But he was determined to continue fighting his case, and return to the life he’d built with his family over the last decade in Miami. And to do so, he would need to remain inside the United States.

Hoping to avoid a beating, Betancourt crossed the border intending to explain his case to Mexican migration authorities — maybe they would listen. “But they didn’t respond,” he said. “They literally pretended not to hear me.”

The American agents forced Betancourt onto the Mexican bus with around 40 other detained passengers. Moments later, they were rolling south through rural Sonora towards an unknown destination in an unfamiliar country.

title: Trump administration tells Congress it will admit 17500 South African refugees - LA Times
authors: Rebecca Santana and Seung Min Kim
description:
The Trump administration plans to limit the number of refugees admitted to the country to 17,500 mostly white South Africans, the administration told Congress on Tuesday, as it continues to transform a program that at one point served as a pathway to safety for people fleeing war and strife from countries around the world.
In a notice to Congress obtained by the Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America.
The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.
The Trump administration has dramatically altered a refugee program that historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support as it welcomed tens of thousands of refugees from countries around the world to new lives in America, and instead the administration has transformed it into a vehicle to resettle white South Africans in America.
The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S. Presidents set the cap on how many refugees the U.S. will approve through the program each year, and historically, they’ve allocated those numbers across various geographic regions while factoring in wars or conflicts that spark humanitarian needs around the globe.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court is considering the Trump administration’s Sept. 21 request to redetain Georgetown University postdoctoral researcher Badar Khan Suri after an appeals court ruling kept him out of immigration detention.

A federal district judge released Khan Suri in May 2025 and the U.S. 4th Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the decision two months ago. Now, if the Supreme Court chooses to take the case — which experts say it appears likely to do — the justices will settle noncitizens’ ability to contest their detention in federal court.

The Supreme Court appeal comes 18 months after federal immigration agents detained Khan Suri for 58 days, drawing on a rarely-used statute to allege he threatened U.S. foreign policy.

Adnan Rashid (GRD ’24), one of Khan Suri’s closest friends who has supported him and his family through their legal proceedings, said he believes the federal government wants to silence the postdoctoral researcher’s speech.

“The government is trying to find a needle in a haystack but there is no needle — he is just a bookish person who sticks to reading and teaching,” Rashid told The Hoya. “They’re trying to find a crime where there is no crime.”

Noor Zafar, one of Khan Suri’s lawyers, said the lower federal courts were right to free Khan Suri from indefinite detention.

“Our client should never have been jailed for exercising his First Amendment rights in the first place and we will continue fighting to keep him free and with his family,” Zafar wrote to The Hoya.

The government’s lawyers have argued, however, that constitutional challenges to detention cannot be heard in federal courts — only in immigration courts, which are overseen by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). Khan Suri’s lawyers have long asserted that immigration courts are politically biased, a product of the Trump administration’s purge of immigration judges.

Khan Suri’s legal team has until Oct. 21 to file an opposing brief. Until then, the Supreme Court cannot formally decide if it will hear the case. No Supreme Court precedent explicitly governs federal judges’ jurisdiction over detention claims.

To justify Khan Suri’s detainment, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Khan Suri was spreading “Hamas propaganda” and antisemitism — citing online posts about him and his connection to his father-in-law, a former Hamas official. He denies these allegations, and the government has published limited evidence to support its claims.

The district court that freed Khan Suri found the government likely violated the First Amendment by targeting Khan Suri for protected speech and familial associations.

In its Supreme Court appeal, the DOJ does not argue that it acted constitutionally — merely that federal courts cannot decide if it did. Their claim centers on three sections of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) they say are meant to “eliminate” district courts from overseeing noncitizens’ detention.

Instead, Trump administration lawyers assert that federal law channels all immigration cases solely into immigration court so noncitizens get “just one bite at the apple — not zero or two.” Under the government’s proposed scheme, Khan Suri would remain detained throughout his lengthy immigration proceedings.

But Khan Suri’s lawyers — and the 4th Circuit — said those INA provisions only apply to deportation proceedings, and detention remains a separate legal issue. In the 4th Circuit’s decision, Judge DeAndrea Benjamin wrote that “no provision within the immigration code deprived” federal courts of jurisdiction over immigration detention.

Jackson Schnabel (SFS ’27), who is currently Khan Suri’s student, said the government’s purported interest in efficiency is baffling.

“It does no good if you have to challenge the illegality of your detention if you have to wait for all of these removal proceedings to go through,” Schnabel told The Hoya. “That just allows the illegal detention to continue — it allows it to exist even when it’s blatantly illegal.”

“If they don’t want there to be a drain on federal resources, they shouldn’t detain people for their speech,” Schnabel added.

In a Monday speech to Georgetown students after the appeal, Khan Suri said constitutional challenges are what “keeps a democracy a democracy.”

Yassine Florez (GRD ’26), a student organizer and close friend of Khan Suri’s family, said he was surprised the appeal came so quickly, but believes the Supreme Court will agree with the 4th Circuit.

“I am confident because we do have the precedent of winning,” Florez told The Hoya.

“He was able to win in the circuit court when no one else could,” Florez added.

The 4th Circuit is one of three federal appeals panels that have recently considered constitutional challenges to immigration detention — and the only one that has sided with noncitizens. Former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil is currently preparing a Supreme Court challenge to a 3rd Circuit decision in January that confined his case to immigration court.

The federal government cited this divide as a reason the Supreme Court should hear the case, positioning Khan Suri as an “ideal vehicle” to clarify case law that will apply to the entire country. In general, circuit splits make the Supreme Court more likely to rule on a legal issue.

Khan Suri expects the Supreme Court to take the case, he said Monday, because they want to block noncitizens from using federal court to secure their freedom.

Florez said that if the Supreme Court takes Khan Suri or Khalil’s case, the impact will reverberate for years.

“The whole goal of this appeal to the Supreme Court is to cement a law that the government can imprison anyone for as long as they want before deciding if they’re guilty or innocent,” Florez said.

“Whether or not they’re pro-justice, this will set a precedent for every case in the future,” Florez added.

Nader Hashemi, Khan Suri’s supervisor at Georgetown, said the case could become “one of those classic Supreme Court cases” that define the current political moment.

“It will speak volumes about what direction politically this country is headed in — in an authoritarian direction, or whether the Supreme Court will establish a guardrail,” Hashemi told The Hoya.

Khan Suri’s case has become a touchpoint for the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and a rallying cry across the Georgetown community. Student protesters have said the case is emblematic of federal crackdowns on academic freedom.

Schnabel, who has attended campus protests and Khan Suri’s legal hearings, said he is disappointed that the legal battle remains ongoing.

“We had the win when the ruling actually came out, but now we need to continue in this part of the fight,” Schnabel said. “But I am still optimistic that the rule of law, the rule of justice, will prevail in the long run — that as facts actually get considered, it will continue to be abundantly clear that what is going on is unconstitutional.”

At Khan Suri’s parallel immigration trial last week, over a dozen students attended the hearing in support as nine witnesses testified that he should remain in the United States.

Hashemi said that while political headwinds — including the Supreme Court’s current conservative majority — are against Khan Suri, he hopes the court looks solely at the facts and case law.

“You have to keep reminding people that his case is still pending, that the Trump administration is unrelenting in its attempt to deport him,” Hashemi said. “The challenge of Badar Khan Suri’s supporters is to keep his case in the public eye and keep reminding people of what’s coming next, what’s at stake here, why his cause matters.”

Darius Wagner (CAS ’27), president of Georgetown’s student government, said Khan Suri’s case is emblematic of the university’s commitment to studying authoritarianism and democracy.

“I think this will only continue to inspire students to keep pursuing those truths, and that is why I think it’s also really important that we all stand by Dr. Badar Khan Suri, because he’s a representation of our best values of our academic freedom and of our founding principles for freedom of speech,” Wagner told The Hoya.

Rashid said that even as Khan Suri faces a constant “onslaught” of litigation, he remains committed to his research and teaching.

“It’s fear, but he has hope,” Rashid said. “He believes in American democracy and freedom of speech and the Constitution. He believes in it, and that’s one of the reasons why he has hope.”

In an interview after his immigration hearing, Khan Suri said he hopes to live a “happy, cheerful life” as an academic.

“Someday, somewhere I’m sure I will get justice,” Khan Suri told The Hoya last Wednesday.

text:
By REBECCA SANTANA and SEUNG MIN KIM

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration plans to limit the number of refugees admitted to the country to 17,500 mostly white South Africans, the administration told Congress Tuesday, as it continues to transform a program that at one point served as a pathway to safety for people fleeing war and strife from countries around the world.

In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America. The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.

The Trump administration has dramatically altered a refugee program that historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support as it welcomed tens of thousands of refugees from countries around the world to new lives in America, and instead the administration has transformed it into a vehicle to resettle white South Africans in America.

The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S.

Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration’s decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.

“For more than four decades, America’s refugee program has provided a lifesaving pathway for people fleeing violence and persecution,” said Naomi Steinberg, HIAS vice president for refugee and immigration policy and advocacy, in a statement. “But again, this administration is diminishing and distorting this legacy in service of its political whims. That is why we will never stop speaking out for a return to a program that welcomes refugees from around the world who have been persecuted because of who they are and what they believe.”

Presidents set the cap on how many refugees the U.S. will approve through the program each year, and historically, they’ve allocated those numbers across various geographic regions while factoring in wars or conflicts that spark humanitarian needs around the globe. HIAS said an average of 92,000 people a year have been admitted to the U.S. since the program was launched in 1980.

Last year, the Trump administration initially set the cap at 7,500 — again predominantly Afrikaners — but later increased the total to 17,500 after it said that “unforeseen developments in South Africa created an emergency refugee situation.”

During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration built the system back up, setting a goal of admitting 125,000 refugees in Biden’s last year in office.

When Trump once again returned to the White House, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been slated to come to the U.S. Then the administration reopened the program, but limited it to white South Africans.

Afrikaners are the descendants of mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first arrived in South Africa in the 17th century. They are just one of South Africa’s white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.

title: After ICE shooting, Venezuelan man's quick release from Austin hospital raises questions

text:
About four hours after Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was admitted to an Austin hospital with a gunshot wound, the Venezuelan man was discharged Sunday and taken 135 miles south to an immigration detention center where some detainees have complained about inadequate medical care.

The bullet fired by a federal immigration officer is still lodged to his back, according to Garces Perez and his immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. After he began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” Garces Perez was taken to another hospital for treatment, the lawyer said.

His lawyers, Democratic leaders and immigrant advocates have questioned whether Garces Perez received proper medical treatment and whether he was taken into custody before he could fully heal.

Garces Perez was working as a DoorDash delivery driver when he was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during a traffic stop in North Austin. His lawyer said that Garces Perez did have a work permit and a driver’s license but expired in December. After he was taken to the hospital, Lincoln-Goldfinch said she and Garces Perez’s wife were not allowed to visit him.

On Monday evening, after he called into a news conference to say that he has not received any medication, he was transported to a second hospital after he complained of losing feeling on the left side of his body, his lawyer said.

“Wilber tells me that after he spoke publicly, guards at the Pearsall detention center forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

By Tuesday afternoon, Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela was back at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall.

Doctors who have treated immigrants injured by ICE say that while Garces Perez’s treatment may seem harsh, it appears that medical staff and ICE officers treated him like any other person in this situation.

DHS released a statement Tuesday saying Garces Perez is receiving “medical care around the clock, including pain medication.” The statement also said ICE officers do not control the medical treatment for the bullet lodged in his back.

“ICE does not and would not advise, nor be the authority on, a medical procedure for an illegal alien at a hospital,” the statement said.

Marc F. Stern, a doctor and an assistant professor at the University of Washington, said he doesn’t like to see any patient recovering in a detention center, but unless ICE forced the medical staff to release Garces Perez prematurely it is common for patients with a lodged bullet to be discharged. He added that in many cases attempting to remove a bullet does more harm than good.

“We’d all like to believe the system works but under the current administration the rule of law has suffered a lot,” Stern said. “So do we have the confidence that all of this is happening correctly? I would hope so.”

Brian Elmore, a doctor who has treated injured immigrants in Mexico and is a current Global Emergency Medical fellow at the University of Virginia, said he recently discharged a Maryland man who also had a bullet lodged in his back. He said it is important to have a post-discharge treatment plan.

“In somebody that isn’t detained, these patients would have close follow-up with their trauma surgery team and be discharged with pain medication,” he said. “The problem with these patients is that they are often discharged in conditions where they receive inappropriate or absent medical care.”

Naureen Shah, director of immigration policy with the American Civil Liberties Union, recently wrote a report titled “Agents of Chaos and Cruelty,” which she said documents ICE’s pattern of excessive force and civil rights violations under the Trump administration.

Shah said that even if a doctor discharged him, the detention center Garces Perez is in is not ideal.

“It’s probably one of the worst places to take a person who has a bullet lodged to his back,” she said.

The ACLU recently filed a $10 million claim against the ICE facility in Pearsall, saying a client experienced medical neglect and mistreatment in detention.

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, said Tuesday that ICE should immediately release Garces Perez, who has a pending removal order and has applied for political asylum, so that he can “receive medical treatment.”

“Mr. Garces Perez is not receiving the care he needs in detention,” Casar wrote in a letter signed by over 100 Democratic members of Congress. “While he remains in the United States, he should be allowed to receive medical care and pursue all legal options available to him. Finally, Mr. Garces Perez and the ICE agent responsible must remain in Texas until a thorough, independent investigation into the shooting is complete.”

Gov. Greg Abbott, who has ordered state police to work with ICE officers operating in Texas, has not directly discussed the shooting. Asked about the shooting at an unrelated Tuesday news conference, the governor said details remain “sketchy.”

“There’s not full information yet available about exactly what happened and what the status is right now,” he added. “But we’ll work to stay on top of it.”

Tuesday afternoon, Austin Mayor Kirk Watson and the city’s police chief, Lisa Davis, addressed questions about Garces Perez’s medical treatment.

Speaking at a news conference, Davis said it is hospital policy to not allow family members to visit patients who are detained while receiving medical attention, but she could not speak to why Garces Perez was released when he was.

“If APD were to bring someone in that was under arrest and detained … if families showed up, no, they would not be allowed to come back and talk with that person,” Davis said. “That is what the protocol is.”

Watson said that when he arrived at Dell Seton Medical Center, he was concerned to hear that Garces Perez’s wife was not given any update on his condition and was seeking clarity on rumors that Garces Perez had died.

“By the time I got down to the hospital, he had obviously already been taken away from the hospital by the ICE officers, and nobody had been told that — I may have been the first one that was told,” Watson said. “That wasn’t part of the hospital operation, it was because of my pursuit of trying to get to the truth about what was going on.”

During the news conference, Davis also showed new footage from an off-duty APD detective’s dashcam and cell phone camera, as well as the bodycam footage from APD officers who arrived on the scene.

The off-duty detective’s footage first showed Garces Perez pulled over and two ICE officers speaking with him. Davis said there was a brief vehicle pursuit, which APD is still investigating, that finished under an overpass where the shots were fired.

Davis confirmed that there is no evidence of a foot chase.

The bodycam footage was muted as APD officers first interact with the ICE officers, but the audio began as APD officers removed Garces Perez from his vehicle and provided medical help. The ICE officers had not provided medical assistance prior to APD’s arrival. The footage was muted to preserve APD’s investigation, Davis said.

APD officers then called 911, and emergency medical services arrived three minutes later.

Elmore questioned why ICE officers didn’t immediately provide aid.

“Any law enforcement officer should have basic first aid skills and been capable of assessing Wilber for life-threatening injuries and administering aid,” he said.

title: Federal judge questions ICE credibility in hearing on Oregon arrests - Minnesota Lawyer
description:
Preliminary injunction bars ICE warrantless arrests without evasion risk.
Four immigrants testify about ICE arrest encounters in Oregon.
The Ashland arrest was among four arrests described in testimony and declarations that lawyers said showed that federal agents have continued making arrests that violate the injunction.
“We’re confident that the judge is going to make a good decision that restores the validity of the force of his injunction, preventing warrantless arrests in Oregon,” Cunnings said.
They are asking the court to order the government to provide all documents related to warrantless arrests, including body camera footage.
text:
In Brief

Judge Mustafa Kasubhai questions federal government’s credibility.

Innovation Law Lab alleges routine warrantless arrests in Oregon.

Preliminary injunction bars ICE warrantless arrests without evasion risk.

Four immigrants testify about ICE arrest encounters in Oregon.

PORTLAND, Ore. — A federal deportation officer acknowledged under oath in federal court that his written report for the arrest of a man in Ashland was inaccurate, prompting U.S. District Court Judge Mustafa Kasubhai to question the federal government’s credibility in documenting warrantless immigration arrests in Oregon.

“Right now your client [the federal government] doesn’t have a lot of credibility when it comes to documentation,” Kasubhai said during closing arguments Sept. 21, referencing the officer’s testimony and other evidence heard during a two-day hearing.

The testimony and arguments came as lawyers for Innovation Law Lab claimed the federal government is “routinely, openly and brazenly” violating a preliminary injunction prohibiting warrantless immigration arrests in the state. The organization sued the Trump administration after Operation Black Rose began, a monthslong federal immigration enforcement campaign conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that started in late September 2025 and resulted in more than 1,500 arrests statewide.

Kasubhai on Feb. 4 granted a preliminary injunction barring U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from conducting warrantless arrests in Oregon unless agents first determine that a specific person is likely to evade authorities before a warrant can be obtained.

The government has “not halted their illegal warrantless arrest policy and practice,” wrote lawyers with Innovation Law Lab in a motion filed Sept. 4. “In fact, the Defendants have doubled down on their illegal policy or practice by issuing instructions to their agents that blatantly violate the Court’s injunction with respect to the subclass.”

They also cite data from the Portland Immigration Rights Council and the Deportation Data Project showing continued and growing arrest activity after the injunction. There were 109 arrests in January, 41 arrests in February, 30 in March, 64 in April, 83 in May, 186 in June and 174 in July.

The Trump administration arrested a record number of people across the U.S. in July.

Alyssa Walker Keller, co-executive director for PIRC, wrote in a declaration and testified in court that after “unprecedented” reported detentions in the fall and winter, there was a “sudden drop” in reports of detentions to the organization’s hotline in February 2026.

“While detentions were still happening there were less than five per week. This lasted for around two to three months. We believe that this was in large part due to the preliminary injunction issued by the District Court,” Walker Keller said.

The hotline has now experienced a “sustained increase” in calls since May, she said.

Walker Keller said most reports involve arrests after a traffic stop in the street, at a local courthouse, or in public parking lots.

The Ashland arrest was among four arrests described in testimony and declarations that lawyers said showed that federal agents have continued making arrests that violate the injunction. Lawyers said testimony from the government’s witness, a deportation officer identified only as J.G., also confirmed the government has failed to follow the reporting ordered by Kasubhai in February.

Four immigrants in Oregon testify in court about ICE enounters

Innovation Law Lab’s motion cites declarations from individuals who describe being boxed in by vehicles, handcuffed, searched and transported before federal agents even confirmed who they were.

The four individuals testified during an eight-hour evidentiary hearing on Sept. 18.

The witnesses included a Medford McDonald’s employee who filed a declaration saying he was boxed in by two vans around 4:05 a.m. on June 13 as he arrived for work. The man, identified only as CJVM, testified in federal court remotely, describing himself as a two-year resident of Medford with a wife and two daughters who first arrived in the country in May 2024 seeking political asylum.

CJVM, who said he no longer works for the restaurant, remembered five men and one woman surrounding his vehicle. He acknowledged reaching over to the passenger seat to try to reach his cellphone to record as officers began to shout. He estimated 30 seconds passed before agents broke the driver-side window.

CJVM said agents forcibly grabbed his arm and handcuffed him.

Agents took a picture of his face and eventually ran his information, discovering he had an active asylum application and was complying with release terms. CJVM said agents apologized and let him go. He also said the same cars kept showing up at the McDonald’s parking lot at the same time for about three consecutive weekends, prompting the manager to arrange transportation for employees to reduce risk when driving to work.

CJVM said in court that he was “still afraid” and had “kept the trauma of what happened that day.”

Another man, identified only as HDGH, said he was arrested alongside a friend, MTM, after they were followed by ICE officers from a Walmart parking lot after buying supplies for a fishing trip on July 26.

The 22-year-old said in court he has lived in Medford since 2021, except for six months when he lived in California.

Agents followed the two for 30 minutes to Emigrant Lake, he recalled. HDGH said agents handcuffed both men and identified the men only after they were taken to the Medford ICE office.

HDGH said agents “tried to pressure” them to self-deport, offering money, but both refused. He described the agents as “angry” after he refused, when asked to describe why he felt pressured.

“When we got to Portland, they said they had to let us go and let us go a few blocks from the office. I understand that a federal judge ordered ICE to release us and that is the only reason we were released,” HDGH said in his declaration.

A Eugene resident, HFMJ, said he works as a landscaper to support three children. He and his roommate were traveling to work around 7:15 a.m. on July 3 when ICE vehicles began following their car. HFMJ said agents arrested his coworker and then approached the car.

“They told me to ‘get out of the car, we’re arresting you. We have an arrest warrant.’ But they never showed me any papers,” HFMJ said.

HFMJ said in court he was not asked his name or anything about his identity before being handcuffed. Agents did not pull their IDs or identify the two men until they were at the ICE office.

HFMJ also described being pressured to sign documentation he did not understand. Kasubhai questioned if officers explained he was being asked to sign a voluntary deportation order. HFMJ said they did not.

He was released, and now every Monday reports to ICE with an app on his cellphone as a condition of that release, HFMJ said.

And JCCV said he was arrested after leaving the parking lot of a Walmart in Hood River on June 19.

The 34-year-old has lived in The Dalles for a year and a half, according to his testimony.

JCCV said he has an ongoing asylum case. The man said he was also approved for Temporary Protected Status but no longer has TPS after the Trump administration terminated it for Venezuela. JCCV said his work authorization has not expired. JCCV said his wife and his children, a 10-year-old daughter and 14-year-old son, live with him in The Dalles.

JCCV, a delivery driver for Walmart through the Spark app and also a DoorDash and Instacart driver, remembered being cut off in the road as he returned to pick up another order.

JCCV said officers took his belongings and put his hands in handcuffs without asking for ID or showing any warrant.

He said agents took him to Cascade Locks, about 25 minutes away, before he was first questioned and asked his name. Agents then drove JCCV to Portland, where he waited for hours and was told to sign a paper.

JCCV said he was “intimidated” into signing and then taken to the Tacoma detention center. At Tacoma, JCCV said an officer gave him documents eight or 10 days into detention describing the arrest. It included false information, he said, claiming that he was in a Toyota Camry. He was driving a 2010 Toyota Corolla.

JCCV told the court that the owner of the car in the paperwork is his brother and that, after reviewing the paperwork, he believes he was mistakenly detained. He said his brother was at the same place for the same work at the same time.

JCCV has since been released from detention.

Deportation officer testifies in court and acknowledges authoring inaccurate report

The government called deportation officer JG as its witness. The deportation officer said he currently works out of the Medford office and said he’s been with ICE for 11 months. He is a former Grants Pass police officer and former officer with the Department of Veterans’ Affairs, according to his testimony.

He said he has 15 years of experience total as a law enforcement officer.

JG said he was physically present in the encounters involving HDGH and CJVM.

In the case of CJVM, JG said officers had run the license plate “a couple weeks” before the encounter. Their target, he said, had a final order for removal. CJVM was not that target, he acknowledged.

Agents had a photo of the target but said it was dark out and that CJVM placed a hand over his face, limiting agents when they attempted to identify the driver. He estimated CJVM was handcuffed for two minutes.

In the arrest of HDGH, JG testified that officers that morning were running license plates of cars in the Medford Walmart lot. They ran the plate of the car HDGH was in and discovered the registered owner, MTM, was reportedly in the country unlawfully.

Officers followed the vehicle to Emigrant Lake because ICE has instituted a policy barring vehicle stops. That policy came in the wake of two fatal ICE shootings in Maine and Houston.

In court, JG acknowledged he authored a report about the arrest that would make it seem as if he already knew who HDGH was prior to the encounter.

JG said he wrote the narrative for the driver and “pretty much” wrote it identical to the narrative for HDGH’s arrest.

JG, reading the narrative, said he had written that the Medford office had initiated an investigation to locate and apprehend HDGH. That was not possible, he said.

“I did not even know he existed,” JG said.

Judge also questions government claiming warrants perpetual

The judge also ordered supplemental briefs on Sept. 18, which were discussed Sept. 21, after Assistant U.S. Attorney Ariana N. Garousi argued that a 2023 warrant for JCCV was still valid. That 2023 warrant preceded an eight-day detention when he first arrived in the United States.

The judge said when someone is released from custody it “generally means” a warrant is resolved. If someone is wanted back in custody, would another warrant not then have to be issued, he asked?

Garouisi argued that yes, a previous warrant in an immigrant’s file, even if it has already been executed, can be used for future arrests. Garouisi cited a federal law that reads the Attorney General may, at any time, revoke a bond or parole, rearrest the alien under the original warrant, and detain the alien.

Kasubhai said the precondition is a revocation of a bond or parole. He questioned where in the evidence it showed JCCV’s bond or parole was revoked.

Jordan Cunnings with Innovation Law Lab described the argument as “pretty astonishing.”

“The government is making a pretty astonishing argument that once they have probable cause to arrest someone, even if they’ve later determined that person is not a flight risk or a danger to the community and can live at peace while their immigration proceedings are ongoing, that initial warrant can be used again at any time to detain someone for any reason or for no reason at all,” she said. “The law doesn’t support that, nor does the Constitution.”

Innovation Law Lab asks court for more reporting as relief

Innovation Law Lab is asking Kasubhai to enforce the injunction against the federal government to protect other immigrants in Oregon who they say are being harmed every day.

They said the administration is failing to fully comply with the injunction’s reporting requirements, which required a report of the facts and circumstances surrounding warrantless immigration arrests conducted in Oregon every 30 days.

Of the more than 500 arrests in Oregon since February, the government has reported about 25 as warrantless, according to its testimony.

Innovation Law Lab’s motion argues that ICE has not consistently provided the required documentation for warrantless arrests and has not produced complete records when plaintiffs requested information on April 20, May 18, July 10, and Aug. 21 regarding specific civil immigration arrests they believed were warrantless.

Cunnings said Innovation Law Lab was happy to see “the depth of the unreliability of the documents” the government is producing and “falsification of information” come to light.

“We’re confident that the judge is going to make a good decision that restores the validity of the force of his injunction, preventing warrantless arrests in Oregon,” Cunnings said.

Innovation Law Lab said the government is violating the order in two ways, repeatedly conducting warrantless arrests and failing to document and report them. They are asking the court to order the government to provide all documents related to warrantless arrests, including body camera footage.

JG said Oregon deportation officers received body cameras about a month ago.

On Sept. 4, the judge ordered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to turn over discovery about warrantless arrests in Oregon ahead of the Sept. 18 hearing, and ordered the administration to produce any document redacted or withheld in unredacted form within 7 days of the order.

He also ordered the names, contact information and narrative descriptions of events of any noncitizens in documents related to events that took place Oct. 29 through Oct. 31, 2025, when one of the plaintiffs, M-J-M-A, was arrested in Woodburn, as well as the names of any agents, from documents related to that same period.

On Sept. 21, Kasubhai ordered additional supplemental briefs be filed within seven days and said he would work on issuing his order.

Presidents set the cap on how many refugees the U.S. will approve through the program each year, and historically, they’ve allocated those numbers across various geographic regions while factoring in wars or conflicts that spark humanitarian needs around the globe. HIAS said an average of 92,000 people a year have been admitted to the U.S. since the program was launched in 1980.

Last year, the Trump administration initially set the cap at 7,500 — again predominantly Afrikaners — but later increased the total to 17,500 after it said that “unforeseen developments in South Africa created an emergency refugee situation.”

During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration built the system back up, setting a goal of admitting 125,000 refugees in Biden’s last year in office.

When Trump once again returned to the White House, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been slated to come to the U.S. Then the administration reopened the program, but limited it to white South Africans.

Afrikaners are the descendants of mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first arrived in South Africa in the 17th century. They are just one of South Africa’s white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.

text:
A month after a man was shot and killed by a federal agent in Maine, his family learned that one of the officer’s bullets had struck his young daughter’s empty car seat.

Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian man, was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer on July 13 at an intersection in Biddeford.

“The only justification given for Johan’s death was that it was in the interest of public safety,” Sean Murphy, an attorney for the family, told some members of Congress on Tuesday. “You know what actually keeps the public safe? Not shooting innocent and law-abiding fathers whose only dream is to build a better life for his family.”

Murphy was one of several people who testified during a public forum focused on recent fatal ICE shootings.

The agent who shot Durán Guerrero was identified as David Brouillette by multiple people who know him. Brouillette has not responded to several requests for comment. The Department of Homeland Security has declined to identify the agent involved.

The forum on Tuesday was convened by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. Since December, Blumenthal and Garcia have hosted five public forums focused on what they have described as “lawless and abusive tactics” by immigration officials under the Trump administration.

A spokesperson for DHS, which oversees ICE, did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday morning about the scheduled forum.

Murphy told the lawmakers that Durán Guerrero had gone to bed early the night of July 12, sharing a quick kiss with his partner Karolina Alvarez while she folded their laundry.

“Neither of them had any clue that kiss was to be their last,” Murphy testified.

Since being retained by the family, Murphy said he’s met Durán Guerrero’s parents, who both attended a public hearing that was held in Biddeford last month by Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, and other House Democrats. Murphy recalled visiting the funeral home and hearing the mother’s cries.

Durán Guerrero’s body was repatriated to Colombia and his family there held a service earlier this month, according to attorney Benjamin Gideon, who is also representing the family.

Gideon said that he and Alvarez watched the service remotely from Maine. He said Alvarez also received several non-evidentiary items from the Office of the Maine Attorney General during an informational meeting on Aug. 27, which is when they learned about the bullet hole in the car seat.

Murphy testified that the attorney general’s office is “is the first and only governmental agency that has confirmed that they are investigating the deadly use of force by a federal agent.”

A spokesperson for the attorney general’s office declined to comment on their investigation Tuesday.

DHS announced in July that its Office of Inspector General was also conducting a routine investigation. Gideon and Murphy said they’ve heard nothing from the federal government in more than two months.

Vice President JD Vance told Maine reporters during a visit in August that the federal government was investigating. His office has not responded to requests for comment since then.

“Apparently, he thought he would blow smoke when he came to Maine,” Gideon said.

Murphy, who previously worked in Puerto Rico as a federal prosecutor, said Tuesday that he has not seen any efforts by the U.S. government to quickly preserve important digital evidence and interview potential witnesses.

“These are all considerations that were standard, but for whatever — well, for very obvious reasons — are not present any more,” Murphy said following a question form Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va. “And we need to bring them back.”

Congressional members also heard testimony on Tuesday from a mother whose son, Ruben Ray Martinez, was shot by ICE in Texas in March 2025, and the children of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was shot by ICE in Houston this summer.

They heard from the parents of Renée Nicole Macklin Good, who was shot while observing federal agents in Minneapolis in January, and from a witness who recorded the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti in the same city less than three weeks later.

“We were told that DHS was going to change,” Blumenthal said during the forum. “We were told it was going to be a more restrained agency. We were told it was going to cut down on violence. Again and again, those promises were proven to be false.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents mistakenly targeted a US citizen in a Chicago suburb on Sunday, leaving him on the ground with various injuries, according to the Evanston Police Department.

Evanston police officers were dispatched Sunday morning after an unknown caller reported hearing two men arguing and someone saying an individual would be taken into custody, according to an Evanston Police Department news release.

When officers arrived at the scene, they found one man on the ground with several bystanders helping him. The man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and Evanston police officers called for an ambulance, the release said.

Witnesses told officers they believed ICE agents were attempting to detain the man, police said.

One responding officer, who was not at the scene, located two SUVs near an intersection and spoke with one person who identified himself as a federal agent conducting a “fugitive investigation.” The person was wearing plain clothes and a vest marked “POLICE” with federal law enforcement markings, according to police.

Agents later determined the man they had targeted was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a US citizen, Evanston police said. He was released.

The Department of Homeland Security told CNN that ICE agents conducting a targeted enforcement operation encountered a person who resembled their target and “immediately identified themselves as law enforcement.”

“The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself,” a DHS spokesperson told CNN. “ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself.”

Surveillance video obtained by CNN appears to show two agents and the man in an upright struggle before federal officials pull him to the ground.

It’s unclear what happens after the man is brought to the ground, as the individuals move out of the camera’s view.

Moments later, at least three drivers pull into the nearby parking lot and exit their vehicles, joining other bystanders, some recording.

An Evanston officer also noticed blood on the agent’s hands, which the federal official said resulted from an injury he received while trying to detain the man, according to the local police news release. The agent declined medical treatment.

Five federal agents were operating in separate vehicles to search the area, police said.

Evanston police officers later contacted the man who had been targeted at a local hospital and an evidence technician photographed and documented his injuries.

DHS said the man refused assistance from ICE agents, but did not address the man’s injuries in its statement. A federal agent also told Evanston police they left the area where protesters began to gather because they feared they would be attacked, according to the release from local police.

“ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” a DHS spokesperson said.

As the Evanston Police Department continues its investigation, officers are preserving available body camera footage and interviewing witnesses, police said.

The incident comes a year after the launch of “Operation Midway Blitz,” the federal government’s immigration crackdown in Chicago and surrounding areas.

This story has been updated with additional information.

authors: Jack Brook, Dorany Pineda, environmental issues, apnews.com, jack-brook, dorany-pineda

text:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A 36-year-old Costa Rican man whose family says he complained of missing insulin shots and meals to manage his diabetes is the third detainee to die in less than six months at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Louisiana.

Carlos Josue Marchena Marchena was found unresponsive Sept. 18 at Winn Correctional Center in Winnfield, ICE said in a statement. It said staff began lifesaving measures before he was taken by ambulance to a hospital where he was later pronounced dead.

The man’s sister, his girlfriend and a detainee held in the cell beside Marchena’s told The Associated Press that he complained of missed meals and shots and not drinking enough water to control his type 1 diabetes as he was moved between facilities in multiple states. Marchena’s condition worsened after he arrived at Winn, and he died less than a week later, his family said.

The official cause of death is pending further medical examination.

The correctional center had recently been found to have fallen short of federal standards, including for medical care, by the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General.

Two other ICE detainees have died at the complex since April.

Nearly 60 ICE detainees have died since January 2025

Marchena is at least the 58th ICE detainee to die since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, according to tracking by AP. Immigrant advocates say the deaths are a sign that authorities are failing to properly oversee the detention of tens of thousands of immigrants swept up in the administration’s aggressive deportation strategy.

ICE said Marchena’s medical care was appropriate. “Marchena received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals,” an agency statement said.

Sufficient food, water and insulin at regular intervals is crucial with type 1 diabetes for managing blood sugar levels to avoid a life-threatening health condition, said Dr. Rajesh Garg, who heads the diabetes unit at the Harbor-UCLA Medical Center.

“If they are under any stress, then they need even more care and then they need to test their blood sugar at regular times,” Garg said. “If there isn’t proper food and water, that is going to stress his system.”

Scott Sutterfield, a spokesperson for LaSalle Corrections, the contractor managing the facility with the Winn Parish Sheriff’s Office, said the death is under review and declined to answer questions. He said the company is committed to “the highest standards of care.”

Winn Parish Sheriff’s Office and the Winn Parish Coroner’s Office did not respond to requests for comment.

Medical examiners and coroners have ruled diabetes was a contributing factor in at least six of the ICE detainees’ deaths during Trump’s second presidency. Detainees with diabetes have frequently complained in court filings of inconsistent access to insulin and other medications.

The deaths come amid mounting scrutiny of ICE detention facilities and whether they are medically neglecting detainees and forcing them to live in inhumane conditions, charges that ICE denies.

Detainee says man was vomiting and looking pale

Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General issued a report in June that said an unannounced inspection at Winn found violations of standards governing medical care, food service, use of force and other subjects. Among violations, it reported frozen food not being stored properly.

Medical staff at Winn failed to keep updated treatment documents and laboratory testing records, which could “negatively impact detainee health care and safety,” the report warned. It said ICE agreed with nine recommendations to improve conditions at Winn, and had implemented several of them.

Marchena’s sister, Franciny Marchena, said her brother told her no one was checking his blood sugar levels to ensure they were stable.

“A person who is healthy and taking their diabetes medication has no reason to collapse the way my brother did,” she told AP, speaking in Spanish from Costa Rica.

His sister said his health began to worsen about two weeks ago when he was in an immigration detention center in Michigan and was put in a security cell after an argument with another detainee.

Detainee says man was vomiting and looking pale

After being transferred to Winn, Marchena told his sister and girlfriend that he had chest pain and was not getting enough to drink or eat, including because the food was sometimes spoiled. It was not known if he had an underlying heart condition.

Marchena also voiced these concerns to Luis Herrera Andy, a Honduran man detained at Winn in the adjacent cell, who noted Marchena only received irregular insulin shots.

A doctor gave Marchena pills for his chest pain but he returned angry, Herrera said, recalling his words: “This place is crap. They don’t help you with anything here. You could even die here.”

The day before Marchena was found dead, he had stomach pain, headaches, chills, and was vomiting, Herrera said. He was a pale purple color and wet with sweat.

Hours before his death, Marchena’s girlfriend Ana Leon Castro said, he called around midnight to say the pills weren’t helping.

“All they gave him was a pill — that was it for the treatment,” Leon Castro said.

Cardiac arrest — when the heart suddenly stops pumping — can occur from too little or too much insulin in a diabetic person, said Garg at Harbor-UCLA. Vomiting, headaches, nausea and stomach pain are all symptoms that can indicate a life-threatening insulin deficiency, though there could be other causes such as an infection.

He leaves behind four children

Marchena was the first Costa Rican detainee to die in an ICE facility under Trump’s second presidency.

He entered the U.S. without legal status in February 2021, ICE said in a statement.

ICE said Marchena had prior misdemeanor convictions for retail fraud and property destruction before he was arrested in January by the Ottawa County Sheriff’s Department in Michigan for assault. In July, an immigration judge ordered him to be deported, according to DHS.

His sister Franciny said Marchena, who worked as a ride service driver and had four children, had requested bail and voluntary deportation to Costa Rica, but it was denied. ICE did not respond when asked about the denial.

___

Pineda reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press reporter Ryan Foley contributed from Iowa.

text:
By MORIAH BALINGIT

WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge in Rhode Island has struck down a Trump administration directive that would have barred some immigrants from accessing certain federal programs, including Head Start preschools, community health clinics and adult education initiatives.

U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy, who was appointed by President Donald Trump in 2019, temporarily barred his administration from moving forward with the rule last year, so it was never implemented. On Monday, she made the injunction permanent.

Officials from the Republican administration had said the directive would stop “illegal aliens” from accessing federal benefits by reclassifying broad swaths of social services programs under a Clinton-era law, the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act.

But the rule also would have swept up many immigrants in the U.S. legally, including work and student visa holders. It also would have barred services from Temporary Protected Status holders, who are granted work permits if the U.S. government determines conditions in their home country are too dangerous to return, along with recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, who were brought to the country illegally as children and receive temporary protection from deportation and work authorization.

Those groups, which are considered “nonqualified aliens” under the law, are already unable to access full Medicaid benefits and federally funded food aid and cash assistance.

The Trump administration issued its directive in July 2025. Democratic attorneys general from 20 states and the District of Columbia sued.

They said the change upended three decades of policy allowing people to access community health clinics, domestic violence shelters and Head Start centers without proving their immigration status. They warned the harms could spread, deterring any immigrant from seeking services and throwing up barriers even for U.S. citizens unable to document their legal status. The new rules also would have put administrative burdens on underfunded social service agencies, including Head Start operators, which might have been forced to close if they were unable to comply with the directive’s new requirements, the lawsuit said.

In her ruling, McElroy declared the directive “unlawful” and said the Trump administration did not follow the proper avenues to rewrite the rules. She called the administration’s actions “procedurally invalid.” She added that the administration still could pursue rule changes through the federal notice-and-comment process, which officials bypassed when they issued the directive last year.

Requests for comment were sent to the departments named as defendants in the wide-ranging lawsuit. The Administration for Children and Families, a division of the Department of Health and Human Services that oversees Head Start, said it does not comment on ongoing litigation. The Labor Department referred inquiries to the Justice Department, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a statement, New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was among those who sued, hailed the judge’s ruling.

“From cancer screenings to food banks to early childhood education, the federal government’s attempts to decimate the social safety net would have been catastrophic for working families,” James said.

text:
AUSTIN (Nexstar) — At least three agencies are now investigating Sunday’s ICE shooting in north Austin, as questions remain about what led federal immigration agents to shoot a Venezuelan food delivery driver.

On Sunday, federal immigration agents shot 28-year-old Venezuelan national Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in north Austin while he was working as a food delivery driver. Outside of that, few details have been confirmed about what led to the encounter between Garces Perez and ICE agents.

Who is investigating?

According to DHS’s initial statement, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is leading the investigation with Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) assistance. Austin police and the Texas Rangers are also conducting their own review, creating multiple reviews into the same shooting.

“I think DHS is 100% capable of doing it fully and fairly without (FBI assistance),” Federal Law Enforcement Officers Association (FLEOA) President Mathew Silverman told KXAN on Monday. FLEOA represents all sorts of federal law enforcement officers, including ones who work at DHS. “It just seems that FBI does have their hand in a lot of this stuff and FBI also has the resources and abilities to be able to do things a lot quicker.”

However, several Democratic elected officials and immigrant-rights advocates have expressed skepticism of the federal government investigating previous ICE shootings this year.

That skepticism has emerged elsewhere in Texas. In August, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said federal officials failed to provide any information on the July 7 fatal ICE shooting of 52-year-old Mexican immigrant Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston.

“From my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate,” Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said at a news conference on Sunday.

During the same event, Lisa Davis, Austin’s police chief, said the Austin Police Department’s Special Investigations Unit, which typically investigates officer-involved shootings, was on scene and working with the Texas Rangers.

“The city is investigating this like it would any officer-involved shooting,” Watson said in an interview with KXAN on Monday. “I’m appreciative that the Texas Rangers are also involved in this because that will make our investigation more robust… I want everybody to know that I think that Austinites need to feel safe and I think an investigation that has real credibility is the thing that will bring about that feeling of, well, a greater feeling of safety.”

In a response to Watson’s comments, DHS posted on social media, “If any Austinites feel unsafe in their city, it is because sanctuary politicians have enabled criminal illegal aliens to roam their streets with impunity.” ICE has not responded to our inquiries or requests for comment.

Austin leaders hold news conference to discuss the city’s investigation

Editor’s Note: The above video contains the exact location and nature of the apparent bullet wound as first responders work to treat the man shot by ICE.

Austin leaders held a joint news conference Tuesday to provide an update into the investigation — including releasing footage taken by an off-duty APD detective and body camera footage of the first officers arriving on scene.

“We believe that it is important that we are transparent as possible surrounding the incident that involved ICE this past Sunday,” Watson said. “Austinites deserve to know what happened,” Watson said at the conference.

APD Chief Davis released that footage during Tuesday’s conference, which captured two black SUVs pulled over to the side of the road in between a blue vehicle that would later to be involved in the shooting.

The off-duty detective then turns into a nearby shopping center and after coming outside, begins rolling on his cellphone, which captured the sound of gunshots. The detective then notifies the department to get officers to the scene.

APD then showed some body camera footage of the first officers arriving at the scene. While the beginning of the footage is muted, you can later hear the officers speaking with the man who was shot.

Davis stated that before the ICE-involved shooing, a pursuit had occurred “though some side neighborhoods.” That footage was not shown Tuesday.

Davis asked that anyone with information on this incident to come forward to help investigators better understand what happened.

APD continues to work with its local, state and federal partners in this investigation.

When asked about the department’s partnership with federal investigators, Davis said they speak daily and APD’s Special Investigations Unit continues to work side by side with the Texas rangers to look through footage.

“Our commitment remains the same,” Davis said. “Follow the facts, follow the evidence and be as transparent and thorough in this investigation.”

Disputes in early reporting

According to Garces Perez’s attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, ICE agents came out of nowhere.

“He was an active DoorDash driver, he was making a delivery. He was in a part of Austin that’s a fairly populated intersection and he said he was driving and large black truck just came and side-swiped him,” Lincoln-Goldfinch told NewsNation on Tuesday. “There were no sirens or lights. He thought it was just an aggressive driver and he pulled over and did a bit of a U-turn and at some point realized that these were police officers.”

Lincoln-Goldfinch claims Garces Perez attempted to comply once he realized who was in the black car, “but they rammed the side of his car again… they rammed him again, and then the officer got out and shot through the passenger side of the car into his back,” she said.

On Sunday night, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, released a statement calling Garces Perez “an illegal alien from Venezuela, who illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal.”

Lincoln-Goldfinch pushed back on those claims, saying he entered the country in 2024 using CBP One, a mobile application for asylum seekers to schedule appointments at designed points of entry on the Southern border. President Donald Trump ended the practice of using CBP One for asylum seekers when he took office.

“He was inspected and admitted to the country. He had a work permit. He was seeking asylum,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said at a news conference. “He changed his address with the immigration court and a notice of hearing was sent to his old address — he didn’t know he had a hearing. So he didn’t go so he got a deportation order in absentia, which is a very common thing.”

On Monday, San Antonio Federal Judge Orlando L. Garcia ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement to not deport Garces Perez, setting a court date for Sept. 30.

Given the discrepancies in early account, Lincoln-Goldfinch says “there needs to be many investigations as well as a lawsuit, which we are filing.”
