title: Amid opposition, Clearfield County commissioners approve ICE contract extension
description:
The Clearfield County commissioners voted Tuesday to extend a contract to operate the Moshannon Valley Processing Center on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after hearing strong public pushback.
The Moshannon Valley Processing Center, with beds for about 1,800 people, is the largest ICE detention center on the east coast.
Clearfield County District Attorney Ryan Sayers was the only speaker in support of continuing the county’s relationship with ICE.
Advocates call on Clearfield County commissioners to vote ‘no’ on ICE contract extension Glass said that he doesn’t fault those in the community who have taken well-paid jobs at the center, but he doesn’t believe the county should be involved in federal immigration policy.
Several members of Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation have been allowed to visit Moshannon Valley this year, after being denied access in the past.
text:
The Clearfield County commissioners voted Tuesday to extend a contract to operate the Moshannon Valley Processing Center on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after hearing strong public pushback.

Speakers called on the board to reject the six-month extension, citing three deaths and complaints about physical and psychological abuse, unfit food, lack of access to adequate health care, and retaliation for protesting the conditions.

The Moshannon Valley Processing Center, with beds for about 1,800 people, is the largest ICE detention center on the east coast. The county serves as a pass-through for about $5 million a month in federal money that ICE pays private prison operator The GEO Group to run the center. The county receives $200,000 a year.

“Those gathered here today represent community members who refuse to stand by,” said Clearfield County resident Sam Mosier, the first of nine speakers. “We stand against these practices, including the use of the Moshannon facility and the inhuman treatment of individuals who are seeking nothing more than a better life for themselves and their families.”

Mosier added the county’s continued involvement would leave a stain on its legacy.

“When history looks back on these times, … this will demonstrate to the world that human dignity matters more to our community and financial gain,” he said.

Clearfield County District Attorney Ryan Sayers was the only speaker in support of continuing the county’s relationship with ICE. He said that as the county’s chief law enforcement officer, he believes immigration laws should be enforced.

“The citizens of Clearfield County deserve leaders and civil servants who will help uphold those laws and support those that do this work each and every day,” Sayers said, noting both of his parents work in the center. “That is why I stand here today with ICE, with the men and women, … that work hard every day to take care of those at the GEO institution and carry out their lawful responsibilities.”

The board voted 2-1 to accept the contract extension. Democratic Commissioner Dave Glass cast the dissenting vote. After the vote, the meeting room erupted in shouts and a chant of “Shame on you.” Absent an affirmative vote, the county’s contract with ICE was set to expire Sept. 28.

Advocates call on Clearfield County commissioners to vote ‘no’ on ICE contract extension

Glass said that he doesn’t fault those in the community who have taken well-paid jobs at the center, but he doesn’t believe the county should be involved in federal immigration policy.

“There’s a right way and a wrong way to do things. This is the wrong way,” he said “We’re in the middle of it. We shouldn’t be in the middle of it. I don’t want to even tangentially support this, and I think there’s a better way.”

Commissioner John Sobel said he didn’t doubt the sincerity of the speakers’ beliefs, but added he doesn’t share their concerns that the facility is poorly or inhumanely run.

“In my many contacts with the folks at GEO, and particularly the director, I have not found evidence of a consistent policy or pattern of behavior of intentional abuse or improper behavior,” Sobel said.

Sobel added that while opponents are concerned about the county taking an administrative fee, which some speakers described as “blood money,” the center provides tax revenue to Decatur Township and the Phillipsburg-Osceola School District.

“If we reject the contract, that makes it easier for GEO to go away, and in the long run, that could impact monies that these other entities are probably dependent on. I’m very uncomfortable doing that,” he said.

Sobel also encouraged those opposed to the agreement with ICE to lobby their U.S. representatives and senators to change federal policy. Several members of Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation have been allowed to visit Moshannon Valley this year, after being denied access in the past.

Democratic U.S. Sen. John Fetterman’s office earlier this month published a letter to acting ICE Director David J. Venturella urging him to ensure the agency paid a local emergency medical clinic for services provided to detainees and staff at Moshannon Valley.

Moshannon Valley Emergency Medical Services is owed more than $230,000 by ICE, Fetterman’s office said, as a result of a lapse in an agreement between the agency and the Veterans Administration, which had handled medical payment processing related to immigration detention.

“We do try to intervene and see if there’s something we can do to help folks there at the institution,” Sobel said. “But in the end, this is ultimately a decision that has to be made at the federal level, and that’s really who you need to be making your argument to.”

More than 10,000 people were processed through Moshannon Valley between January and August, Commissioner Tim Winters noted. The center held 1,711 people on Tuesday, he said, adding that he believes immigration reform is needed.

“This transcends party lines completely. We need comprehensive immigration reform in the United States,” Winter said. “Unfortunately, the situation we are in now involves various federal policies, federal agencies, and I want to be very clear on this: A ‘no’ vote today will have absolutely no effect on the operations of the Moshannon Valley Processing Center. It will continue to operate tomorrow the same as it did yesterday.”

He said a vote against extending the contract would mean the county no longer has the ability to investigate claims of poor conditions, which he said had not been proven.

“Both Commissioner Sobel and myself have went there unannounced, eaten the same food. The claims are overblown,” he said.

Moshannon Valley was built as a privately operated federal prison that opened in 2006 and closed in 2021, after the Biden administration banned new federal contracts with for-profit prison operators.

It reopened later in 2021 as an ICE facility operated by GEO Group under contract with the county, in an arrangement that skirted the private prison ban. The Trump administration reversed the ban in 2025.

Immigration rights advocates note that there’s now evidence that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security intends to buy the facility. The agency issued a request for proposals last month for turnkey detention sites including one in its “Philadelphia Area of Responsibility. According to ICE, that includes all of Pennsylvania, Delaware and West Virginia. DHS said it intends to award 10-year contracts that would allow it to expand operations in the facilities.

And The GEO Group’s CEO, George C. Zoley, told investors in an earnings call in August that the company is in an “active process” to sell some of its facilities, which the company hopes to continue managing under a long-term contract.

Jasmine Rivera, executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, said in a call with reporters last week that she believes the six month contract extension is needed for the parties to complete their due diligence before a sale.

At Tuesday’s meeting, speakers strongly condemned ICE’s policies and practices, comparing it to a concentration camp

Sean Inlow, a retired state police detective, urged the commissioners to reject the contract on “legal, moral and personal grounds.”

Inlow suggested that the arrest and detention of people awaiting due process in the immigration system is criminal.

“If the county commissioners are going to accept this contract and they’re going to support this program, then you are participating in a criminal enterprise,” he said. “In my view, as a state trooper, I could not make those arrests.”

He added that the county’s involvement in the Trump administration’s mass deportation plan reflects badly on its people.

“Personally speaking, I’m sick of this creeping Trumpist intimidation,” Inlow said. “I’m not hopeful, but I hope that you guys decline this contract because what we’re doing is morally wrong, criminally wrong, personally wrong.”

name: Human Rights
title: Deaths in Detention: Mortality Rate for People Detained by ICE More Than Doubles Under ...
description:
The mortality rate for people in ICE custody has more than doubled from the first Trump administration and is at its highest point in more than a decade.
As egregious as the current mortality rate is, it still does not include an accurate death toll resulting from the neglect in ICE detention centers because of hidden deaths like Trejo Ricano’s.
Beyond recorded in-custody deaths, ICE has hidden a growing number of fatalities due to recent shifts in reporting mandates.
That transparency is critical if we are to achieve the radical reform to put a stop to the alarming rise in deaths connected to ICE detention.
Amid record deaths, documented abuses, and signs of profit-seeking, the expansion of immigration detention facilities demands urgent action.
text:
While detained at Stewart Detention Center in Georgia, Prisciliano Trejo Ricano experienced severe symptoms, including coughing up blood and severe pain. After weeks struggling to access medical care, he was transferred to a nearby hospital. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) formally released him from custody when he was in a coma. He died from an aggressive form of leukemia less than two weeks later.

Trejo Ricano’s name does not appear on the ICE website as one of the people who died while in ICE custody, and ICE will not be investigating what led to his death so shortly after being released from Stewart due to recent policy changes.

The mortality rate for people in ICE custody has more than doubled from the first Trump administration and is at its highest point in more than a decade. At least 57 people have died in immigration detention since the start of the second term, more than double the number of deaths recorded from the previous four years combined. As egregious as the current mortality rate is, it still does not include an accurate death toll resulting from the neglect in ICE detention centers because of hidden deaths like Trejo Ricano’s.

Beyond recorded in-custody deaths, ICE has hidden a growing number of fatalities due to recent shifts in reporting mandates. In 2021, the Department of Homeland Security implemented a federal policy requiring ICE to report and investigate any deaths occurring within 30 days of release from ICE custody. This measure ensured that ICE could be held accountable and prevented it from releasing severely ill individuals to dodge accountability and reporting requirements. The Trump administration rescinded that policy in June in yet another move to evade oversight and transparency.

By eliminating these reporting requirements, ICE shields itself from accountability for the human cost of its medical failures. ICE is then incentivized to discharge critically ill individuals just before they die, artificially skewing official mortality statistics. Ultimately, erasing these accountability metrics only emboldens the agency to continue operating with minimal transparency, leaving detained immigrants even more vulnerable to systemic neglect and abuse.

Despite federal efforts to obstruct meaningful oversight and obscure these fatalities, the ACLU remains dedicated to exposing the full extent of hidden deaths in ICE custody. Through targeted Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and litigation, we are fighting to ensure the deaths of these individuals are tracked so that ICE is held accountable for the true cost of its detention conditions.

In 2022, we submitted our first FOIA request seeking more information about ICE’s pattern of deathbed releases. This request sought documents related to four deaths, along with additional documents that would lead to more information about ICE’s policies and practices around these deaths and potentially uncover additional unreported deaths. When the government failed to respond to this FOIA request, we filed a lawsuit to obtain responsive documents. After successfully obtaining some records, the ACLU submitted another FOIA request for similar information in July this year. In addition to requesting records related to certain deathbed releases, that FOIA request also asks for documents relating to the latest elimination of the requirement for ICE to report and investigate the deaths of those people who die shortly after being released from detention. The ACLU is committed to shed light on these hidden deaths. That transparency is critical if we are to achieve the radical reform to put a stop to the alarming rise in deaths connected to ICE detention.

Alongside the rapid growth of detention operations, the administration has systemically dismantled key internal oversight mechanisms within DHS. The limited oversight mechanisms that were in place to ensure accountability in immigration detention, including the Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman and the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, have been effectively gutted, shutting down essential avenues for public complaints and accountability.

“These offices have obstructed immigration enforcement by adding bureaucratic hurdles and undermining DHS’s mission,” a DHS spokesperson said in defense of the cuts. "Rather than supporting law enforcement efforts, they often function as internal adversaries that slow down operations.” By stripping away internal checks and balances, DHS has created a vacuum of oversight, furthering concerns that officers are now empowered to operate in the shadows.

Compounding with this lack of oversight, the rapid expansion of detention facilities has further strained already problematic ICE operations. The agency is consistently failing to meet basic human needs, subjecting tens of thousands of people every day to systemic and dangerous medical neglect, unacceptable sanitation conditions, and unsafe housing. For many, these dire conditions have resulted in preventable medical crises and fatalities. Without radical systemic reform and restored oversight, the current number of deaths in and outside of detention will almost certainly continue to climb.

Environmental and operational conditions inside detention facilities directly contribute to the surge in rising deaths. Overcrowding and staffing shortages create dangerous conditions for people in detention. Unsanitary conditions mean that disease runs rampant, and several facilities have reported outbreaks of measles and tuberculosis that have triggered multi-week quarantines. For those with preexisting medical or mental health conditions, slow response times and inadequate care can turn manageable illnesses into life threatening emergencies. In addition to medical neglect, reports document rampant physical abuse, excessive force, and solitary confinement. These egregious and inhumane conditions coerce people into abandoning their immigration and asylum claims and signing voluntary departure orders to third countries.

Facing increased scrutiny, DHS has also recently announced a pause on the purchase of additional warehouses for immigration detention. Still, some of the facilities the agency has already acquired will continue to be developed for mass detention. Amid record deaths, documented abuses, and signs of profit-seeking, the expansion of immigration detention facilities demands urgent action. We encourage members of the House and Senate to co-sponsor the Dignity for Detained Immigrants Act. The bill would repeal mandatory detention, end family detention, and create a presumption of release and impose a higher burden of proof to detain primary caregivers and vulnerable populations. It would also phase out the use of private detention facilities and jails over a three-year period and require DHS to establish civil detention standards that provide, at minimum, the level of protection in the American Bar Association’s Civil Immigration Detention Standards. The bill would also mandate the DHS inspector general to conduct unannounced inspections with meaningful penalties for failure to comply with standards and require DHS to admit members of congress to detention facilities for unannounced inspections. The question is no longer whether the system is broken, but whether we are willing to confront and dismantle what it has become.

WASHINGTON — On Sept. 25 and Sept. 29, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals is facing a direct test of executive accountability in two high-stakes J.G.G. v. Trump hearings. Both hearings stem from the Trump administration’s March 2025 decision to invoke the wartime Alien Enemies Act to send more than 100 Venezuelan men to CECOT, El Salvador’s notorious mega-prison, without due process and in defiance of D.C. District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg’s order to halt the removal flights. The American Civil Liberties Union and ACLU of D.C. are counsel in this case.

The Sept. 25 hearing focuses on whether the men sent to CECOT are entitled to finally get hearings, either remotely or back in the United States, to show that they are not part of the Tren de Aragua gang and that their removal from the United States under the Alien Enemies Act without a hearing was illegal.

The Sept. 29 hearing focuses on accountability — specifically, whether Trump officials will face consequences for openly defying a federal judge. It will be en banc, meaning all 11 active judges will hear the argument — a procedure rarely used in the D.C. Circuit.

More than 200 former judges have filed an amicus brief urging the court not to let the administration escape accountability. In opinions issued in connection with prior proceedings in this case, judges on the circuit have already written that the government’s actions forming the basis of Judge Boasberg’s contempt inquiry raised “grave rule-of-law concerns.” As Judge Pan wrote, “When the political branches cease to honor the judgments and decisions of the judiciary, the carefully calibrated structure of our government collapses, and we are no longer a society that is protected by the rule of law.”

text:
SEATTLE — A federal judge in Seattle on Tuesday tossed the Trump administration’s lawsuit against Washington seeking the state’s voter rolls, in line with many rulings across the country.

This marks the 25th case that the U.S. Department of Justice has lost in its push to access sensitive voter information. The Justice Department has sued many states for voter rolls, and has yet to have a judge rule in its favor. An appeals court has also ruled against it in a lawsuit against Michigan. The federal government has appealed many of its other losses, as well.

Both sides had been waiting for weeks for a decision from U.S. District Court Judge Kymberly Evanson after an early August hearing in federal court in Seattle.

In her order Tuesday, Evanson, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, said the Trump administration’s argument is “not persuasive as a matter of statutory interpretation, nor is it consistent with the purpose” of federal law.

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown called the decision “the likeliest of victories for democracy.”

“Trump’s DOJ is now 0 for 25 nationwide in efforts to plunder the private information of states’ voters,” he continued in a statement. “We should not have to spend election season defending voters from their president, but victory after victory reminds us there is hope for the rule of law.”

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said the decision “reaffirms that my office has every right to protect voter’s private data.”

“These baseless demands for state voter rolls are part of a broader pattern of federal overreach in states’ elections,” he added. “The DOJ does not have the authority or any reason to interfere with state election administration.”

Since that hearing, the Justice Department has threatened Hobbs over election records, directing him early this month to preserve documents from the 2024 election. Failing to do so “may constitute spoliation of evidence, which may subject you to civil and criminal sanctions,” according to the letter to Hobbs.

The conflict here began last September when Hobbs refused to provide the Trump administration with the personal information contained in the state’s voter rolls.

Hobbs reported he’d be willing to provide voter names, addresses, genders, years of birth, voting records, registration dates and registration numbers. But he wouldn’t give dates of birth, driver license numbers and the last four digits of social security numbers, since that information is protected under Washington law.

In the hearing last month, Tera Heintz, of the Washington state attorney general’s office, called the demand “unprecedented and dangerous.”

“There is simply no authority for DOJ’s claim that they should be able to superintend on a line-by-line, individual-by-individual basis who is allowed to register and vote in state and federal elections,” she said. “That is not DOJ’s authority. It usurps the constitutional authority.”

Hobbs, a Democrat, feared the information would be shared with immigration authorities to fuel President Donald Trump’s crackdown, or that it could be used as pretext to remove voters from the rolls. Trump has repeatedly claimed massive voter fraud without evidence. Federal officials insisted the request was to ensure the state was properly updating its voter list under federal law.

The federal government filed the litigation in December, but the case was delayed for months as the Justice Department’s attorneys failed to serve Washington state officials with the suit.

The Trump administration alleges the records are needed to ensure states are complying with National Voter Registration Act requirements to remove voters who are ineligible from their voter rolls and the Help America Vote Act prohibition on processing voter registration applications without verifying the applicants’ identity. Also the Civil Rights Act of 1960, which federal attorneys claim forces election officials to provide this voter information to the U.S. attorney general if it is demanded.

The state counters that this argument is wrong, that these federal laws don’t authorize the voter roll demand. The Civil Rights Act provision was meant to help prevent racial discrimination in elections in the segregated South.

In the hearing, Evanson noted many other courts have decided similar cases across the country.

“Is there any meaningful basis on which to distinguish this case?” Evanson asked Justice Department attorney Raymond Yang.

He responded that the cases are mostly identical, but other judges have “misconstrued” federal law.

The Department of Justice didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.

At least 16 states led by Republicans have provided or said they would provide their full voter registration lists, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.

This is just one of the state’s flashpoints with the Trump administration over elections. Washington has also been at odds with the president over his unsuccessful efforts to restrict mail-in voting.

text:
The reporters, activists, and politicians all leaned forward in the heat, straining to hear the voice coming out of the cell phone, which was held to a microphone by a woman who alternately listened and translated what the voice was saying. The voice belonged to Wilber Rafael Garcés Peréz, a 28-year-old Venezuelan immigrant who had been shot by an ICE agent the day before in North Austin. Perez had been delivering food for DoorDash when he was stopped, shot in the upper back, then taken to Dell Seton Medical Center. His wife, Elizdar, didn’t know where he was until the next morning, when his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, talked to him at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, in Pearsall, where Perez had been transferred.

Here we all were on Monday afternoon, more than a hundred of us, standing under an oak tree in front of Lincoln-Goldfinch’s law office in Central Austin. It was an astonishing crowd to gather in the middle of a summer’s day, and the sense of frustration and anger was palpable, especially from the two dozen activists holding signs. “ICE: Stop shooting our neighbors” read one; ”Migration is a human right” read another. There were some twenty news cameras—CNN was there and NBC Nightly News—and everyone stood, sweated, and filmed the impassioned words of a dozen speakers, including Lincoln-Goldfinch, Congressmen Greg Casar and Lloyd Doggett, and Garcés Peréz.

Then, by chance, Garcés Peréz called his wife from Pearsall just as Lincoln-Goldfinch opened up the press conference to questions. His attorney asked if he wanted to tell his own story in his own words—and he said yes.

“He’s in a lot of pain,” said Fabiana Meléndez Ruiz, the translator, who does PR for Lincoln-Goldfinch’s firm. “They did not take out the bullet because it was close to his spine.” Garcés Peréz said he had also suffered a fractured clavicle.

He told her his version of what happened. “He was driving to do a DoorDash delivery,” translated Ruiz, “when an SUV rode next to him and tried to hit him, and he thought it was an aggressive driver.” Garcés Peréz said he tried to give up peacefully. “He did a U-turn to try and find a spot to park so that he could go with them, and they basically ran into him and then shot him.”

A few reporters winced and leaned closer. One of them asked if Garcés Peréz received any medical attention at Dell Seton, one of the best hospitals in Austin. Ruiz listened and translated. “He says no. He was complaining that he was in a lot of pain, and he’s like, ‘Are you going to take out the bullet wound?’ And the doctor said, ‘Hey, they’re in a hurry to get you out of here.’ When he arrived at the detention center at 4 a.m., he also complained about the pain, and he had to sleep on the floor.”

The shooting had happened around 12:30 p.m. on Sunday, at the intersection of Anderson Square and Research Boulevard in North Austin, under the highway overpass. In the aftermath, Garcés Peréz’s dark-blue Toyota Corolla sat under the overpass, its passenger-side door bashed in and at least two bullet holes in a back window. The shooting led to protests at the site, which then led to DPS troopers firing pepper balls into a crowd. By Sunday evening, politicians like Casar and state Representative James Talarico were demanding an independent inquiry (Homeland Security Investigations, with the assistance of the FBI, is leading a probe into the matter). Mayor Kirk Watson was visibly angry when he spoke to the public later. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry,” he said.

Earlier in the press conference, Lincoln-Goldfinch told us that Elizdar had wanted her husband to stay home that day, but he had decided to earn some money instead. “At twelve-thirty, she received a call from him, shouting that he had been shot and he was in pain and then the call cut off and she knew nothing else,” said Lincoln-Goldfinch. Elizdar raced to Seton, but guards wouldn’t let her see him. She still hasn’t seen him.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Peréz entered legally in 2024, had a work permit, and was seeking asylum. But then he moved—and though he notified the court of his new address, when the court sent a hearing notification, it went to his former address. “He didn’t go, and so he got the deportation order, which is a very common thing,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Still, the attorney wasn’t going to let the government off the hook. “There is absolutely zero justification for having shot him,” she said loudly. “And this is why we’re calling for a stop to ICE traffic stops. ICE officers are overarmed, overpaid, undertrained, and violent. They don’t know how to safely conduct traffic stops.”

Lincoln-Goldfinch filed a writ of habeas corpus in federal court to get Garcés Peréz out, as well as a temporary restraining order to keep him from being deported, which was granted this afternoon. Late yesterday, a member of Congressman Joaquin Castro’s staff visited Garcés Peréz at the detention center and reported that the detainee had lost feeling on his left side. Lincoln-Goldfinch hopes to visit him today. The next step is getting Elizdar to see her husband. And maybe removing the bullet from his back.

text:
A Winnipeg-born Canadian citizen has been deported back to Canada after a harrowing nine and a half months behind bars in a California ICE detention centre, where he says he endured poor food, mouldy walls and lack of proper medical care.

Clayton Herman landed in Vancouver on Aug. 26 with little more than the clothing on his back and a cellphone, after being escorted to the plane by detention officers who stood guard until the hatch was sealed and the plane rolled onto the tarmac.

Herman says he's ambivalent about leaving the life he built in Ojai, Calif., where he had become part of the community.

"One relief is that I'll never have to be held in chains again, in a concrete blockhouse behind razor wire," Herman said in an interview from the home of a friend of a friend who put him up for a few weeks.

Herman had been taken into custody in the U.S. in October 2025, after he was accused of violating his supervision conditions based on readings from what he called a "glitchy" location monitoring device.

He had entered the U.S. legally through a port of entry 20 years earlier, but had long overstayed his visa. He had reported regularly in person to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement since 2022, as he waited for his visa overstay case to be heard in court.

After being held for eight months, he was released in mid-June, but was taken back into custody at an ICE office on July 21, when he went for a routine check-in as his case moved through the U.S. immigration system.

Lack of ID can trap people in cycle: SEED Winnipeg

Though he's now back in Canada, Herman still faces challenges.

He knows when he leaves his current accommodations, he could be unhoused for a while, since he has no job and no identification.

Herman had to surrender a temporary emergency travel document issued by Global Affairs Canada as he passed through customs in the Vancouver airport.

"If I have to rough it for a while, I have no fear of that. I've done that before," Herman said. "And it's better than being in that inhumane conditions of that filthy, concrete, razor-wired blockhouse down south."

People who lose ID documents face barriers to getting housing, jobs, health-care and government benefits, said Jennifer Bogoch, a manager at SEED (Supporting Employment and Economic Development) Winnipeg. The non-profit runs a program that helps people get ID documents for free.

"It's really a fundamental piece of being included in society," Bogoch said.

Losing identification can make it hard to access the stability and other documentation a person needs to get ID, trapping them in a vicious cycle, she said.

"It takes time, it takes money to replace it. Those barriers can really be compounded for people who are living on a low income, who are experiencing trauma, who are without stable housing, who don't have a safe place to keep it."

Herman says he needs to find a place to live before he can be reunited with his beloved cats, Poquito and Butters, who he had to leave behind in California.

Other detainees face worse fate: prof

Sharry Aiken, a law professor at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont., says there are thousands of people locked up in ICE detention centres who are suffering a worse fate than Herman.

Some detainees have been deported to countries where they have no connection.

Others, many from Latin America and other nations in the global South, face "a prospect not of departure to Canada, but potentially removal to countries where their very lives are at risk," Aiken said in a July interview with CBC News.

Among them are Haitian detainees, who no longer have the temporary protected status granted after a 2010 earthquake that killed more than 300,000, could be sent back to a country the U.S. State Department has told citizens to avoid due to the risk of "crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care."

And Aiken notes many migrants in the U.S. who try to flee to Canada are turned away because of the Safe Third Country Agreement, under which refugees who first arrive in the U.S. are barred from seeking asylum in Canada, barring certain exceptions.

That agreement needs to end because of the "brazen cruelty" of ICE enforcement and detention, said Aiken.

"Canada is continuing to remove people to the United States and subject them to detention and deportation," as a result of that agreement, she said.

"We shouldn't have it. It should be suspended in light of what's going on."

Canada and the U.S. continue to use that agreement to "manage asylum claims at our shared border," a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said.

Temporary measures currently in place for Haitians have been extended until the end of October, Remi Lariviere wrote in a statement emailed Tuesday.

Canada has "a proud humanitarian tradition" and "a robust framework" to monitor changes in the U.S. refugee protection system, the statement said.

While Herman is working to put his life together in Canada, he's also dedicating himself to protesting the conditions in ICE facilities.

He's started by writing a 12-page document that details the facility in Adelanto, Calif., where he was held — a for-profit ICE detention centre run by the Geo Group that Herman describes as a "hellhole."

He wants to let the world know what is going on behind its gates, he said.

"I feel sorry for what people are going through down there."

text:
A man is recovering from injuries he sustained Sunday morning after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him in a Chicago suburb.

In one video verified by NBC News, a Black man is seen sprawled on the street, near a curb, behind a black SUV in Evanston, Illinois. Two agents wearing ICE-style vests are seen standing over him. One has his face covered and his vest reads “POLICE” and the other appears to be pinning the man down to the ground. The man is shouting at them and can be heard saying, “I’m a f------ U.S. citizen.”

According to Evanston police, the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and officers requested an ambulance.

Police said they are investigating the incident, which was filmed by bystanders and gained attention after being posted on social media.

One bystander in the background of the video is heard saying the ICE officers used force against the man. Other bystanders begin shouting at the man on the ground, asking him if he is OK. The ICE officers eventually get in the black SUV and drive off, leaving the man on the ground. The bystanders begin trying to help the man and call Evanston police.

“I saw two agents pinning down a gentleman. They were using very rough force on him, and it looked like they really did hurt him because we had to call 911,” Miguel Angel Olivares, one of the people who witnessed the encounter, told NBC Chicago on Monday.

“When we saw him, he had his jaw swollen and he had a little blood on his shirt. I’m not sure if it was the agent’s or it was his blood,” Olivares said.

In a news release Sunday, Evanston police said they spoke to an ICE agent who said federal immigration officers “had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking.” After the man refused to provide identification, he was “detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention.”

An Evanston police officer reported observing blood on the agent’s hands. The agent said he was injured while attempting to handcuff the individual and declined medical treatment, according to the news release from Evanston police. “Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen. He was released.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that their officers encountered a person who resembled someone they were targeting in an enforcement operation in Evanston on Sunday.

“ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself. ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the DHS statement reads. “DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.”

DHS did not state anything about the injuries the man suffered and why ICE officers did not appear to render aid.

Neither the police nor DHS identified the man who was injured.

“Two and a half centuries after the cause of liberty found its home on this continent, I can report to you with pride that America is back, and our country is stronger today than ever before.” (Watch)

text:
CLEARFIELD — The Clearfield County Board of Commissioners voted 2-1 on Tuesday to approve a six-month contract extension for the operation of Moshannon Valley Processing Center.

Commissioners Tim Winters and John Sobel voted in favor of the extension, and Commissioner Dave Glass voted against.

Sobel and Winters said that rejecting the contract would impact tax money contributed to the Philipsburg-Osceola Area School District, and it would eliminate any oversight they have of Moshannon, the largest immigration detention facility in the Northeast. Both commissioners told the roughly 60 protesters to direct their energy toward their elected U.S. representatives and senators, along with those in charge of enacting federal immigration policy.

“I will be the first to say, our oversight ability is very small, but we still have it,” Winters said. “If we vote no, we have no communication; we have no place in this. We can only vote on the proposal before us.”

Opponents of Moshannon have long called on the county to end its relationship with GEO Group and ICE, for which it receives $200,000 per year.

“It makes me so angry that every day I go to work, a portion of my money goes to harm these people who are desperate for our help,” William Fescemyer, a member of Indivisible: Outcry, said at the meeting prior to the vote. “I don’t know how to convince you that this is so unbelievably evil. It betrays that flag. It betrays our country.”

In September 2021, the county entered into five-year agreements with ICE and GEO Group and has served as a middleman between the government agency and the private contractor that owns and operates Moshannon. The setup offered a workaround to former President Joe Biden’s 2021 executive order banning private federal prisons, which President Donald Trump reversed in 2025.

Stay informed

Sign up for Talk of the Town, an update of the news that matters to your community — from the PA Wilds to Happy Valley.

Email address

The contract extension modifies the staffing plan and changes the contracting officer, but “all other terms and conditions remain unchanged,” according to a copy of the document obtained through a public records request.

Since the facility reopened as an immigration detention facility, it has drawn criticism for poor-quality food, inadequate healthcare, and inhumane conditions. The facility’s population has only risen as the Trump administration has escalated federal immigration policy and quickened deportations at a historic rate.

It’s possible Clearfield County commissioners won’t have a role to play after the contract extension expires in March, as ICE reviews its detention operations in Pennsylvania.

In mid-July, ICE published a request for information on “turn-key detention services” for four regions across the country, including central Pennsylvania.

When asked about what the RFI means for Moshannon, an ICE spokesperson previously told Spotlight PA that the agency is “evaluating options, including the potential purchase of turnkey detention facilities where appropriate, or other contracting solutions to support continuity of operations.”

GEO Group’s founder and CEO George Zoley told shareholders in a second-quarter earnings call in early August that the company is “engaged in an active process for the sale of several of our turnkey facilities, subject to mutual agreement on price and our continued management of those facilities under long-term support services contracts.”

In late August, ICE published a request for proposal for several turnkey detention facilities, naming Moshannon explicitly as a “Historical Location” in the facility-specific requirements portion of the request.

“The Contractor shall furnish the proposed detention facility and provide all management, supervision, personnel, labor, equipment, vehicles, supplies, materials, and services necessary to provide safe, secure, humane, and compliant detention services for ICE detainees,” the request says.

Though ICE and GEO Group haven’t confirmed whether Moshannon is up for sale, they haven’t denied that possibility.

Jeff Migliozzi, communications director at advocacy group Freedom for Immigrants, told Spotlight PA he thinks the federal government’s approach to buying detention facilities circumvents accountability and further obscures their operations, as there is no precedent for states to regulate the federal government.

“If, in fact, the federal government purchases Moshannon,” he said, “it will only become more difficult to monitor and expose what is happening inside, and that is very intentional on the part of the federal government.”

If ICE were to contract directly with GEO Group and cut the commissioners out of the equation, Sobel said he’s concerned that he and his colleagues won’t have as much access to GEO Group officials to check on whether someone is receiving medical care or quality food. Sobel said that he has appreciated the relationship with GEO Group and its communication when questions or concerns arise.

The intergovernmental agreement allows commissioners to enter the facility with 24-hour notice, but the officials have been denied access in the past.

While Migliozzi acknowledged that the Clearfield County commissioners provide minor oversight, he was skeptical they could prevent problems endemic to the U.S. detention system.

“It’s not like one form of ownership correlates to a more humane experience,” Migliozzi said. “We see consistently across the board that human rights abuses are occurring inside.”

text:
A 36-year-old immigrant from Costa Rica died last week in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, according to an agency notification sent to lawmakers on Monday.

Carlos Josue Marchena-Marchena was found unresponsive Sept. 18 at the Winnfield Correctional Center in Louisiana, according to ICE.

"Upon arrival at WPMC, medical staff and EMS continued resuscitative efforts," ICE said in its notification to Congress. "Despite life-saving efforts, at approximately 8 a.m., an on-site physician at WPMC pronounced Marchena deceased."

Marchena is the 55th person to die in ICE custody during the second Trump administration -- the 25th person to die in ICE detention this year -- and the second person to die at the detention facility in Louisiana this year, according to ABC News' analysis of ICE data.

"While in custody, Marchena received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals," ICE said.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that ICE officers arrested the 36-year-old Marchena for entering the U.S. without inspection in 2021.

According to DHS, Marchena has convictions for retail fraud and destruction of personal property and an arrest for assault, however, ABC News has not verified this claim from the Department of Homeland Security.

DHS said Marchena received proper medical care while in custody.

"ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay," the agency said in a statement.

Attorney information for Marchena was not immediately available.

text:
From the Mexican restaurant where he works in North Austin, Juan Perez has seen U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detain more and more people in the area.

That includes construction workers, stopping at the gas station or the Dollar Tree for ice before their work day begins. And lone drivers, whose cars are left unattended after they’re hauled away. On Saturday, Perez saw one guy taken away. On Thursday, another man, trying to flee, ran through the restaurant’s parking lot. Perez did not see if ICE caught him.

“It’s been going on for a month here and they’ve just been — respectfully — terrorizing the whole area,” Perez, 28, said as he looked past a mostly empty restaurant and onto the street on Monday. “I just guess they’re easy targets because a lot of people, a lot of construction people gotta put gas or whatever in the mornings.”

The restaurant sits among a group of small businesses near the intersection where an ICE officer on Sunday shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old immigrant from Venezuela. To some in the area, a violent encounter was all but inevitable as they have seen federal agents — often in unmarked cars, sometimes accompanied by Texas Department of Public Safety troopers — pick up the pace of their hunting for immigrants.

“It’s just sad,” Perez said, shaking his head. “If you were just going after rapists … I understand that. But I mean, you’re going after hardworking people.”

The shooting occurred amid a surge of ICE activity in Austin that is injecting fear into Latino residents, citizens and undocumented alike, according to others who work in the area, local activists and elected officials from Austin City Hall to Congress.

Garces Perez’s violent arrest has placed a spotlight on the soaring number of ICE arrests, and renewed scrutiny on the willingness of Texas’ GOP leaders to help President Donald Trump pursue his mass deportation campaign.

ICE has divided Texas into five jurisdictions, and street arrests in the San Antonio jurisdiction, which includes Austin, have skyrocketed since the beginning of the year, according to a Texas Tribune analysis.

Since 2022, when the practice of apprehending undocumented people in the interior of the country was far less common under the Biden administration, the San Antonio jurisdiction has seen a 32.2-point increase in field-based arrests — one of the largest jumps in the country, the data review shows.

“It’s ‘Hey, Mexican, come here,’ type of enforcement,” Austin City Council member Chito Vela, whose district includes the site of Garces Perez’s shooting, said of the increased ICE presence. “We’re talking about gas stations and, you know, parking lots of grocery stores — that kind of like really random enforcement of immigration laws that we have seen over the last 30 days.”

Mario Tapia launched a magazine 12 years ago for Latinos in Central Texas. Since Trump returned to the White House, he has been publishing videos of ICE arrests on Instagram. He said the earliest videos he received from followers in April 2025 were difficult to initially confirm as ICE arrests because the officers drove unmarked cars and wore vests that simply said “police.”

But soon it became clear that the authorities were from ICE, he said, as more videos emerged, followed by accounts from relatives of those detained. He said he has documented two types of arrests during Trump’s second term: some are initiated by DPS traffic stops, with troopers calling ICE if they confirm the person they pulled over is undocumented, while others are solo ICE pursuits, like the one that led to Garces Perez’s shooting.

Tapia said most of the reports he receives are from North Austin, including the site of the shooting.

“I understand this subject polarizes a lot of people,” he said Monday. “But I wish people would notice what this all means not just for the undocumented immigrant community, but in general for the entire Hispanic community. There’s fear.”

Texas has played a starring role in the president’s immigration crackdown. Shortly after Trump’s return to Washington, Gov. Greg Abbott directed DPS — and other state agencies — to help the federal government. After years of patrolling the U.S.-Mexico border as part of Abbott’s Operation Lone Star initiative, the state agency has redirected some resources from the border to assist ICE in the interior of the state.

As of Monday evening, top Texas GOP officials — including the governor and the lieutenant governor — had yet to weigh in publicly on Garces Perez’s shooting.

The increased ICE presence has put people on edge across the state capital.

Austin City Council member Zohaib “Zo” Qadri, whose district covers central Austin, said his office has received reports from University of Texas at Austin students when they see something that makes them suspicious.

“The governor has weaponized DPS to kinda go around and terrorize folks in Austin,” Qadri said. “The president has, you know, weaponized ICE to go around and terrorize folks in Austin.”

Sulma Franco, the director of immigration campaigns at the Austin nonprofit Grassroots Leadership, said her group has also seen an uptick in immigration arrests on Austin’s streets since Trump’s return to office.

“It’s terrible that Texas is turning into a laboratory for these racist laws,” she said. “It’s frustrating to see our community in constant fright.”

Maria Elizabeth has witnessed the fear. The 30-year-old works at a restaurant behind a convenience store that serves Latin American cuisine, down the street from where ICE shot Garces Perez.

“People don’t want to stop by,” Elizabeth said. “They’re scared of the police, they’re scared of ICE.”

On Monday afternoon, the picnic tables near the counter were empty. Down the street, people began leaving candles and other objects to mark where Garces Perez was shot.

Sam Stark of the Austin Current contributed to this report.

authors: Taylor Romine, Priscilla Alvarez, Andy Rose

text:
A Venezuelan man who was wounded Sunday when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot him is back in the hospital and asking a court to intervene before he can be removed from the country.

The man, identified as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was delivering orders for DoorDash at the time of the confrontation, his attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said. This is the latest shooting incident involving the agency since the Trump administration started its immigration crackdown.

Federal authorities haven’t said what led to the shooting of Garces Perez, who was taken to a hospital Monday evening after earlier being detained at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, according to his attorney. She also filed a petition in federal court Monday asking a judge to block the government from deporting Garces Perez and release him from custody while his case is pending.

The local district attorney called for an independent investigation into what happened.

This is at least the third shooting involving immigration agents in Texas since President Donald Trump started his second term, and is part of a larger trend of shootings by federal agents since stricter immigration enforcement began.

At least 20 people have been shot by on-duty ICE and US Customs and Border Protection agents during the second Trump administration, eight fatally, prior to Sunday, according to a CNN analysis.

Here is what we know so far about the latest shooting:

Venezuelan man shot in North Austin by immigration agent

Garces Perez was driving in North Austin on Sunday when he was shot in the torso just before 1 p.m., officials said.

DoorDash said he was working as a Dasher at the time of the shooting.

ICE officers were conducting targeted immigration enforcement operations Sunday based on license plate checks when they came across a vehicle registered to Garces Perez, who had a deportation order, according to a source familiar with the incident.

Officers conducted a vehicle stop and questioned Garces Perez, who had a brief exchange with the officers before he fled the scene in his car, the source said. They told him they were ICE agents and that he was going to be arrested; Garces Perez then fled the scene in his car, the source said.

It is unclear whether Garces Perez’s car came to a complete stop or was moving during the initial exchange. The shooting happened later.

During a news conference Monday, Garces Perez called in from ICE custody and gave his own account of the shooting with the help of an interpreter.

Garces Perez said the SUV tried to hit him, which he originally interpreted as an aggressive driver. When he realized ICE agents were in the vehicle, Garces Perez said he asked to pull over to be detained but the federal official denied his request.

Garces Perez said when he attempted a U-turn to park the car, the SUV ran into his car and he was then shot, according to the translator.

He said after he was shot, an officer went into his car and “forcibly turned it off.” He told the officer he was in pain and felt like he was going to pass out shortly before EMTs arrived.

The Department of Homeland Security has not given a detailed account of what happened or responded to CNN’s request for comment on the circumstances of the incident.

Homeland Security Investigations, the agency’s investigative branch, will lead the investigation with assistance from the FBI, DHS said in a post on X without providing further details.

CNN reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment on Garces Perez’s account of events.

“I see ICE following their same PR pattern in this case,” Lincoln-Goldfinch told CNN on Monday. “There is no evidence to be seen that Wilber was doing anything but driving his car down the road.”

Video of the shooting was also captured by Heidi Clark, who was livestreaming to Facebook while driving down Research Boulevard. As she drove toward the intersection with Anderson Square, loud tire screeches interrupted her as she spoke.

“Woah!” Clark said as she turned her phone camera toward the scene and a person could be seen in the distance running out of an SUV toward a blue sedan.

Video from after the shooting showed a blue Toyota Corolla with damage to the front passenger door and at least two apparent bullet holes in the right rear window, according to footage shared by CNN affiliate KVUE and several witness videos taken at the scene.

Garces Perez stable but ‘not doing well’ after gunshot wound, he said

Before returning to the hospital, Garces Perez told reporters Monday that he was “not doing well” and was in a lot of pain, adding that doctors had not removed the bullet because it was too close to his spine.

“They sent him to (an ICE facility) with a bullet in his back without pain medication, and he slept overnight in a processing center without a bed,” his lawyer said.

Garces Perez also relayed, through the interpreter, that he was in a cold room with no bed at the ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, about 100 miles southwest of Austin.

Rep. Joaquin Castro of Texas said someone from his office visited Garces Perez on Monday, and reported that ICE was taking him back to the hospital as he was still reporting a lot of pain, he said in a video he posted on X.

Garces Perez has lost movement on the “entire left side of his body,” Lincoln-Goldfinch told CNN’s Erin Burnett Monday evening, which means he could be “facing paralysis.”

Later Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a video on social media that she was told by a fellow inmate that Garces Perez had been taken to a hospital. She told CNN she didn’t have an update on his condition.

CNN has reached out to DHS about his comments on his injury and the conditions of the processing center.

Video taken after the shooting and obtained by CNN shows Garces Perez sitting on a curb with his hands cuffed behind his back as he’s detained by authorities. His shirt is cut open during the video to reveal what appears to be a gaping gunshot wound in his back.

Differing accounts of legal status by DHS and attorney

DHS and Garces Perez’s attorney have different accounts about his legal status.

DHS said in a post on X that Garces Perez is an undocumented immigrant from Venezuela who had a final order for removal, adding he is stable and “in federal custody pending removal.”

But his attorney said Garces Perez entered the country on an asylum claim, where he was allowed into the country and issued a work permit. He had been protected from deportation by a parole program that included Venezuelans, which the Trump administration ended last year, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

“He had a pending court date, and the immigration court changed his court date without notifying him,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said, which ended up with Garces Perez receiving a removal order in absentia.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said she used “back channels” to find out where Garces Perez is being held. ICE recently removed the location of detainees with final removal orders from an online database, complicating their attorneys’ efforts to prevent their deportation, The Associated Press reported Monday.

Local district attorney demands independent investigation

The Travis County District Attorney’s office, which covers most of Austin, said in a statement Sunday night that “it is critical that all the facts come to light and that an independent investigation be completed.”

“We are requesting that the Austin Police Department and our office, the Travis County District Attorney, be co-equal partners in the investigation,” the statement said, and asked for access to evidence the federal government has in this case.

The statement is reminiscent of the requests the Hennepin County Attorney’s office has made in Minneapolis regarding the shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. DHS turned over some evidence to state officials last July but hasn’t released findings in their investigations.

Austin’s Democratic Mayor Kirk Watson said during a news conference Sunday that is important for the city to be involved in the investigation, adding “Austinites have a right to know what happened.”

“While I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all,” Watson said of the shooting. “It’s happened in other cities with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”

CNN has reached out to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s office for comment.

The League of United Latin American Citizens, the Latino civil rights organization founded in Texas, also called on measures to curtail DHS, saying Congress should establish an independent oversight of immigration, and guarantee any DHS or ICE official who violates a person’s constitutional rights will be investigated and prosecuted, they said in a statement Sunday.

“No agency should be the sole judge of its own conduct,” Roman Palomares, LULAC chair and national president, said in a statement. “When the government takes or endangers a life, the Constitution demands due process and accountability, and those protections belong to every person in this country.”

Protests erupt in reaction to shooting

In the past several months, Texas has been at the center of the debate on immigration enforcement. In July, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant, in Houston during a traffic stop. ICE agents tried to conduct a traffic stop as part of a “targeted operation” and Salgado Araujo attempted to evade arrest, an agency spokesperson said in a statement to CNN at the time.

Earlier this month, two teens who are US citizens said they were attacked by ICE agents in Alamo, Texas, after they recorded an immigration stop, with video showing one being repeatedly punched in the head while pinned to the pavement. DHS told CNN in a statement at the time “two anti-ICE agitators” refused to follow verbal commands and were detained after “they attempted to obstruct officers conducting a vehicle stop.”

“This is a pattern – it’s a disturbing pattern – and it’s got to stop,” said US Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat who represents part of Austin.

Just hours after Garces Perez was shot, protesters gathered near the busy intersection where the shooting took place. Protesters were seen lining the streets, some chanting, some holding Mexican flags.

“I’ve lived in Austin all my life, but from what I’ve been seeing right now, I’ve never felt more betrayed,” Jaasiel Avilva, a 22-year-old Army veteran and son of Mexican immigrants, told CNN. “It’s just domestic terrorism.”

Janney Olvera, 13, told CNN affiliate KEYE she and her mother went to the protest fresh from finishing cheerleading practice.

“We’re not getting any justice,” Olvera told the outlet as she held a Mexican flag to honor her Mexican and Guatemalan heritage. “This is supposed to protect our streets? I don’t think so.”

text:
A Kentucky State University student-athlete was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement while traveling through the Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport with the university's basketball team Aug. 7, a lawyer coordinating the student's case told The Courier Journal.

Since her arrest, Aminata Seck, 26, has been moved between at least four detention centers without consistent medical care, according to previous reporting. She is currently being held in Grayson County as of Sept. 21, according to the Grayson County Detention Center's inmate listings.

Here's what to know about the case:

Who is Aminata Seck?

Seck is a student-athlete at Kentucky State University. She joined the school's basketball team in 2024, where she plays the center position, according to KSU's 2025-26 women's basketball roster. In March, Seck was named to the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference All-Conference Third Team with Elite 16 honors due to her strong academic performance.

"Seck played a key role for the team throughout the 2025-26 season, leading the squad on the boards while consistently contributing on both ends of the floor," a university report reads.

Seck transferred to KSU from Langston University, a historically Black university in Langston, Oklahoma.

"Out of respect for the privacy of those involved, Kentucky State University does not have information to share," a spokesperson for the school said in a statement to The Courier Journal.

The KSU women's basketball roster lists Seck's hometown as Dakar, Senegal.

Why was Aminata Seck taken into ICE custody?

Sadiqa Reynolds, an attorney helping coordinate Seck's case and former president and CEO of the Louisville Urban League, told The Courier Journal that Seck's team was headed to New York for a tournament when she was taken into custody after going through security at the Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport.

According to previous reporting, Reynolds said Seck may have missed a student visa deadline because she was having back surgery. Seck is currently suffering from an ACL injury, Reynolds told The Courier Journal.

What happens next in the Aminata Seck case?

Seck remains in ICE custody in Leitchfield. Reynolds previously told The Courier Journal that Seck has had trouble getting consistent access to ice for her injury and is in "so much pain."

"She needs surgery. She needs medical attention," Reynolds said in a social media post. "Kentucky State has done what they can and now we must step up."

Reynolds praised Seck's coach, Amani Williams, who she said has gone "above and beyond" advocating for her player.

"She has treated her like a mother would treat their child," Reynolds said. "I think we have to celebrate some of these heroes who have really been behind the scenes doing everything they could possibly do to keep people safe. And even though it maybe hasn't worked … nobody should have to do all of this."

Based on available court records, it is currently unclear whether Seck has filed a habeas corpus petition, a lawsuit challenging prolonged or unlawful ICE detentions.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

September 22, 2026

MEDIA CONTACT

Spencer Tilger | media@refugeerights.org

IRAP ANNOUNCES NEW INITIATIVE TO ADVANCE MIGRATION SOLUTIONS FOR THE FUTURE

The Immigration Solutions Accelerator will design and champion actionable solutions for durable protections for displaced people in the United States and Europe

(New York, NY) – Today, the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP) launched the Immigration Solutions Accelerator, a policy and advocacy shop dedicated to advancing lawful pathways rooted in the rights of displaced people. The Accelerator leverages IRAP’s expertise gained from representing our clients to advance lawful pathways globally that are responsive to the migration needs of the future.

“In an era defined by increasing xenophobia, mass displacement, and climate disasters, the need for pragmatic, scalable immigration solutions rooted in human rights and dignity cannot be overstated,” said IRAP President Sharif Aly. “The Immigration Solutions Accelerator exists to provide those solutions by drawing upon the expertise of our staff, clients, and partners. With this launch, IRAP reaffirms our commitment to defending immigrant communities in the present while also laying the groundwork for a better future. Everyone should have a safe place to call home and a safe way to get there.”

title: A Shooting in Austin Exposes the Terror of ICE's Shadow Surge - Texas Monthly
authors: svillarreal, Bekah Stolhandske McNeel, Michael Hardy, Sam Karas, Peter Holley, Naina Srivastava, Robert Downen, Dan Solomon, Eric Benson, Sean O'Neal
description:

This was the spot where Carlos had sat with Garcés Perez until being shooed away.
text:
The Crestview-Wooten neighborhood, where on Sunday an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, wears its identity proudly. There’s a Mexican market on one block, a supermercado on the next, and paleterias, a panaderia, and Latino-owned salons and body shops nearby. It sits just south of Rundberg and the trend-resistant “Taco Mile,” named for its concentration of authentic taco joints. North Austin neighborhoods have been seeing increased ICE activity for months. Locals have reported high-speed chases, and in August, Congressman Greg Casar chastised the department for staking out schools and churches in the area.

North Austin has been under what observers call a shadow surge, and on September 20, it burst into view when an ICE agent shot Garcés Perez while he was out on a DoorDash delivery, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. The agent in a black Expedition collided with the Venezuelan’s Toyota Corolla and then fired into the vehicle, striking Garcés Perez in the upper left shoulder. Witnesses say he was taken conscious from the scene.

The incident is the latest in a series of shootings by ICE agents as President Donald Trump and his advisers continue to pressure ICE to hit three thousand arrests per day. While Operation Midway Blitz, in Chicago, and Operation Metro Surge, in Minneapolis, seemed designed to draw protests and media coverage, the more-ubiquitous shadow surges across the country have been even more deadly—and disturbingly imprecise. When an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July, the Department of Homeland Security admitted that Salgado hadn’t even been the target of the stop. Six days later, an ICE agent in Maine shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, with ICE later admitting that he was also not the intended target of that operation. Reports also show that while arrests and detentions have soared to all-time highs this summer, deportations have remained level, largely because the immigrants being picked up do not have criminal records or deportation orders, or have open asylum cases.

A DHS spokesperson said in an email that Garcés Perez had “illegally entered our country under the Biden administration.” It’s not clear yet whether that means he was one of the more than 616,000 Venezuelans granted Temporary Protected Status under President Biden—a status the second Trump administration terminated—or whether he had always been in the country illegally. Much of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement has targeted those with legal statuses granted by Biden, including legal refugee status. Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client has an open asylum case and a valid work permit.

In the Crestview neighborhood on Sunday evening, I parked my car in an empty lot next to a white pickup with a wheelbarrow and rolls of chicken wire in the bed and a bumper sticker that read “Dios es [heart].” A Latino man with a black American flag cap and work jeans greeted me with a nod. “Just getting water. You need some?” he asked as he tossed me a cold plastic bottle without waiting for the answer. He told me he worked in landscaping, was from Mexico, and was a legal permanent resident. We stood drinking our water in silence, listening to the angry shouts growing louder from the protest about a hundred feet away as Austin police officers in riot gear arrived alongside a dozen or so state troopers.

The two groups—law enforcement and protesters—stood on either side of the access road as cars honked and inched their way forward while some passengers hung out of windows. On one side was a mix of families with kids waving Mexican flags and twentysomethings in balaclavas waving middle fingers. On the other side, about two dozen officers chatted among themselves, looking relatively unbothered. A water bottle flew over the cars, aimed at the officers.

“Whew. They’re angry,” I said, looking at the protesters.

“Yes, because immigration and police,” the landscaper said, “they are almost the same thing.” He said that the previous week, he had seen a car pulled over by the police—ICE officers arrived three minutes later and took the driver away, he said.

The Austin Police Department’s relationship with immigration enforcement has changed over the past several months, and officials immediately distanced themselves from the shooting, with Chief Lisa Davis emphasizing that APD officers had not been involved but would be investigating. “This has happened in the city of Austin,” Davis said at a news conference immediately after the shooting. “The city of Austin deserves answers on what occurred.”

Tensions with local police forces cooperating with ICE are high across the state, including in Austin. In January, an APD response to a disturbance call led to ICE taking a woman and her five-year-old daughter, a U.S. citizen, into custody and later deporting them. On March 4, APD adopted new rules limiting officers’ cooperation with ICE on the civil warrants the agency issues—saying officers didn’t have to call ICE if they encountered someone with such a warrant. In mid-April, Governor Greg Abbott threatened to terminate roughly $2.5 million in state public-safety grants unless the city adjusted its new policy. About a week later, Davis announced that APD would revise the March policy, restoring a process under which officers should, when operationally feasible, contact ICE about a valid ICE-issued warrant—while still limiting how long APD could hold someone for ICE.

The nuance of to what extent APD can or cannot refuse to cooperate with ICE is difficult to discuss rationally once the PepperBalls start flying.

“You are complicit!” a protester shouted as officers headed back to their cars after securing the scene of the shooting, where a special investigations team had been working. As they backed away from the access road, some protesters rushed forward across northbound Research Boulevard, disappearing in pursuit of the officers between the stacks of concrete box culverts and utility vaults under the overpass. For a moment it looked like a scene from a dystopian film. After a few pops erupted, the crowd came sprinting back. Once everyone had regrouped—police in the parking lot of the Crestview Crossing shopping center, protesters across the street—rocks started flying. The officers formed a line, holding PepperBall guns, and fired at the curb in front of the crowd, releasing clouds of irritant. The more experienced among the protesters donned their respirators. Twenty minutes later, the police were gone, and the protest began to reorganize around the spot where Garcés Perez—by then reported to be in serious but stable condition in ICE custody at Dell Seton Medical Center—had been shot.

Over at the Crestview Crossing shopping center, it was relatively quiet, a helicopter still circling overhead. Only then did the door of the center’s paleteria open. A couple emerged, looking distressed. “I talked to him,” said the husband, aged sixty, who asked only to be identified as Carlos. “We saw where he was shot. In the back.”

Carlos had also talked to the ICE agent, he said, who told him he had shot Garcés Perez because the Venezuelan man had not stopped when the officer said to stop. “So he shot him,” Carlos repeated. “But the police don’t have nothing to do with this,” he added, gesturing at the remnants of the confrontation. He said he understood the anger and fear in the community, but he didn’t feel that screaming and throwing rocks were doing any good. “I’m scared. . . . I’m just trying to help my people, but this is not good for nobody. Nobody.”

Later, I drove to Dell Seton Medical Center to see whether anyone there had answers about Garcés Perez. Everyone—lawyers, family, press—had been kicked off the campus, I found out. DHS replied to my inquiry with an emailed statement: “The illegal alien’s condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal.” The statement also said that Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI would be investigating the shooting. Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client was released from the hospital after only a few hours. This morning CBS confirmed that Garcés Perez is being held at the detention center in Pearsall, south of San Antonio.

Back at the scene of the shooting, a vigil had formed. Austinites filled the U.S. 183 underpass, mingling with cars and motorcycles in a mass of honking, tejano music, revving engines, and waving flags. Without the police presence, anger had softened into a sort of binding agent, pulling the crowd members close together, ebbing and flowing, making space for neighbors as they joined.

Someone put down a circle of tea lights and flowers around the spot where Garcés Perez fell, asking anyone with a lighter to come help. People did, and the crowd filled the street around the circle as the traffic lights blinked red overhead, marking the intersection as a place to take caution.

This was the spot where Carlos had sat with Garcés Perez until being shooed away. Carlos recalled saying to the younger man: “This is not American people, my friend. The way they are doing this, this is something else.” What that something else was, he didn’t know.

text:
In a new survey, homebuilders around the country say ramped-up Immigration and Customs Enforcement crackdowns are creating huge headaches for their businesses.

Why it matters: The labor strain comes on top of other challenges for the industry: rising mortgage rates, higher prices for key inputs driven by tariffs and the Iran war, as well as growing competition for resources with builders of data centers.

What they're saying: "ICE is becoming a very large issue and causing labor shortages," says a Houston builder in a survey conducted earlier this month by John Burns Research and Consulting, which regularly asks homebuilders about market conditions.

A builder in Richmond, Virginia, says: "ICE has had significant impacts to vendors throughout Virginia/Maryland in the last 90 days. ... This has had a major impact on cycle times and the ability to start new houses."

Jacksonville, Florida: "Current immigration enforcement efforts in our region are causing a strain on both the labor force, labor costs and cycle times."

The intrigue: The remarks in the homebuilder survey were unprompted, says Rick Palacios, director of research at the consulting firm.

"All we asked about on the topic in our survey was construction cycle times," he says. "The comments on 'ICE and immigration' were completely unsolicited."

Zoom in: The strains come after three straight months of record ICE arrests — in August the agency said it arrested 50,925 people across the country, the highest number of "illegal aliens" arrested in a single month.

Between the lines: These arrests have been less conspicuous than high-profile raids that came early in the year, but impactful — called a "shadow surge" by one of the administration's opponents.

Zoom out: Immigration raids discourage legally authorized workers from reporting to job sites, Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders, recently said.

Higher mortgage rates and rising material costs are also weighing on the industry, he said.

Building material costs are up by a median 6.7% from last year, according to one NAHB survey.

The other side: "ICE is not arresting people legally in the country," said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis.

"There is no shortage of American minds and hands to grow our labor force."

The administration has said its new Office of Immigration Policy will help employers navigate immigration policies.

The big picture: Immigrants made up more than 26% of the construction workforce in 2024, the most recent Census Bureau data on the industry.

But in certain trades, the share is much higher — immigrants make up 57% of those working on drywall and 53% of roofers, according to an analysis of that data released earlier this year by NAHB.
